'Veraṃ' means the fivefold enmity, such as killing living beings. 'Kenaci' means for any reason. 'Paññāya' means by not obtaining the wisdom of insight. 'Dhammassa' means by not seeing the path of stream-entry. Again, he spoke the inspired verses to show steadfastness, due to the desire not to return.

Taṃ sutvā sunando sārathi “ayaṃ kumāro evarūpaṃ rajjasiriṃ kuṇapaṃ viya chaḍḍetvā attano adhiṭṭhānaṃ abhinditvā “pabbajissāmīti araññaṃ paviṭṭho, mama iminā dujjīvitena ko attho, ahampi tena saddhiṃ pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the charioteer Sunanda thought: “This prince, having abandoned such royal splendor like a corpse, without breaking his own resolve, has entered the wilderness, saying, ‘I will go forth.’ What use is this wretched life to me? I too shall go forth with him.” Then he spoke this verse:

43.

43.

“Ahampi pabbajissāmi, rājaputta tavantike;

Avhāyassu maṃ bhaddante, pabbajjā mama ruccatī”ti.

“I too will go forth, O prince, in your presence. Call me, good sir; the going forth pleases me.”

Tattha tavantiketi tava santike. Avhāyassūti “ehi pabbajāhī”ti pakkosassu.

Here, 'tavantike' means 'in your presence.' 'Avhāyassu' means 'summon him, saying, “Come, go forth!”'

Evaṃ tena yācitopi mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ idāneva taṃ pabbājessāmi, mātāpitaro idha nāgacchissanti, atha nesaṃ parihāni bhavissati, ime assā ca ratho ca pasādhanabhaṇḍañca idheva nassissanti, ‘yakkho so, khādito nu kho tena sārathī’ti garahāpi [M 6.0022] me uppajjissatī”ti cintetvā attano ca garahāmocanatthaṃ mātāpitūnañca vuḍḍhiṃ sampassanto asse ca rathañca pasādhanabhaṇḍañca tassa iṇaṃ katvā dassento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Even when thus entreated, the Great Being thought, 'If I were to ordain him now, my parents would not come here, and they would suffer loss; these horses, chariot, and ornaments would perish right here; and blame would accrue to me, people saying, “He is a yakkha! Has the charioteer been devoured by him?”' Considering this, and foreseeing both the removal of blame from himself and the welfare of his parents, and making the horses, chariot, and ornaments a debt for the charioteer to repay, he spoke this verse:

44.

44.

“Rathaṃ niyyādayitvāna, anaṇo ehi sārathi;

Anaṇassa hi pabbajjā, etaṃ isīhi vaṇṇita”nti.

“Having returned the chariot, come, charioteer, free from debt. For the going forth of one free from debt—this is praised by the sages.”

Tattha etanti etaṃ pabbajjākaraṇaṃ buddhādīhi isīhi vaṇṇitaṃ pasatthaṃ thomitaṃ.

Here, 'this' refers to this act of going forth, praised, extolled, and commended by the sages, such as the Buddhas.

Taṃ sutvā sārathi “sace mayi nagaraṃ gate esa aññattha gaccheyya, pitā cassa imaṃ pavattiṃ sutvā ‘puttaṃ me dassehī’ti puna āgato imaṃ na passeyya, rājadaṇḍaṃ me kareyya, tasmā ahaṃ attano guṇaṃ kathetvā aññatthāgamanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintento gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, the charioteer thought: “If, after I have gone to the city, he goes elsewhere, and his father, hearing of this, returns and, not seeing him, says, ‘Show me my son,’ he would inflict royal punishment on me. Therefore, I will speak of my own good deed and get him to promise not to go elsewhere.” Reflecting thus, he spoke two verses:

45.

45.

“Yadeva [V 6.0022] tyāhaṃ vacanaṃ, akaraṃ bhaddamatthu te;

Tadeva me tvaṃ vacanaṃ, yācito kattumarahasi.

“Whatever word of yours I performed, may good fortune be yours. That very word of mine, you ought to do when asked.”

46.

46.

“Idheva tāva acchassu, yāva rājānamānaye;

Appeva te pitā disvā, patīto sumano siyā”ti.

“Stay right here for now, until I bring the king; perhaps your father, seeing you, will be pleased and glad of mind.”

Tato [P 6.0019] mahāsatto āha –

Then the Great Being said:

47.

47.

“Karomi te taṃ vacanaṃ, yaṃ maṃ bhaṇasi sārathi;

Ahampi daṭṭhukāmosmi, pitaraṃ me idhāgataṃ.

“I will do that word you speak to me, O charioteer; I too wish to see my father, should he come here.”

48.

48.

“Ehi samma nivattassu, kusalaṃ vajjāsi ñātinaṃ;

Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ mayhaṃ, vutto vajjāsi vandana”nti.

“Go now, dear one, turn back, and convey news of my well-being to my kinsmen; to my mother and father, as you have been told, convey my homage.”

Tattha karomi tetanti karomi te etaṃ vacanaṃ. Ehi samma nivattassūti samma sārathi, tattha gantvā ehi, ettova khippameva nivattassu. Vutto vajjāsīti mayā vutto hutvā “putto vo temiyakumāro vandatī”ti vandanaṃ vadeyyāsīti attho.

There, 'karomi te' means 'I do this word for you'. 'Ehi samma nivattassu' means 'O dear charioteer, having gone there, come back; turn back from here quickly.' 'Vutto vajjāsi' means 'having been told by me, you should speak the homage, saying, “Your son, Prince Temiya, pays homage”'—this is the meaning.

Iti vatvā mahāsatto suvaṇṇakadali viya onamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena bārāṇasinagarābhimukho mātāpitaro vanditvā sārathissa sāsanaṃ [M 6.0023] adāsi. So sāsanaṃ gahetvā kumāraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rathamāruyha nagarābhimukho pāyāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, the Great Being, bowing down like a golden banana plant with the five-point prostration while facing the city of Bārāṇasī, paid homage to his parents and gave a message to the charioteer. Taking the message, the charioteer circumambulated the prince, mounted the chariot, and set out toward the city. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

49.

49.

“Tassa pāde gahetvāna, katvā ca naṃ padakkhiṇaṃ;

Sārathi rathamāruyha, rājadvāraṃ upāgamī”ti.

‘‘Having taken hold of his feet and having circumambulated him, the charioteer mounted the chariot and approached the palace gate.’’

Tassattho – bhikkhave, evaṃ vutto so sārathi, tassa kumārassa pāde gahetvā taṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rathaṃ āruyha rājadvāraṃ upāgamīti.

The meaning is this: O monks, when spoken to in this way, that charioteer took the prince's feet, circumambulated him, mounted the chariot, and approached the palace gate.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe candādevī sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā “kā nu kho me puttassa pavattī”ti sārathissa [V 6.0023] āgamanamaggaṃ olokentī taṃ ekakaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā uraṃ paharitvā paridevi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

At that moment, Queen Candā opened the lion-window, and wondering, ‘‘What is the news of my son?’’ she looked down the road for the charioteer's arrival. Seeing him returning alone, she struck her breast and lamented. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

50.

50.

“Suññaṃ mātā rathaṃ disvā, ekaṃ sārathimāgataṃ;

Assupuṇṇehi nettehi, rodantī naṃ udikkhati.

‘‘The mother, seeing the empty chariot and the charioteer returning alone, with eyes full of tears, looks upon him while weeping.’’

51.

51.

“Ayaṃ so sārathi eti, nihantvā mama atrajaṃ;

Nihato nūna me putto, pathabyā bhūmivaḍḍhano.

‘‘This is that charioteer coming, having slain my son; surely my son is slain, he who would have been a benefit to the earth.’’

52.

52.

“Amittā nūna nandanti, patītā nūna verino;

Āgataṃ sārathiṃ disvā, nihantvā mama atrajaṃ.

‘‘Surely my enemies now rejoice, surely my foes are delighted, seeing the charioteer returning after having slain my son.’’

53.

53.

“Suññaṃ mātā rathaṃ disvā, ekaṃ sārathimāgataṃ;

Assupuṇṇehi nettehi, rodantī paripucchi naṃ.

‘‘The mother, seeing the empty chariot and the charioteer returning alone, with eyes full of tears, weeping, questioned him.’’

54.

54.

“Kiṃ nu mūgo kiṃnu pakkho, kiṃnu so vilapī tadā;

Nihaññamāno bhūmiyā, taṃ me akkhāhi sārathi.

‘‘Was he mute? Was he crippled? Did he wail then, as he was being struck down into the earth? Tell me that, charioteer.’’

55.

55.

“Kathaṃ hatthehi pādehi, mūgapakkho vivajjayi;

Nihaññamāno bhūmiyā, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

‘‘How, though mute and crippled, did he ward you off with his hands and feet? As he was being struck down into the earth, tell me this when questioned.’’

Tattha mātāti temiyakumārassa mātā. Pathabyā bhūmivaḍḍhanoti so mama putto bhūmivaḍḍhano hutvā pathabyā nihato nūna. Rodantī paripucchi nanti taṃ rathaṃ ekamantaṃ ṭhapetvā mahātalaṃ [P 6.0020] abhiruyha candādeviṃ vanditvā ekamante ṭhitaṃ sārathiṃ paripucchi. Kinnūti kiṃ nu so mama [M 6.0024] putto mūgo eva pakkho eva. Tadāti yadā naṃ tvaṃ kāsuyaṃ pakkhipitvā kuddālena matthake pahari, tadā. Nihaññamāno bhūmiyāti tayā bhūmiyaṃ nihaññamāno kiṃ nu vilapi. Taṃ meti taṃ sabbaṃ aparihāpetvā me akkhāhi. Vivajjayīti “apehi sārathi, mā maṃ mārehī”ti kathaṃ hatthehi pādehi ca phandanto taṃ apanudi, taṃ me kathehīti attho.

Herein, ‘mother’ refers to Prince Temiya’s mother. ‘Pathabyā bhũmivaᄃᄃhano’ means, ‘My son, who was a benefit to the earth, has surely been slain upon the earth.’ ‘Rodantĩ paripucchi naᅃ’ means that the charioteer, having placed the chariot to one side, ascended to the great terrace, paid respects to Queen Candādevĩ, and as he stood to one side, she questioned him. ‘Kiᅃ nũ’ means, ‘Was my son indeed mute and indeed crippled?’ ‘Tadā’ refers to when you, having placed him in the pit, struck him on the head with a spade. ‘Nihaᄃᅃamāno bhũmiyā’ means, ‘As he was being struck down by you into the earth, did he indeed wail?’ ‘Taᅃ me’ means, ‘Tell me all that without omission.’ ‘Vivajjayĩ’ means, ‘Tell me how, struggling with his hands and feet, he pushed you away, as if saying: ‘Go away, charioteer, do not kill me!’’’

Tato sārathi āha –

Then the charioteer said:

56.

56.

“Akkheyyaṃ [V 6.0024] te ahaṃ ayye, dajjāsi abhayaṃ mama;

Yaṃ me sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā, rājaputtassa santike”ti.

‘‘I will tell you, noble lady, if you grant me safety; whatever I heard or saw in the prince’s presence.’’

Tattha dajjāsīti sace abhayaṃ dadeyyāsi, so idaṃ “sacāhaṃ ‘tava putto neva mūgo na pakkho madhurakatho dhammakathiko’ti vakkhāmi, atha ‘kasmā taṃ gahetvā nāgatosī’ti rājā kuddho rājadaṇḍampi me kareyya, abhayaṃ tāva yācissāmī”ti cintetvā āha.

Here, ‘dajjāsĩ’ means ‘if you would grant safety.’ He spoke after thinking, ‘If I say, ‘Your son was neither mute nor crippled but is of sweet speech and a speaker of Dhamma,’ then the king, becoming angry, might ask, ‘Why did you not bring him back?’ and might even inflict royal punishment on me. I will first ask for safety.’

Atha naṃ candādevī āha –

Then Queen Candādevĩ said to him:

57.

57.

“Abhayaṃ samma te dammi, abhīto bhaṇa sārathi;

Yaṃ te sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā, rājaputtassa santike”ti.

‘‘I grant you safety, friend; speak without fear, charioteer, whatever you heard or saw in the prince’s presence.’’

Tato sārathi āha –

Then the charioteer said:

58.

58.

“Na so mūgo na so pakkho, visaṭṭhavacano ca so;

Rajjassa kira so bhīto, akarā ālaye bahū.

‘‘He was neither mute nor crippled, and his speech is articulate. He was indeed afraid of kingship; he made many pretenses.’’

59.

59.

“Purimaṃ sarati so jātiṃ, yattha rajjamakārayi;

Kārayitvā tahiṃ rajjaṃ, pāpattha nirayaṃ bhusaṃ.

‘‘He remembers a former birth wherein he exercised kingship; having exercised kingship there, he reached a terrible hell.’’

60.

60.

“Vīsatiñceva vassāni, tahiṃ rajjamakārayi;

Asītivassasahassāni, nirayamhi apacci so.

‘‘For twenty years he exercised kingship there; for eighty thousand years he was cooked in hell.’’

61.

61.

“Tassa rajjassa so bhīto, mā maṃ rajjābhisecayuṃ;

Tasmā pitu ca mātucca, santike na bhaṇī tadā.

‘‘Afraid of that kingship, thinking, ‘May they not anoint me to rule!’ he therefore did not speak then in the presence of his father and mother.’’

62.

62.

“Aṅgapaccaṅgasampanno[M 6.0025], ārohapariṇāhavā;

Visaṭṭhavacano pañño, magge saggassa tiṭṭhati.

‘‘Endowed with all major and minor limbs, possessing height and stature, wise and with articulate speech, he stands on the path to heaven.’’

63.

63.

“Sace [V 6.0025] tvaṃ daṭṭhukāmāsi, rājaputtaṃ tavatrajaṃ;

Ehi taṃ pāpayissāmi, yattha sammati temiyo”ti.

‘‘If you wish to see the prince, your own son, come, I will lead you to where Temiya dwells.’’

Tattha visaṭṭhavacanoti apalibuddhakatho. Akarā ālaye bahūti tumhākaṃ vañcanāni bahūni akāsi. Paññoti paññavā. Sace tvanti rājānaṃ dhuraṃ katvā ubhopi te evamāha. Yattha sammati temiyoti yattha vo putto mayā gahitapaṭiñño hutvā acchati, tattha pāpayissāmi, idāni papañcaṃ akatvā lahuṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti āha.

Herein, ‘visaᄃᄃhavacano’ means speech that is unhindered. ‘Akarā ālaye bahũ’ means ‘he performed many deceptions toward you.’ ‘Paᄃᄃo’ means possessing wisdom. ‘Sace tvaᅃ’ means he spoke thus to both parents, addressing the king primarily. ‘Yattha sammati temiyo’ means ‘I will lead you to where your son remains, after having made a promise to me.’ He said, ‘Now, without delay, it is fitting to go quickly.’

Kumāro [P 6.0021] pana sārathiṃ pesetvā pabbajitukāmo ahosi. Tadā sakko tassa manaṃ ñatvā tasmiṃ khaṇe vissakammadevaputtaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta vissakammadevaputta, temiyakumāro pabbajitukāmo, tvaṃ tassa paṇṇasālañca pabbajitaparikkhārañca māpetvā ehī”ti pesesi. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā vegena gantvā tiyojanike vanasaṇḍe attano iddhibalena ramaṇīyaṃ assamaṃ māpetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānañca pokkharaṇiñca āvāṭañca akālaphalasampannaṃ rukkhañca katvā paṇṇasālasamīpe catuvīsatihatthappamāṇaṃ caṅkamaṃ māpetvā antocaṅkame ca phalikavaṇṇaṃ ruciraṃ vālukaṃ okiritvā sabbe pabbajitaparikkhāre māpetvā “ye pabbajitukāmā, te ime gahetvā pabbajantū”ti bhittiyaṃ akkharāni likhitvā caṇḍavāḷe ca amanāpasadde sabbe migapakkhino ca palāpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

The prince, however, having sent the charioteer away, desired to go forth. At that moment, Sakka, knowing his mind, summoned the devaputta Vissakamma and sent him, saying, ‘My dear Vissakamma, Prince Temiya wishes to go forth. Go and create a leaf-hut and the requisites for an ascetic, then return.’ He agreed, saying ‘Very well,’ and went swiftly. In a forest grove three leagues in extent, he created a delightful hermitage by his psychic power, with places for night and day, a lotus pond, a well, and trees bearing out-of-season fruits. Near the leaf-hut, he made a walking path twenty-four cubits in length and scattered beautiful, crystal-colored sand along it. After creating all the requisites for an ascetic, he wrote on the wall, ‘Let those who wish to go forth take these and do so.’ Then he drove away all fierce beasts and birds with unpleasant sounds and returned to his own abode.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto taṃ disvā sakkadattiyabhāvaṃ ñatvā, paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā vatthāni apanetvā, rattavākacīraṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ajinacammaṃ ekaṃse katvā jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ bandhitvā kājaṃ aṃse katvā kattaradaṇḍamādāya paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā pabbajitasiriṃ samubbahanto aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānento paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kaṭṭhattharaṇe nisinno pañca abhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā sāyanhasamaye paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ṭhitakārarukkhato paṇṇāni gahetvā[M 6.0026], sakkadattiyabhājane aloṇake atakke nidhūpane udake sedetvā amataṃ viya paribhuñjitvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi.

At that moment, the Great Being, seeing this and knowing it to be Sakka’s gift, entered the leaf-hut and removed his royal garments. He put on one red bark-cloth as a lower garment and draped another over his body. He placed an antelope skin on one shoulder, tied his hair into a matted bundle, slung a carrying pole over his shoulder, and took a walking staff. Emerging from the leaf-hut and bearing the splendor of a renunciant, he paced back and forth on the walking path, uttering this inspired utterance: 'Ah, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!' He then re-entered the leaf-hut, sat on a wooden pallet, and attained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. In the evening, he left the hut and, at the end of the walking path, gathered leaves from a kāraka tree. Placing them in the bowl provided by Sakka, he softened them in water without salt, seasoning, or smoke. He consumed them as if they were nectar, cultivated the four divine abidings, and dwelt there.

Kāsirājāpi sunandasārathissa vacanaṃ sutvā mahāsenaguttaṃ pakkosāpetvā taramānarūpova gamanasajjaṃ kāretuṃ āha –

The King of Kāsī, having heard the charioteer Sunanda's words, summoned the commander-in-chief Mahāsenagutta and, in great haste, ordered him to prepare for the journey, saying:

64.

64.

“Yojayantu [V 6.0026] rathe asse, kacchaṃ nāgāna bandhatha;

Udīrayantu saṅkhapaṇavā, vādantu ekapokkharā.

“Let the horses be yoked to the chariots; bind the girths on the elephants. Let the conches and small drums sound; let the single-faced drums be played.

65.

65.

“Vādantu bherī sannaddhā, vaggū vādantu dundubhī;

Negamā ca maṃ anventu, gacchaṃ puttanivedako.

“Let the braced kettledrums be beaten; let the sweet-sounding great drums resound. Let the townspeople follow me as I go to advise my son.”

66.

66.

“Orodhā ca kumārā ca, vesiyānā ca brāhmaṇā;

Khippaṃ yānāni yojentu, gacchaṃ puttanivedako.

“Let the women of the harem, the princes, the merchants, and the brahmins quickly yoke their vehicles, as I go to advise my son.”

67.

67.

“Hatthārohā anīkaṭṭhā, rathikā pattikārakā;

Khippaṃ yānāni yojentu, gacchaṃ puttanivedako.

“Let the elephant riders, members of the royal guard, charioteers, and foot soldiers quickly yoke their vehicles, as I go to advise my son.”

68.

68.

“Samāgatā jānapadā, negamā ca samāgatā;

Khippaṃ yānāni yojentu, gacchaṃ puttanivedako”ti.

“The countryfolk have assembled, and the townspeople have gathered; let them quickly yoke their vehicles, as I go to advise my son.”

Tattha [P 6.0022] udīrayantūti saddaṃ muñcantu. Vādantūti vajjantu. Ekapokkharāti ekamukhabheriyo. Sannaddhāti suṭṭhu naddhā. Vaggūti madhurassarā. Gacchanti gamissāmi. Puttanivedakoti puttassa nivedako ovādako hutvā gacchāmi. Taṃ ovaditvā mama vacanaṃ gāhāpetvā tattheva taṃ ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisiñcitvā ānetuṃ gacchāmīti adhippāyenevamāha. Negamāti kuṭumbikajanā. Samāgatāti sannipatitā hutvā.

In this context, 'udīrayantu' means let them release a sound. 'Vādantu' means let them play. 'Ekapokkharā' refers to single-faced drums. 'Sannaddhā' means well-bound or tightly braced. 'Vaggū' means having a sweet sound. 'Gacchaṃ' means 'I shall go.' 'Puttanivedako' means 'I go as one who informs and advises my son.' He spoke with this intention: 'I go to advise him, make him accept my words, place him right there on a heap of jewels, anoint him as king, and bring him back.' 'Negamā' refers to the householders or merchant class. 'Samāgatā' means having gathered together.

Evaṃ raññā āṇattā sārathino asse yojetvā rathe rājadvāre ṭhapetvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Being thus commanded by the king, the charioteers yoked the horses, placed the chariots at the palace gate, and informed the king. Clarifying this matter, the Teacher said:

69.

69.

“Asse ca sārathī yutte, sindhave sīghavāhane;

Rājadvāraṃ upāgacchuṃ, yuttā deva ime hayā”ti.

“The charioteers, with the horses yoked—swift-moving Sindh steeds—approached the palace gate and said: 'Your Majesty, these horses are yoked!'”

Tattha [M 6.0027] asseti sindhave sindhavajātike sīghavāhane javasampanne asse ādāya. Sārathīti sārathino. Yutteti rathesu yojite. Upāgacchunti te rathesu yutte asse ādāya āgamaṃsu, āgantvā ca pana “yuttā, deva, ime hayā”ti ārocesuṃ.

In this context, 'asse' refers to having taken Sindh horses, born in the Sindh region, which are swift-moving and endowed with great speed. 'Sārathī' refers to the charioteers. 'Yutte' means yoked to the chariots. 'Upāgacchuṃ' means they came with the horses yoked to the chariots and, upon arrival, announced: 'Your Majesty, these horses are yoked.'

Tato [V 6.0027] sārathīnaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā rājā upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

Then, upon hearing the words of the charioteers, the king spoke half a stanza:

70.

70.

“Thūlā javena hāyanti, kisā hāyanti thāmunā”ti.

“The stout fail in speed; the lean fail in strength.”

Taṃ sutvā sārathinopi upaḍḍhagāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing this, the charioteers also spoke half a stanza:

“Kise thūle vivajjetvā, saṃsaṭṭhā yojitā hayā”ti.

“Avoiding both the lean and the stout, well-matched horses are yoked.”

Tassattho – deva, kise ca thūle ca evarūpe asse aggaṇhitvā vayena vaṇṇena javena balena sadisā hayā yojitāti.

The meaning is: Your Majesty, by avoiding such horses as are either lean or stout, steeds that are similar in age, color, speed, and strength have been yoked.

Atha rājā puttassa santikaṃ gacchanto cattāro vaṇṇe aṭṭhārasa seniyo sabbañca balakāyaṃ sannipātāpesi. Tassa sannipātentasseva tayo divasā atikkantā. Atha catutthe divase kāsirājā nagarato nikkhamitvā gahetabbayuttakaṃ gāhāpetvā assamapadaṃ gantvā puttena saddhiṃ paṭinandito paṭisanthāramakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then the king, intending to go to his son, assembled the four castes, the eighteen divisions of the army, and the entire body of troops. Three days passed during this assembly. On the fourth day, the King of Kāsī departed from the city, took what was necessary to bring with him, and went to the hermitage. After being joyfully greeted by his son, he engaged in friendly conversation. Clarifying this matter, the Teacher said:

71.

71.

“Tato rājā taramāno, yuttamāruyha sandanaṃ;

Itthāgāraṃ ajjhabhāsi, sabbāva anuyātha maṃ.

“Then the king, in great haste, mounted the yoked chariot and addressed the women of the harem: 'All of you, follow me.'

72.

72.

“Vāḷabījanimuṇhīsaṃ, khaggaṃ chattañca paṇḍaraṃ;

Upādhī rathamāruyha, suvaṇṇehi alaṅkatā.

“Taking the yak-tail whisk, the turban, the sword, and the white parasol, and wearing sandals adorned with gold, he mounted the chariot.

73.

73.

“Tato sa rājā pāyāsi, purakkhatvāna sārathiṃ;

Khippameva upāgacchi, yattha sammati temiyo.

“Then the king set forth, with the charioteer in the lead, and quickly approached the place where Temiya was dwelling.

74.

74.

“Tañca [P 6.0023] disvāna āyantaṃ, jalantamiva tejasā;

Khattasaṅghaparibyūḷhaṃ, temiyo etadabravi.

“Seeing him approaching, blazing as if with majesty and surrounded by a host of warriors, Temiya said this:

75.

75.

“Kacci nu tāta kusalaṃ, kacci tāta anāmayaṃ;

Sabbā ca rājakaññāyo, arogā mayha mātaro.

“I trust you are well, father? I trust you are free from illness? And are all the royal princesses, my mothers, healthy?

76.

76.

“Kusalañceva [V 6.0028][M 6.0028] me putta, atho putta anāmayaṃ;

Sabbā ca rājakaññāyo, arogā tuyha mātaro.

“I am well, my son, and indeed free from illness. All the royal princesses, your mothers, are healthy.

77.

77.

“Kacci amajjapo tāta, kacci te suramappiyaṃ;

Kacci sacce ca dhamme ca, dāne te ramate mano.

“I trust you are not a drinker of intoxicants, father? I trust that liquor is disagreeable to you? I trust your mind delights in truth, in righteousness, and in giving?

78.

78.

“Amajjapo ahaṃ putta, atho me suramappiyaṃ;

Atho sacce ca dhamme ca, dāne me ramate mano.

“I am not a drinker of intoxicants, my son, and liquor is disagreeable to me. Indeed, my mind delights in truth, in righteousness, and in giving.

79.

79.

“Kacci arogaṃ yoggaṃ te, kacci vahati vāhanaṃ;

Kacci te byādhayo natthi, sarīrassupatāpanā.

“Are your draft animals healthy? Do your vehicles carry you well? Do you have no illnesses, no afflictions tormenting the body?

80.

80.

“Atho arogaṃ yoggaṃ me, atho vahati vāhanaṃ;

Atho me byādhayo natthi, sarīrassupatāpanā.

“Indeed, my draft animals are healthy, and my vehicles carry me well. Indeed, I have no illnesses, no afflictions tormenting my body.

81.

81.

“Kacci antā ca te phītā, majjhe ca bahalā tava;

Koṭṭhāgārañca kosañca, kacci te paṭisanthataṃ.

“Are your borderlands prosperous, and is the center of your kingdom populous? Are your granaries and treasuries well-provided?

82.

82.

“Atho antā ca me phītā, majjhe ca bahalā mama;

Koṭṭhāgārañca kosañca, sabbaṃ me paṭisanthataṃ.

“Indeed, my borderlands are prosperous, and the center of my kingdom is populous. My granaries and treasuries are all well-provided.

83.

83.

“Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Patiṭṭhapentu pallaṅkaṃ, yattha rājā nisakkatī”ti.

“Welcome to you, great king; your coming is most fortunate. Let them set out a throne where the king may sit.”

Tattha upādhī rathamāruyhāti suvaṇṇapādukā ca rathaṃ āropentūti attho. Ime tayo pāde puttassa tattheva abhisekakaraṇatthāya “pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni gaṇhathā”ti āṇāpento rājā āha. Suvaṇṇehi alaṅkatāti idaṃ pādukaṃ sandhāyāha. Upāgacchīti upāgato ahosi. Kāya velāyāti? Mahāsattassa kārapaṇṇāni pacitvā nibbāpentassa nisinnavelāya. Jalantamiva tejasāti rājatejena jalantaṃ viya. Khattasaṅghaparibyūḷhanti kathāphāsukena amaccasaṅghena parivutaṃ, khattiyasamūhehi [V 6.0029] vā parivāritaṃ. Etadabravīti kāsirājānaṃ bahi khandhāvāraṃ nivāsāpetvā [M 6.0029] padasāva paṇṇasālaṃ āgantvā taṃ vanditvā nisinnaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto etaṃ vacanaṃ abravi.

Herein, Upādhī rathamāruyha means that golden sandals were also placed on the chariot. The king spoke these three lines, commanding, 'Take the five items of royal regalia,' for the purpose of anointing his son right there. Adorned with gold refers to these sandals. He approached means he had arrived. At what time? At the time when the Great Being, having boiled leaves from the kāra tree, was seated while cooling them. As if blazing with splendor means as if blazing with royal power. Surrounded by a host of warriors means surrounded by an assembly of ministers comfortable in conversation, or by a multitude of warriors. He spoke thus means that the king of Kasi, having encamped outside, came on foot to the leaf hut; having paid respects to the seated king, Temiya spoke these words while making friendly conversation.

Kusalaṃ anāmayanti ubhayenapi padena ārogyameva pucchati. Kacci amajjapoti kacci majjaṃ na pivasīti pucchati. “Appamatto”tipi pāṭho, kusaladhammesu nappamajjasīti attho. Suramappiyanti surāpānaṃ appiyaṃ. “Suramappiyā”tipi pāṭho, surā appiyāti attho. Dhammeti dasavidhe rājadhamme. Yogganti yuge yuñjitabbaṃ te tava assagoṇādikaṃ. Kacci vahatīti kacci arogaṃ hutvā vahati. Vāhananti hatthiassādi sabbaṃ vāhanaṃ. Sarīrassupatāpanāti sarīrassa upatāpakarā. Antāti paccantajanapadā. Phītāti iddhā subhikkhā, vatthābharaṇehi vā annapānehi vā paripuṇṇā gāḷhavāsā. Majjhe cāti raṭṭhassa majjhe. Bahalāti gāmanigamā ghanavāsā. Paṭisanthatanti paṭicchāditaṃ guttaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ vā. Yattha rājā nisakkatīti yasmiṃ pallaṅke rājā nisīdissati, taṃ paññāpentūti vadati.

Kusalaṃ anāmayam: with both terms, he inquires about well-being, specifically asking about health. Kacci amajjapo: he asks, 'Do you not drink intoxicants?' Appamatto is also a reading, meaning 'not heedless in wholesome qualities.' Suramappiyaṃ means 'liquor is disagreeable.' Suramappiyā is also a reading, meaning 'liquor is disagreeable.' Dhamme refers to the ten royal duties. Yoggaṃ means 'what is to be yoked,' i.e., your horses, oxen, etc. Kacci vahati means 'are they healthy and able to carry loads?' Vāhanaṃ means 'all conveyances like elephants and horses.' Sarīrassupatāpanā means 'what torments the body.' Antā means 'the border regions.' Phītā means 'prosperous, abundant in food, well-supplied with clothing, ornaments, food, and drink, densely inhabited.' Majjhe ca means 'in the middle of the kingdom.' Bahalā means 'villages and towns with dense populations.' Paṭisanthataṃ means 'covered, guarded, or full.' Yattha rājā nisakkati means 'the couch where the king will sit'; he says, 'Let them prepare that.'

Rājā mahāsatte gāravena pallaṅke na nisīdati. Atha [P 6.0024] mahāsatto “sace pallaṅke na nisīdati, paṇṇasanthāraṃ paññāpethā”ti vatvā tasmiṃ paññatte nisīdanatthāya rājānaṃ nimantento gāthamāha –

The king, out of respect for the Great Being, did not sit on the couch. Then the Great Being, thinking, 'If he does not sit on the couch, have a seat of leaves prepared,' invited the king to sit on it once it was prepared, reciting this verse:

84.

84.

“Idheva te nisīdassu, niyate paṇṇasanthare;

Etto udakamādāya, pāde pakkhālayassu te”ti.

“Sit right here on this prepared spread of leaves; taking water from here, wash your feet.”

Tattha niyateti susanthate. Ettoti paribhogaudakaṃ dassento āha.

Herein, niyate means ‘well-spread’. Etto means, showing the water for use, he spoke.

Rājā mahāsatte gāravena paṇṇasanthārepi anisīditvā bhūmiyaṃ eva nisīdi. Mahāsattopi paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā taṃ kārapaṇṇakaṃ nīharitvā rājānaṃ tena nimantento gāthamāha –

The king, out of respect for the Great Being, did not sit even on the seat of leaves, but sat on the ground itself. The Great Being, for his part, entered the leaf hut, brought out that dish of kāra leaves, and inviting the king with it, spoke this verse:

85.

85.

“Idampi paṇṇakaṃ mayhaṃ, randhaṃ rāja aloṇakaṃ;

Paribhuñja mahārāja, pāhuno mesidhāgato”ti.

“This leafy dish of mine, O king, is cooked and without salt; partake of it, great king, for you have come here to me as a guest.”

Atha [M 6.0030] naṃ rājā āha –

Then the king said to him:

86.

86.

“Na [V 6.0030] cāhaṃ paṇṇaṃ bhuñjāmi, na hetaṃ mayha bhojanaṃ;

Sālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecana”nti.

“I do not eat greens, nor is that my food; I eat the rice of Sāli grain, with a sauce of pure meat.”

Tattha na cāhanti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ.

Herein, na cāhaṃ is a statement of refusal.

Rājā tathārūpaṃ attano rājabhojanaṃ vaṇṇetvā tasmiṃ mahāsatte gāravena thokaṃ paṇṇakaṃ hatthatale ṭhapetvā “tāta, tvaṃ evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjasī”ti puttena saddhiṃ piyakathaṃ kathento nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe candādevī orodhena parivutā ekamaggena āgantvā bodhisattassa assamapadaṃ patvā piyaputtaṃ disvā tattheva patitvā visaññī ahosi. Tato paṭiladdhassāsā patitaṭṭhānato uṭṭhahitvā āgantvā bodhisattassa pāde daḷhaṃ gahetvā vanditvā assupuṇṇehi nettehi roditvā vandanaṭṭhānato uṭṭhāya ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ rājā “bhadde, tava puttassa bhojanaṃ passāhī”ti vatvā thokaṃ paṇṇakaṃ tassā hatthe ṭhapetvā sesaitthīnampi thokaṃ thokaṃ adāsi. Tā sabbāpi “sāmi, evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjasī”ti vadantiyo taṃ gahetvā attano attano sīse katvā “atidukkaraṃ karosi, sāmī”ti vatvā namassamānā nisīdiṃsu. Rājā puna “tāta, idaṃ mayhaṃ acchariyaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having praised his own royal food in such a manner, placed a small portion of the greens on the palm of his hand out of respect for the Great Being and sat conversing affectionately with his son, saying, “My dear, do you eat such food?” At that moment, Queen Candā, surrounded by her retinue, arrived all together and, reaching the Bodhisatta’s hermitage, saw her beloved son. Right there, she fell and fainted. Then, regaining consciousness, she rose from where she had fallen, approached the Bodhisatta, firmly grasped his feet, paid homage, and weeping with tear-filled eyes, rose from her posture of homage and sat to one side. The king then said to her, “Bhadde, behold your son's food,” and placing a small portion in her hand, he also gave small portions to the other women. All of them, saying, “My Lord, do you eat such food?” took it and placed it on their own heads, saying, “You perform an exceedingly difficult task, my lord,” and sat down paying homage. The king then said, “My dear, this appears as an amazing thing to me,” and spoke this verse:

87.

87.

“Accherakaṃ maṃ paṭibhāti, ekakampi rahogataṃ;

Edisaṃ bhuñjamānānaṃ, kena vaṇṇo pasīdatī”ti.

“It appears as an amazing thing to me, regarding one who is alone and secluded; for one eating such food, by what means does the complexion brighten?”

Tattha ekakanti tāta, taṃ ekakampi rahogataṃ iminā bhojanena yāpentaṃ disvā mama acchariyaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Edisanti evarūpaṃ aloṇakaṃ atakkaṃ nidhūpanaṃ randhaṃ pattaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ kena kāraṇena vaṇṇo pasīdatīti naṃ pucchi.

Therein, ‘ekakaṃ’ means, ‘My dear, seeing you sustaining yourself alone and in seclusion with this food, it appears astonishing to me.’ ‘Edisaṃ’ means ‘eating such food—unsalted, unseasoned, unspiced, cooked, and consisting of leaves—by what reason does the complexion brighten?’ Thus he questioned him.

Athassa [P 6.0025] so ācikkhanto āha –

Then, explaining, he said:

88.

88.

“Eko rāja nipajjāmi, niyate paṇṇasanthare;

Tāya me ekaseyyāya, rāja vaṇṇo pasīdati.

“Alone, O King, I lie down on a spread of leaves; by that solitary sleeping, O King, my complexion brightens.”

89.

89.

“Na [M 6.0031] ca nettiṃsabandhā me, rājarakkhā upaṭṭhitā;

Tāya me sukhaseyyāya, rājavaṇṇo pasīdati.

“Nor do sword-bearers attend me, nor royal guards; through that blissful sleep of mine, O King, my complexion brightens.”

90.

90.

“Atītaṃ [V 6.0031] nānusocāmi, nappajappāmināgataṃ;

“I do not grieve over the past, nor do I long for the future.

Paccuppannena yāpemi, tena vaṇṇo pasīdati.

I sustain myself with what is present; for that reason, my complexion brightens.

91.

91.

“Anāgatappajappāya, atītassānusocanā;

Etena bālā sussanti, naḷova harito luto”ti.

“By longing for the future and by lamenting the past, fools wither away, like a green reed that is plucked out.”

Tattha nettiṃsabandhāti khaggabandhā. Rājarakkhāti rājānaṃ rakkhitā. Nappajappāmīti na patthemi. Haritoti haritavaṇṇo. Lutoti luñcitvā ātape khittanaḷo viya.

Therein, ‘nettiṃsabandhā’ means those who have swords girt to them. ‘Rājarakkhā’ means those who guard the king. ‘Nappajappāmi’ means I do not long for. ‘Harito’ means green-colored. ‘Luto’ means like a reed that is plucked out and cast in the sun.

Atha rājā “idheva naṃ abhisiñcitvā ādāya gamissāmī”ti cintetvā rajjena nimantento āha –

Then the king, thinking, “Having consecrated him right here, I will take him and go,” offered him the kingdom, saying:

92.

92.

“Hatthānīkaṃ rathānīkaṃ, asse pattī ca vammino;

Nivesanāni rammāni, ahaṃ putta dadāmi te.

“An elephant corps, a chariot corps, horses and armored infantry, delightful residences—son, I give them to you.

93.

93.

“Itthāgārampi te dammi, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitaṃ;

Tā putta paṭipajjassu, tvaṃ no rājā bhavissasi.

“I give you also the women’s quarters, adorned with all ornaments. Accept them, son, and you shall be our king.

94.

94.

“Kusalā naccagītassa, sikkhitā cāturitthiyo;

Kāme taṃ ramayissanti, kiṃ araññe karissasi.

“Women skilled in dance and song, trained and charming, will delight you with sensual pleasures. What will you do in the forest?

95.

95.

“Paṭirājūhi te kaññā, ānayissaṃ alaṅkatā;

Tāsu putte janetvāna, atha pacchā pabbajissasi.

“I will bring for you adorned maidens from other kings; after fathering sons with them, you may then go forth thereafter.

96.

96.

“Yuvā ca daharo cāsi, paṭhamuppattiko susu;

Rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasī”ti.

“You are young and tender, in the very prime of your youth. Rule the kingdom, good sir; what will you do in the forest?”

Tattha hatthānīkanti dasahatthito paṭṭhāya hatthānīkaṃ nāma, tathā rathānīkaṃ. Vamminoti vammabaddhasūrayodhe. Kusalāti chekā. Sikkhitāti aññesupi itthikiccesu sikkhitā. Cāturitthiyoti caturā vilāsā itthiyo, atha vā caturā nāgarā itthiyo, atha vā caturā [M 6.0032] nāma [V 6.0032] nāṭakitthiyo. Paṭirājūhi te kaññāti aññehi rājūhi tava rājakaññāyo ānayissāmi. Yuvāti yobbanappatto. Daharoti taruṇo. Paṭhamuppattikoti paṭhamavayena uppattito samuggato. Susūti atitaruṇo.

Therein, ‘hatthānīka’ means an elephant corps, starting from ten elephants; likewise for ‘rathānīka’. ‘Vammino’ refers to brave warriors clad in armor. ‘Kusalā’ means skilled. ‘Sikkhitā’ means trained in other feminine duties as well. ‘Cāturitthiyo’ refers to women of charming grace, or clever city women, or clever actresses. ‘Paṭirājūhi te kaññā’ means, 'I will bring for you royal maidens from other kings.' ‘Yuvā’ means one who has reached youth. ‘Daharo’ means youthful. ‘Paṭhamuppattiko’ means one who has emerged into the first stage of life. ‘Susū’ means very young.

Ito paṭṭhāya bodhisattassa dhammakathā hoti –

From this point onward is the Bodhisatta’s discourse on the Dhamma:

97.

97.

“Yuvā care brahmacariyaṃ, brahmacārī yuvā siyā;

Daharassa hi pabbajjā, etaṃ isīhi vaṇṇitaṃ.

“A youth should lead the holy life; a youth should be a follower of the holy life. For the going forth of a young person—this is praised by the seers.

98.

98.

“Yuvā [P 6.0026] care brahmacariyaṃ, brahmacārī yuvā siyā;

Brahmacariyaṃ carissāmi, nāhaṃ rajjena matthiko.

“A youth should lead the holy life; a youth should be a follower of the holy life. I will lead the holy life; I have no desire for a kingdom.

99.

99.

“Passāmi vohaṃ daharaṃ, amma tāta vadantaraṃ;

Kicchāladdhaṃ piyaṃ puttaṃ, appatvāva jaraṃ mataṃ.

“I see a young child, a beloved son obtained with difficulty, dead before reaching old age, calling out 'Mother! Father!'

100.

100.

“Passāmi vohaṃ dahariṃ, kumāriṃ cārudassaniṃ;

Navavaṃsakaḷīraṃva, paluggaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ.

“I see a young maiden, a lovely-to-see princess, like a fresh bamboo shoot, broken, her life destroyed.

101.

101.

“Daharāpi hi mīyanti, narā ca atha nāriyo;

Tattha ko vissase poso, ‘daharomhī’ti jīvite.

“For the young die too, both men and women; who then, in that case, can trust in life, thinking, ‘I am young’?

102.

102.

“Yassa ratyā vivasāne, āyu appataraṃ siyā;

Appodakeva macchānaṃ, kiṃ nu komārakaṃ tahiṃ.

“For one whose life becomes shorter with the end of each night, like fish in a small pool of water, what value is there in youth?

103.

103.

“Niccamabbhāhato loko, niccañca parivārito;

Amoghāsu vajantīsu, kiṃ maṃ rajjebhisiñcasī”ti.

“The world is constantly smitten, and constantly surrounded; while the nights pass unfailingly, why do you anoint me for kingship?”

Kāsirājā āha –

The king of Kāsī said:

104.

104.

“Kena [V 6.0033] mabbhāhato loko, kena ca parivārito;

Kāyo amoghā gacchanti, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“By what is the world oppressed? And by what is it encompassed? What things pass not in vain? Please tell me this, as I am asking you.”

Bodhisatto āha –

The Bodhisatta said:

105.

105.

“Maccunābbhāhato loko, jarāya parivārito;

Ratyo amoghā gacchanti, evaṃ jānāhi khattiya.

“The world is oppressed by death, surrounded by old age. The nights pass not in vain—know this, O Khattiya.

106.

106.

“Yathāpi [M 6.0033] tante vitate, yaṃ yadevūpavīyati;

Appakaṃ hoti vetabbaṃ, evaṃ maccāna jīvitaṃ.

“Just as when the warp is stretched, whatever is woven makes the remainder to be woven less; even so is the life of mortals.”

107.

107.

“Yathā vārivaho pūro, gacchaṃ nupanivattati;

Evamāyu manussānaṃ, gacchaṃ nupanivattati.

“As a full river flowing onward does not turn back; even so the life of humans flowing onward does not turn back.”

108.

108.

“Yathā vārivaho pūro, vahe rukkhepakūlaje;

Evaṃ jarāmaraṇena, vuyhante sabbapāṇino”ti.

“As a full river sweeps away the trees growing on its banks, even so all living beings are swept away by old age and death.”

Tattha brahmacārī yuvā siyāti brahmacariyaṃ caranto yuvā bhaveyya. Isīhi vaṇṇitanti buddhādīhi isīhi thomitaṃ pasatthaṃ. Nāhaṃ rajjena matthikoti ahaṃ rajjena atthiko na homi. Amma tāta vadantaranti “amma, tātā”ti vadantaṃ. Palugganti maccunā luñcitvā gahitaṃ. Yassa ratyā vivasāneti mahārāja, yassa mātukucchimhi paṭisandhiggahaṇakālato paṭṭhāya rattidivātikkamena appataraṃ āyu hoti. Komārakaṃ tahinti tasmiṃ vaye taruṇabhāvo kiṃ karissati.

Herein, ‘a young man might be a celibate’ means he should be young while practicing the holy life. ‘Praised by sages’ means praised and commended by sages such as the Buddhas. ‘I have no need for a kingdom’ means ‘I am not one who has need of a kingdom.’ ‘Saying, “Mother, Father”’ means one who says, “Mother, Father.” ‘Crumbled’ means seized and taken by death. ‘For whom, as the night ends’ means, O great king, for whom, from the time of taking rebirth in the mother’s womb, life becomes shorter with the passing of days and nights. ‘What can youth do then?’ means what will youthfulness accomplish at that age?

Kena mabbhāhatoti kena abbhāhato. Idaṃ rājā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa atthaṃ ajānantova pucchati. Ratyoti rattiyo. Tā hi imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyuñca vaṇṇañca balañca khepentiyo eva gacchantīti amoghā gacchanti nāmāti veditabbaṃ[P 6.0027]. Yaṃ yadevūpavīyatīti yaṃ yaṃ tantaṃ upavīyati. Vetabbanti tantasmiṃ vīte sesaṃ vetabbaṃ yathā appakaṃ hoti, evaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ. Nupanivattatīti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe gataṃ gatameva hoti, na upanivattati. Vahe rukkhepakūlajeti upakūlaje rukkhe vaheyya.

‘By what is it oppressed?’ means by what is it struck? The king asks this, not understanding the meaning of what was said concisely. ‘Nights’ (ratyo) refers to the nights. It should be understood that they are said to 'pass not in vain' because they pass while consuming the life, beauty, and strength of these beings. ‘Whatever is woven’ means whatever of the cloth is woven. ‘What is to be woven’ (vetabbaṃ) means just as the remainder to be woven in the loom becomes small when it is woven, so is the life of mortals. ‘Does not turn back’ means that in each and every moment, what is gone is gone indeed; it does not return. ‘Would sweep away trees on the bank’ means it would sweep away trees growing near the bank.

Rājā [V 6.0034] mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā “kiṃ me gharāvāsenā”ti ativiya ukkaṇṭhito pabbajitukāmo hutvā “nāhaṃ tāva puna nagaraṃ gamissāmi, idheva pabbajissāmi. Sace pana me putto nagaraṃ gaccheyya, setacchattamassa dadeyya”nti cintetvā taṃ vīmaṃsituṃ puna rajjena nimantento āha –

Hearing the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king became extremely disenchanted with household life and, desiring to go forth, he thought: ‘What use is the household life to me? I will not return to the city; I shall go forth right here. If my son should go to the city, I would give him the white parasol.’ Then, to test him, he invited him again with the kingdom, saying:

109.

109.

“Hatthānīkaṃ rathānīkaṃ, asse pattī ca vammino;

Nivesanāni rammāni, ahaṃ putta dadāmi te.

“An elephant corps, a chariot corps, horses and armored infantry, and delightful dwellings—son, I give them to you.”

110.

110.

“Itthāgārampi [M 6.0034] te dammi, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitaṃ;

Tā putta paṭipajjassu, tvaṃ no rājā bhavissasi.

“I will give you the women’s quarters, adorned with every ornament. Accept them, my son; you shall be our king.”

111.

111.

“Kusalā naccagītassa, sikkhitā cāturitthiyo;

Kāme taṃ ramayissanti, kiṃ araññe karissasi.

“Women skilled in dance and song, trained in womanly charms, will delight you with sensual pleasures. What will you do in the forest?”

112.

112.

“Paṭirājūhi te kaññā, ānayissaṃ alaṅkatā;

Tāsu putte janetvāna, atha pacchā pabbajissasi.

“I will bring you adorned maidens from rival kings; after fathering sons with them, then you may go forth to homelessness.”

113.

113.

“Yuvā ca daharo cāsi, paṭhamuppattiko susu;

Rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasi.

“You are young and tender, in the first flush of youth; rule the kingdom, good sir. What will you do in the forest?”

114.

114.

“Koṭṭhāgārañca kosañca, vāhanāni balāni ca;

Nivesanāni rammāni, ahaṃ putta dadāmi te.

“Granaries and treasuries, conveyances and forces, and delightful dwellings—I give them to you, my son.”

115.

115.

“Gomaṇḍalaparibyūḷho, dāsisaṅghapurakkhato;

Rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasī”ti.

“Surrounded by a circle of beautiful princesses, and honored by a retinue of female servants, rule the kingdom, good sir. What will you do in the forest?”

Tattha gomaṇḍalaparibyūḷhoti subhaṅgīnaṃ rājakaññānaṃ maṇḍalena purakkhato.

Herein, ‘surrounded by a circle of beauties’ means honored by a circle of beautiful-limbed royal maidens.

Atha mahāsatto rajjena anatthikabhāvaṃ pakāsento āha –

Then the Great Being, making clear his lack of need for the kingdom, said:

116.

116.

“Kiṃ [V 6.0035] dhanena yaṃ khīyetha, kiṃ bhariyāya marissati;

Kiṃ yobbanena jiṇṇena, yaṃ jarāyābhibhuyyati.

“What is the use of wealth that wastes away? What is the use of a wife who will die? What is the use of youth that must grow old, which is overcome by old age?”

117.

117.

“Tattha kā nandi kā khiḍḍā, kā ratī kā dhanesanā;

Kiṃ me puttehi dārehi, rāja muttosmi bandhanā.

“In such a state, what joy, what sport, what delight, what pursuit of wealth? What are sons and wives to me? O king, I am freed from bondage.”

118.

118.

“Yohaṃ evaṃ pajānāmi, maccu me nappamajjati;

Antakenādhipannassa, kā ratī kā dhanesanā.

“For me, who knows this, death is never heedless; for one seized by the Ender, what delight, what pursuit of wealth?”

119.

119.

“Phalānamiva [P 6.0028] pakkānaṃ, niccaṃ patanato bhayaṃ;

Evaṃ jātāna maccānaṃ, niccaṃ maraṇato bhayaṃ.

“Just as for ripe fruits there is constant fear of falling, so for mortals who are born there is constant fear of death.”

120.

120.

“Sāyameke na dissanti, pāto diṭṭhā bahū janā;

Pāto ete na dissanti, sāyaṃ diṭṭhā bahū janā.

“Of the many people seen in the morning, some are not seen by evening; of the many people seen in the evening, some are not seen by morning.”

121.

121.

“Ajjeva [M 6.0035] kiccaṃ ātapaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena, mahāsenena maccunā.

“The effort should be made this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow? For we can make no pact with Death and his great army.”

122.

122.

“Corā dhanassa patthenti, rāja muttosmi bandhanā;

Ehi rāja nivattassu, nāhaṃ rajjena matthiko”ti.

“Thieves long for wealth; O King, I am freed from bondage. Come, O King, turn back; I have no need for a kingdom.”

Tattha yaṃ khīyethāti mahārāja, kiṃ tvaṃ maṃ dhanena nimantesi, yaṃ khīyetha khayaṃ gaccheyya. Dhanaṃ vā hi purisaṃ cajati, puriso vā taṃ dhanaṃ cajitvā gacchatīti sabbathāpi khayagāmīyeva hoti, kiṃ tvaṃ maṃ tena dhanena nimantesi. Kiṃ bhariyāyāti bhariyāya kiṃ karissāmi, yā mayi ṭhiteyeva marissati. Jiṇṇenāti jarāya anuparitena anubhūtena. Abhibhuyyatīti abhibhaviyyati. Tatthāti tasmiṃ evaṃ jarāmaraṇadhamme lokasannivāse. Kā nandīti kā nāma tuṭṭhi. Khiḍḍāti kīḷā. Ratīti pañcakāmaguṇarati. Bandhanāti kāmabandhanā mutto asmi, mahārājāti jhānena vikkhambhitattā evamāha. Maccu meti mama maccu nappamajjati, niccaṃ mama vadhāya appamatoyevāti. Yo ahaṃ evaṃ pajānāmi, tassa mama antakena adhipannassa vadhitassa [V 6.0036] kā nāma rati, kā dhanesanāti. Niccanti jātakālato paṭṭhāya sadā jarāmaraṇato bhayameva uppajjati.

Herein, ‘that which would perish’ means, O great king, why do you invite me with wealth that would waste away and go to destruction? For either wealth leaves the person, or the person leaves the wealth and departs—in every way, it is bound for destruction. Why do you invite me with such wealth? ‘What of a wife?’ means what shall I do with a wife, who will die while I still remain? ‘Grown old’ means touched and experienced by old age. ‘Is overcome’ means is vanquished. ‘In that’ means in this world, which has the nature of old age and death. ‘What joy?’ means what kind of satisfaction? ‘Sport’ means playing. ‘Delight’ means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘From bondage’ means ‘I am freed from the bond of sensual desire, O great king.’ He says this because it has been suppressed by jhāna. ‘My death’ means my death is not heedless; it is always vigilant for my destruction. For me, who knows this, who am seized and struck down by the Ender, what delight is there, what pursuit of wealth? ‘Always’ means from the time of birth, fear of old age and death always arises.

Ātapanti kusalakammavīriyaṃ. Kiccanti kattabbaṃ. Ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suveti suve vā parasuve vā maraṇaṃ vā jīvitaṃ vā ko jāneyya. Saṅgaranti saṅketaṃ. Mahāsenenāti pañcavīsatibhayabāttiṃsakammakaraṇachannavutirogappamukhādivasena puthusenena. Corā dhanassāti dhanatthāya jīvitaṃ cajantā corā dhanassa patthenti nāma, ahaṃ pana dhanapatthanāsaṅkhātā bandhanā mutto asmi, na me dhanenatthoti attho. Nivattassūti mama vacanena sammā nivattassu, rajjaṃ pahāya nekkhammaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ katvā pabbajassu. Yaṃ pana cintesi “imaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpessāmī”ti, taṃ mā cintayi, nāhaṃ rajjena atthikoti. Iti mahāsattassa dhammadesanā sahānusandhinā matthakaṃ pattā.

‘Striving’ (ātapaṃ) means energy in wholesome actions. ‘Duty’ (kiccaṃ) means what is to be done. ‘Who knows if death will come tomorrow?’ means who can know if there will be death or life tomorrow or the day after? ‘Pact’ (saṅgaraṃ) means an agreement. ‘With a great army’ means with a vast host, consisting of the twenty-five fears, the thirty-two kinds of punishment, the ninety-six diseases, and so forth. ‘Thieves for wealth’ means thieves who long for wealth, even giving up their lives for its sake; but I am freed from the bondage known as the longing for wealth; the meaning is that I have no need for wealth. ‘Turn back’ means ‘By my word, turn back completely; having abandoned the kingdom and made renunciation your refuge, go forth.’ As for what you thought, ‘I will establish him in the kingdom,’ do not think so, for I have no need for a kingdom. Thus the Great Being’s Dhamma teaching reached its conclusion with its connections.

Taṃ sutvā rājānañca candādeviñca ādiṃ katvā soḷasasahassā orodhā ca amaccādayo ca sabbe pabbajitukāmā ahesuṃ. Rājāpi nagare [M 6.0036] bheriṃ carāpesi “ye mama puttassa santike pabbajituṃ icchanti, te pabbajantū”ti[P 6.0029]. Sabbesañca suvaṇṇakoṭṭhāgārādīnaṃ dvārāni vivarāpetvā “asukaṭṭhāne ca mahānidhikumbhiyo atthi, atthikā gaṇhantū”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe akkharāni likhāpetvā mahāthambhe bandhāpesi. Te nāgarā yathāpasārite āpaṇe ca vivaṭadvārāni gehāni ca pahāya nagarato nikkhamitvā rañño santikaṃ āgamiṃsu. Rājā mahājanena saddhiṃ mahāsattassa santike pabbaji. Sakkadattiyaṃ tiyojanikaṃ assamapadaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ ahosi. Mahāsatto paṇṇasālāyo vicāresi, majjhe ṭhitā paṇṇasālāyo itthīnaṃ dāpesi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Bhīrukajātikā etāti. Purisānaṃ pana bahipaṇṇasālāyo dāpesi. Tā sabbāpi paṇṇasālāyo vissakammadevaputtova māpesi. Te ca phaladhararukkhe vissakammadevaputtoyeva attano iddhiyā māpesi. Te sabbe vissakammena nimmitesu phaladhararukkhesu uposathadivase bhūmiyaṃ patitapatitāni phalāni gahetvā paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Tesu yo kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā vitakketi, tassa manaṃ jānitvā mahāsatto ākāse nisīditvā madhuradhammaṃ kathesi. Te janā bodhisattassa madhuradhammaṃ sutvā ekaggacittā hutvā khippameva abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattesuṃ.

Hearing this, starting with the king and Queen Candā, the sixteen thousand women of the harem, the ministers, and all others desired to go forth. The king also had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'Those who wish to go forth into the presence of my son, let them go forth.' Having opened the doors of all the treasuries, such as the gold vaults, he announced: 'In such and such places, there are great treasure jars; those who wish may take them.' He had letters inscribed on golden plates and fastened them to great pillars. The citizens, leaving behind their shops with goods as they were and their homes with open doors, departed from the city and came into the king’s presence. The king, along with the great multitude, went forth into the presence of the Great Being. The hermitage provided by Sakka, three leagues in extent, became full. The Great Being arranged the leaf-huts; he gave the leaf-huts in the middle to the women. Why? Because they are of a timid nature. But he gave the outer leaf-huts to the men. All those leaf-huts were created by the divine son Vissakamma. And the divine son Vissakamma himself, by his psychic power, created the fruit-bearing trees. All of them, on the Uposatha days, gathered the fruits that had fallen to the ground from the fruit-bearing trees created by Vissakamma, consumed them, and practiced the ascetic life. Among them, if anyone entertained a thought of sensual desire, ill will, or harm, the Great Being, knowing their mind, would sit in the air and deliver a sweet discourse. Those people, hearing the Bodhisatta’s sweet discourse, became unified in mind and quickly attained the supernormal powers and meditative attainments.

Tadā eko sāmantarājā “kāsirājā kira bārāṇasinagarato nikkhamitvā vanaṃ pavisitvā pabbajito”ti sutvā “bārāṇasiṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti nagarā nikkhamitvā bārāṇasiṃ patvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā alaṅkatanagaraṃ disvā rājanivesanaṃ āruyha sattavidhaṃ vararatanaṃ oloketvā [V 6.0037] “kāsirañño imaṃ dhanaṃ nissāya ekena bhayena bhavitabba”nti cintento surāsoṇḍe pakkosāpetvā pucchi “tumhākaṃ rañño idha nagare bhayaṃ uppannaṃ atthī”ti? “Natthi, devā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti. “Amhākaṃ rañño putto temiyakumāro ‘bārāṇasiṃ rajjaṃ na karissāmī’ti amūgopi mūgo viya hutvā imamhā nagarā nikkhamitvā vanaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji, tena kāraṇena amhākaṃ rājā mahājanena saddhiṃ imamhā nagarā nikkhamitvā temiyakumārassa santikaṃ gantvā pabbajito”ti ārocesuṃ. Sāmantarājā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā tussitvā “ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā [M 6.0037] “tāta, tumhākaṃ rājā kataradvārena nikkhanto”ti pucchi. “Deva, pācīnadvārenā”ti vutte attano parisāya saddhiṃ teneva pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā nadītīrena pāyāsi.

At that time, a neighboring king, hearing that 'the king of Kasi, having left the city of Bārāṇasī, has entered the forest and become a renunciate,' thought, 'I will seize Bārāṇasī.' He left his city, arrived at Bārāṇasī, entered the city, and saw the city beautifully adorned. Ascending to the royal residence, he examined the seven kinds of precious treasures and pondered, 'The king of Kasi must have had some fear related to this wealth; otherwise, he would not have left it.' He summoned the drunkards who remained and asked, 'Has any danger arisen for your king in this city?' 'No, lord,' they replied. 'Then for what reason did he go?' he asked. 'Our king's son, Prince Temiya, though not mute, acted as if he were mute, saying, "I will not rule the kingdom of Bārāṇasī." He left this city, entered the forest, and embraced the ascetic life. For this reason, our king, along with the populace, left this city, went to Prince Temiya, and became a renunciate,' they explained. Hearing their words, the neighboring king was pleased and thought, 'I too shall become a renunciate.' He asked, 'Sirs, through which gate did your king depart?' 'Through the eastern gate, lord,' they said. Then, with his retinue, he left by that same eastern gate and proceeded along the riverbank.

Mahāsattopi tassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā vanantaraṃ āgantvā ākāse nisīditvā madhuradhammaṃ desesi. So parisāya saddhiṃ tassa santikeyeva pabbaji. Evaṃ aparepi satta rājāno “bārāṇasinagaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āgatā. Tepi rājāno satta rajjāni chaḍḍetvā bodhisattassa santikeyeva pabbajiṃsu. Hatthīpi araññahatthī jātā, assāpi araññaassā jātā, rathāpi araññeyeva vinaṭṭhā, bhaṇḍāgāresu kahāpaṇe assamapade vālukaṃ katvā vikiriṃsu. Sabbepi abhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattetvā jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Tiracchānagatā hatthiassāpi isigaṇe cittaṃ pasādetvā chakāmāvacaralokesu nibbattiṃsu.

The Great Being, knowing of his arrival, went into the forest, sat in the sky, and delivered a sweet discourse. The king, along with his retinue, renounced the world in his very presence. Similarly, seven other kings came thinking, 'We will seize the city of Bārāṇasī.' Those kings also abandoned their seven kingdoms and renounced the world in the presence of the Bodhisatta. The elephants became wild forest elephants, the horses became wild forest horses, and the chariots perished right there in the forest; the coins from the treasuries were scattered like sand throughout the hermitage. All of them developed the supernormal powers and attainments, and at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Brahma world. Even the animals, such as the elephants and horses, having found faith in the company of the sages, were reborn in the six sensual heavens.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi rajjaṃ pahāya nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā chatte adhivatthā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā [P 6.0030] ahosi, sunando sārathi sāriputto, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, mūgapakkhapaṇḍito pana ahameva sammāsambuddho ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Four Noble Truths, said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, the Tathāgata renounced the kingdom and departed.' Then he connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the goddess dwelling in the parasol was Uppalavaṇṇā, Sunanda the charioteer was Sāriputta, the parents were the great royal families (King Suddhodana and Queen Māyā), the remaining assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the wise Mūgapakkha was I myself, the Fully Enlightened One.'

Mūgapakkhajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The end of the first commentary, the Mūgapakkha Jātaka.

[539] 2. Mahājanakajātakavaṇṇanā

[539] 2. The Commentary on the Mahājanaka Jātaka.

Koyaṃ [V 6.0038][M 6.0039] majjhe samuddasminti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā tathāgatassa mahābhinikkhamanaṃ vaṇṇayantā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'Who is this in the middle of the ocean?' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation. One day, the monks were sitting together in the Dhamma hall, praising the Tathāgata's Great Renunciation. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?' When they replied, 'With this one,' he said, 'Not only now, monks, but also in the past the Tathāgata went forth in a Great Renunciation.' Being requested by them, he related the past.

Atīte videharaṭṭhe mithilāyaṃ mahājanako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa dve puttā ahesuṃ ariṭṭhajanako ca polajanako cāti. Tesu rājā jeṭṭhaputtassa uparajjaṃ adāsi, kaniṭṭhassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Aparabhāge mahājanako kālamakāsi. Tassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā rañño accayena ariṭṭhajanako rājā hutvā itarassa uparajjaṃ adāsi. Tasseko pādamūliko amacco rañño santikaṃ gantvā “deva, uparājā tumhe ghātetukāmo”ti āha. Rājā tassa punappunaṃ kathaṃ sutvā kaniṭṭhassa sinehaṃ bhinditvā polajanakaṃ saṅkhalikāhi bandhāpetvā rājanivesanato avidūre ekasmiṃ gehe vasāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Kumāro “sacāhaṃ bhātu verīmhi, saṅkhalikāpi me hatthapādā mā muccantu, dvārampi mā vivarīyatu, sace no verīmhi, saṅkhalikāpi me hatthapādā muccantu, dvārampi vivarīyatū”ti saccakiriyamakāsi. Tāvadeva [P 6.0031] saṅkhalikāpi khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ chijjiṃsu, dvārampi vivaṭaṃ. So nikkhamitvā ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, in Mithilā, a king named Mahājanaka reigned. He had two sons, Ariṭṭhajanaka and Polajanaka. The king gave the viceroyalty to his eldest son and the position of commander-in-chief to the younger. Later, Mahājanaka passed away. After performing the funeral rites for him, Ariṭṭhajanaka became king upon the death of his father and gave the viceroyalty to his brother. A courtier-minister in his service went to the king and said, 'Your Majesty, the viceroy wishes to kill you.' Hearing these words repeatedly, the king’s affection for his younger brother was broken; he had Polajanaka bound in chains and confined in a house not far from the royal palace, placing a guard over him. The prince performed an Act of Truth: 'If I am an enemy to my brother, may these chains on my hands and feet not be loosed, and may the door not open. But if I am not an enemy, may these chains on my hands and feet be loosed, and may the door open.' At that very moment, the chains shattered into pieces and the door opened. He departed and went to a border village, where he took up residence.

Paccantagāmavāsino taṃ sañjānitvā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Rājāpi taṃ gāhāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. So anupubbena paccantajanapadaṃ hatthagataṃ katvā mahāparivāro hutvā “ahaṃ pubbe bhātu na verī, idāni pana verīmhī”ti mahājanaparivuto mithilaṃ gantvā bahinagare khandhāvāraṃ katvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Nagaravāsino yodhā “kumāro kira āgato”ti sutvā yebhuyyena hatthiassavāhanādīni gahetvā tasseva santikaṃ āgamiṃsu, aññepi nāgarā āgamiṃsu. So bhātu sāsanaṃ pesesi “nāhaṃ pubbe tumhākaṃ verī, idāni pana verīmhi, chattaṃ vā me detha, yuddhaṃ vā”ti. Rājā taṃ sutvā [M 6.0040] yuddhaṃ kātuṃ icchanto aggamahesiṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, yuddhe jayaparājayo [V 6.0039] nāma na sakkā ñātuṃ, sace mama antarāyo hoti, tvaṃ gabbhaṃ rakkheyyāsī”ti vatvā mahatiyā senāya parivuto nagarā nikkhami.

The inhabitants of the border village, recognizing him, attended upon him. The king was unable to have him captured. In due course, having brought the border region under his control and having gained a large following, he thought, 'Formerly I was not an enemy to my brother, but now I am.' Surrounded by a great multitude, he went to Mithilā, established a military camp outside the city, and stayed there. The soldiers in the city, hearing that the prince had arrived, for the most part took their elephants, horses, and vehicles and went to him; other townsfolk also joined him. He sent a message to his brother: 'Formerly I was not your enemy, but now I am. Either give up the royal umbrella to me, or give battle.' Hearing this, the king, wishing to fight, summoned his chief queen and said, 'My dear, victory and defeat in battle cannot be known. If any danger befalls me, you must protect the child in your womb.' Then, surrounded by a great army, he marched out of the city.

Atha naṃ yuddhe polajanakassa yodhā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ. Tadā “rājā mato”ti sakalanagare ekakolāhalaṃ jātaṃ. Devīpi tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ suvaṇṇasārādīni gahetvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā matthake kiliṭṭhapilotikaṃ attharitvā upari taṇḍule okiritvā kiliṭṭhapilotikaṃ nivāsetvā sarīraṃ virūpaṃ katvā pacchiṃ sīse ṭhapetvā divā divasseva nikkhami, na koci naṃ sañjāni. Sā uttaradvārena nikkhamitvā katthaci agatapubbattā maggaṃ ajānantī disaṃ vavatthāpetuṃ asakkontī kevalaṃ “kālacampānagaraṃ nāma atthī”ti sutattā “kālacampānagaraṃ gamikā nāma atthī”ti pucchamānā ekikā sālāyaṃ nisīdi. Kucchimhi panassā nibbattasatto na yo vā so vā, pūritapāramī mahāsatto nibbatti.

Then, in the battle, Polajanaka’s soldiers brought the king's life to an end. At that time, a great uproar arose throughout the entire city, crying, 'The king is dead!' The queen, learning of his death, quickly gathered her most valuable gold and jewels, placed them in a basket, spread a soiled cloth over them, and scattered rice grains on top. She then dressed herself in a soiled garment and disfigured her appearance. Placing the basket on her head, she left in the middle of the day, and no one recognized her. Exiting through the northern gate, and never having gone anywhere before, she did not know the way and was unable to determine the direction. Having merely heard that there was a city named Kālacampā, she went about asking, 'Is there anyone going to the city of Kālacampā?' and sat alone in a rest house. Now, the being who had been conceived in her womb was no ordinary person; it was the Great Being who had fulfilled the perfections.

Tassa tejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “tassā kucchiyaṃ nibbattasatto mahāpuñño, mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā paṭicchannayoggaṃ māpetvā tattha mañcaṃ paññāpetvā mahallakapuriso viya yoggaṃ pājento tāya nisinnasālāya dvāre ṭhatvā “kālacampānagaraṃ gamikā nāma atthī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ, tāta, gamissāmī”ti. “Tena [P 6.0032] hi yoggaṃ āruyha nisīda, ammā”ti. “Tāta, ahaṃ paripuṇṇagabbhā, na sakkā mayā yoggaṃ abhiruhituṃ, pacchato pacchato gamissāmi, imissā pana me pacchiyā okāsaṃ dehī”ti. “Amma, kiṃ vadesi, yoggaṃ pājetuṃ jānanasamattho nāma mayā sadiso natthi. Amma, mā bhāyi, āruyha nisīdā”ti. Sā “tāta, sādhū”ti vadati. So tassā ārohanakāle attano ānubhāvena vātapuṇṇabhastacammaṃ viya pathaviṃ unnāmetvā yoggassa pacchimante paharāpesi. Sā abhiruyha sayane nipajjitvāva “ayaṃ devatā bhavissatī”ti aññāsi. Sā dibbasayane nipannamattāva niddaṃ okkami.

By his power, Sakka’s abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting and knowing the reason, thought, 'A being of great merit has been conceived in her womb; it is fitting for me to go.' He created a covered carriage, prepared a bed within it, and, driving the carriage in the guise of an old man, he stood at the door of the rest house where she was sitting and asked, 'Is there anyone here going to the city of Kālacampā?' 'I will go, father,' she replied. 'Then, mother, climb into the carriage and sit down.' 'Father, I am heavy with child and cannot climb into the carriage; I will follow behind, but please make room for this basket of mine.' 'Mother, what are you saying? There is no one who knows how to drive a carriage as well as I do. Mother, do not fear, climb in and sit.' She said, 'Very well, father.' As she was climbing in, by his power he made the earth rise up like a wind-filled leather bellows until it touched the rear of the carriage. Having mounted and lain down upon the couch, she realized, 'This must be a deity.' The moment she lay upon that divine couch, she fell into a deep sleep.

Atha [M 6.0041] naṃ sakko tiṃsayojanamatthake ekaṃ nadiṃ patvā pabodhetvā “amma, otaritvā nadiyaṃ nhāyitvā ussīsake sāṭakayugaṃ atthi, taṃ nivāsehi, antoyogge puṭabhattaṃ atthi, taṃ bhuñjāhī”ti āha. Sā tathā katvā puna nipajjitvā sāyanhasamaye kālacampānagaraṃ patvā dvāraṭṭālakapākāre disvā “tāta, kiṃ nāma nagarameta”nti pucchi. “Kālacampānagaraṃ, ammā”ti. “Kiṃ vadesi, tāta, nanu amhākaṃ nagarato kālacampānagaraṃ saṭṭhiyojanamatthake hotī”ti? “Evaṃ, amma, ahaṃ pana ujumaggaṃ jānāmī”ti. Atha naṃ dakkhiṇadvārasamīpe otāretvā [V 6.0040] “amma, amhākaṃ gāmo purato atthi, tvaṃ gantvā nagaraṃ pavisāhī”ti vatvā purato gantvā viya sakko antaradhāyitvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Then Sakka, having reached a river at a distance of thirty leagues, woke her and said, 'Mother, get down and bathe in the river. There is a pair of garments at the head of the couch—put them on. Inside the carriage is a bundle of food—eat it.' She did so and lay down again. In the evening, they arrived at the city of Kālacampā. Seeing the gate-towers and ramparts, she asked, 'Father, what city is this?' 'The city of Kālacampā, mother.' 'What are you saying, father? Is not Kālacampā sixty leagues from our city?' 'Yes, mother, but I know the direct road.' Then, having her dismount near the southern gate, he said, 'Mother, our village is just ahead. You go and enter the city.' Having spoken, Sakka, as if going on ahead, vanished and returned to his own abode.

Devīpi ekikāva sālāyaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko disāpāmokkho ācariyo kālacampānagaravāsī mantajjhāyako brāhmaṇo pañcahi māṇavakasatehi parivuto nhānatthāya gacchanto dūratova oloketvā taṃ abhirūpaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ tattha nisinnaṃ disvā tassā kucchiyaṃ mahāsattassānubhāvena saha dassaneneva kaniṭṭhabhaginisinehaṃ uppādetvā māṇavake bahi ṭhapetvā ekakova sālaṃ pavisitvā “bhagini, kataragāmavāsikā tva”nti pucchi. “Tāta, mithilāyaṃ ariṭṭhajanakarañño aggamahesīmhī”ti. “Amma, idha kasmā āgatāsī”ti? “Tāta, polajanakena rājā mārito, athāhaṃ bhītā ‘gabbhaṃ anurakkhissāmī’ti āgatā”ti. “Amma, imasmiṃ pana te nagare koci ñātako atthī”ti? “Natthi, tātā”ti. Tena hi mā cintayi, ahaṃ udiccabrāhmaṇo mahāsālo disāpāmokkhaācariyo, ahaṃ taṃ bhaginiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā paṭijaggissāmi, tvaṃ “bhātikā”ti maṃ vatvā pādesu gahetvā paridevāti. Sā mahāsaddaṃ katvā [P 6.0033] tassa pādesu gahetvā paridevi. Te dvepi aññamaññaṃ parideviṃsu.

The queen sat alone in the hall. At that moment, a world-renowned teacher, a brahmin from the city of Kālacampā who was a mantra-reciter and a brahmin of great house, surrounded by five hundred young students, was going out to bathe. Looking from afar, he saw her, beautiful and possessed of great charm, seated there. By the majesty of the Great Being in her womb, at the very moment of seeing her, affection for a younger sister arose in him. Leaving the young students outside, he entered the hall alone and asked, "Sister, from which village do you come?" "Father, I am the chief queen of King Ariṭṭhajanaka of Mithilā." "Mother, why have you come here alone?" "Father, the king was killed by Polajanaka, and so, being afraid and wishing to protect the child in my womb, I have come here." "Mother, do you have any relatives in this city?" "I have none, father." "Then do not worry. I am a northern brahmin of a great house, a world-renowned teacher. I shall establish you in the position of a sister and care for you. Call me 'brother,' clasp my feet, and lament that you have found your brother after so long." She let out a loud cry, clasped his feet, and lamented. They both wept together.

Athassa antevāsikā mahāsaddaṃ sutvā khippaṃ upadhāvitvā “ācariya, kiṃ te hotī”ti pucchiṃsu. So āha – “kaniṭṭhabhaginī me esā, asukakāle nāma mayā vinā jātā”ti. Atha māṇavā “tava bhaginiṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya mā cintayittha ācariyā”ti āhaṃsu. So māṇave paṭicchannayoggaṃ āharāpetvā taṃ tattha nisīdāpetvā “tātā, vo [M 6.0042] gantvā brāhmaṇiyā mama kaniṭṭhabhaginibhāvaṃ kathetvā sabbakiccāni kātuṃ vadethā”ti vatvā gehaṃ pesesi. Te gantvā brāhmaṇiyā kathesuṃ. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇīpi uṇhodakena nhāpetvā sayanaṃ paññāpetvā nipajjāpesi. Atha brāhmaṇopi nhātvā āgato bhojanakāle “bhaginiṃ me pakkosathā”ti pakkosāpetvā tāya saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjitvā antonivesaneyeva taṃ paṭijaggi.

Then his disciples, hearing the sound of weeping, quickly ran up and asked, "Teacher, what is the matter with you?" He said, "This is my younger sister; she was born at a time when I was away." Then the young brahmins said, "Teacher, since you have found your sister, do not worry; we shall do what is necessary." He had the young men bring a covered carriage from his house, had her seated in it, and said, "Dears, go and tell the brahmin's wife that she is my younger sister and tell her to perform all necessary duties." Having said this, he sent her to his house. They went and told the brahmin's wife. Then the brahmin's wife had her bathed with warm water, prepared a bed, and had her rest. Then the brahmin, having bathed and returned, at mealtime said, "Call my sister." He had her called and ate together with her, and then cared for her like a sister within the inner residence.

Sā na cirasseva suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi, “mahājanakakumāro”tissa ayyakasantakaṃ nāmamakāsi. So vaḍḍhamāno dārakehi saddhiṃ kīḷanto ye taṃ rosenti, te asambhinnakhattiyakule jātattā mahābalavatāya ceva mānathaddhatāya ca daḷhaṃ gahetvā paharati. Tadā te mahāsaddena rodantā “kena pahaṭā”ti vutte “vidhavāputtenā”ti vadanti. Atha kumāro cintesi “ime maṃ ‘vidhavāputto’ti abhiṇhaṃ vadanti, hotu, mama mātaraṃ pucchissāmī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ [V 6.0041] mātaraṃ pucchi “amma, ko mayhaṃ pitā”ti? Atha naṃ mātā “tāta, brāhmaṇo te pitā”ti vañcesi. So punadivasepi dārake paharanto “vidhavāputto”ti vutte “nanu brāhmaṇo me pitā”ti vatvā “brāhmaṇo kiṃ te hotī”ti vutte cintesi “ime maṃ, brāhmaṇo te kiṃ hotī’ti abhiṇhaṃ vadanti, mātā me idaṃ kāraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ na kathesi, sā attano manena me na kathessati, hotu, kathāpessāmi na”nti. So thaññaṃ pivanto thanaṃ dantehi ḍaṃsitvā “amma, me pitaraṃ kathehi, sace na kathessasi, thanaṃ te chindissāmī”ti āha. Sā puttaṃ vañcetuṃ asakkontī “tāta, tvaṃ mithilāyaṃ ariṭṭhajanakarañño putto, pitā te polajanakena mārito, ahaṃ taṃ anurakkhantī imaṃ nagaraṃ āgatā, ayaṃ brāhmaṇo maṃ bhaginiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā paṭijaggatī”ti kathesi. So taṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya “vidhavāputto”ti vuttepi na kujjhi.

Not long after, she gave birth to a son with golden-hued skin and gave him his grandfather's name, Mahājanaka-kumāra. As he grew up, while playing with other boys, if they provoked him, he would firmly grab and strike them, for he was born of an unbroken Khattiya lineage and possessed great strength and pride. Then, crying out loudly, when asked, "Who struck you?" they would say, "The widow's son struck me!" Then the prince thought, "They frequently call me 'the widow's son.' I will ask my mother." One day, he asked his mother, "Mother, who is my father?" Then his mother, wishing to protect him, deceived him, saying, "Dear, the brahmin is your father." The next day, while striking the boys, when he was called "widow's son," he retorted, "Is not the brahmin my father?" When they replied, "What is this brahmin to you? You and your mother came from another land," he then reflected, "My mother is not telling me the truth. I will make her speak." While nursing, he bit the nipple of her breast and said, "Mother, tell me who my father is. If you do not tell me, I will bite off your nipple." Unable to deceive her son any longer, she said, "Dear, you are the son of King Ariṭṭhajanaka of Mithilā. Your father was killed by Polajanaka. Protecting you, I came to this city. This brahmin, having placed me in the position of a sister, cares for me." Hearing this, from then on, even when called "widow's son," he no longer became angry.

So soḷasavassabbhantareyeva tayo vede ca sabbasippāni ca uggaṇhi[P 6.0034], soḷasavassikakāle pana uttamarūpadharo ahosi. Atha so “pitu santakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā mātaraṃ pucchi “amma, kiñci dhanaṃ te hatthe atthi, udāhu no, ahaṃ vohāraṃ katvā dhanaṃ uppādetvā [M 6.0043] pitu santakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ mātā āha – “tāta, nāhaṃ tucchahatthā āgatā, tayo me hatthe dhanasārā atthi, muttasāro, maṇisāro, vajirasāroti, tesu ekeko rajjaggahaṇappamāṇo, taṃ gahetvā rajjaṃ gaṇha, mā vohāraṃ karī”ti. “Amma, idampi dhanaṃ mayhameva upaḍḍhaṃ katvā dehi, taṃ pana gahetvā suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gantvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. So upaḍḍhaṃ āharāpetvā bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gamikehi vāṇijehi saddhiṃ nāvāya bhaṇḍaṃ āropetvā puna nivattitvā mātaraṃ vanditvā “amma, ahaṃ suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gamissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mātā āha – “tāta, samuddo nāma appasiddhiko bahuantarāyo, mā gaccha, rajjaggahaṇāya te dhanaṃ bahū”ti. So “gacchissāmeva ammā”ti mātaraṃ vanditvā gehā nikkhamma nāvaṃ abhiruhi.

Within sixteen years, he learned the three Vedas and all the arts. At the age of sixteen, he possessed a most excellent appearance. Then he thought, "I will take back my father's kingdom," and asked his mother, "Mother, do you have any wealth on hand? I will engage in trade, acquire wealth, and take my father's kingdom." His mother replied, "Dear son, I did not come empty-handed. I have three essential treasures: the essence of pearls, the essence of emeralds, and the essence of diamonds. Each one is sufficient to seize a kingdom. Take these and claim the kingdom; do not engage in trade." "Mother, give me half of this wealth. Taking it, I will go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, bring back much wealth, and then take the kingdom." He had half brought, prepared it as capital, and loaded the goods onto a ship with merchants bound for Suvaṇṇabhūmi. Then he returned, paid respects to his mother, and said, "Mother, I am going to Suvaṇṇabhūmi." His mother said, "Dear son, the ocean is vast and full of dangers; do not go. You have sufficient wealth to seize the kingdom." But he replied, "I will indeed go, Mother," and having paid respects to her, he left the house and boarded the ship with seven hundred others.

Taṃ divasameva polajanakassa sarīre rogo uppajji, anuṭṭhānaseyyaṃ sayi. Tadā satta jaṅghasatāni nāvaṃ abhiruhiṃsu. Nāvā sattadivasehi satta yojanasatāni gatā. Sā aticaṇḍavegena gantvā attānaṃ vahituṃ nāsakkhi, phalakāni bhinnāni, tato tato udakaṃ uggataṃ, nāvā samuddamajjhe nimuggā. Mahājanā rodanti paridevanti, nānādevatāyo namassanti. Mahāsatto pana neva rodati na paridevati, na devatāyo namassati, nāvāya pana nimujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā sappinā sakkharaṃ omadditvā kucchipūraṃ khāditvā dve maṭṭhakasāṭake telena temetvā daḷhaṃ nivāsetvā kūpakaṃ nissāya ṭhito nāvāya nimujjanasamaye kūpakaṃ abhiruhi. Mahājanā [V 6.0042] macchakacchapabhakkhā jātā, samantā udakaṃ aḍḍhūsabhamattaṃ lohitaṃ ahosi. Mahāsatto kūpakamatthake ṭhitova “imāya nāma disāya mithilanagara”nti disaṃ vavatthapetvā kūpakamatthakā uppatitvā macchakacchape atikkamma mahābalavatāya usabhamatthake pati. Taṃ divasameva polajanako kālamakāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya mahāsatto maṇivaṇṇāsu ūmīsu parivattanto suvaṇṇakkhandho viya samuddaṃ [P 6.0035] tarati. So yathā ekadivasaṃ, evaṃ sattāhaṃ tarati, “idāni puṇṇamīdivaso”ti velaṃ pana oloketvā loṇodakena mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathiko hoti.

On that very day, a disease arose in King Polajanaka’s body, and he lay on a bed from which he could not rise. At that time, seven hundred people had boarded the ship. The ship traveled seven hundred leagues in seven days. Moving with extreme speed, it could no longer bear its own weight; its planks broke apart, water gushed in from all sides, and the ship sank in the middle of the ocean. The great crowd of people wept and lamented, paying homage to various deities. The Great Being, however, neither wept nor lamented, nor did he pay homage to any deities. Knowing the ship was sinking, he mixed ghee with sugar and ate his fill, soaked two fine cloths in oil and fastened them tightly around him, and stood leaning against the mast. When the ship was sinking, he climbed to the top of the mast. The other people became food for fish and turtles, and the water all around for a distance of half an usabha became blood-red. The Great Being, standing atop the mast, determined the direction, thinking, 'In this direction lies the city of Mithilā.' Then, leaping from the top of the mast, he cleared the area where the fish and turtles were feeding and, by his great strength, landed at a distance of an usabha. That very day, King Polajanaka passed away. From then on, the Great Being, tossed among the jewel-colored waves, crossed the ocean like a golden mass. He swam thus for seven days. Observing the time and knowing, 'Today is the full moon day,' he rinsed his mouth with saltwater and undertook the Uposatha observance.

Tadā [M 6.0044] ca “ye mātupaṭṭhānādiguṇayuttā samudde marituṃ ananucchavikā sattā, te uddhārehī”ti catūhi lokapālehi maṇimekhalā nāma devadhītā samuddarakkhikā ṭhapitā hoti. Sā satta divasāni samuddaṃ na olokesi, dibbasampattiṃ anubhavantiyā kirassā sati pamuṭṭhā. “Devasamāgamaṃ gatā”tipi vadanti. Atha sā “ajja me sattamo divaso samuddaṃ anolokentiyā, kā nu kho pavattī”ti olokentī mahāsattaṃ disvā “sace mahājanakakumāro samudde nassissa, devasamāgamapavesanaṃ na labhissa”nti cintetvā mahāsattassa avidūre alaṅkatena sarīrena ākāse ṭhatvā mahāsattaṃ vīmaṃsamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, a celestial maiden named Maṇimekhalā had been appointed by the Four Great Kings as the guardian of the ocean with the command: 'Rescue those beings who, endowed with virtues such as devotion to their parents, are not fit to die in the ocean.' For seven days she did not look upon the ocean; it is said that while enjoying divine bliss, her mindfulness was lost. Some say she had gone to an assembly of the gods. Then, as she looked upon the ocean, thinking, 'Today is the seventh day that I have not looked upon the ocean; what is happening there?' she saw the Great Being. She thought, 'If Prince Mahājanaka perishes in the ocean, I will not be granted admission to the assembly of the gods.' Standing in the sky not far from the Great Being, with her body beautifully adorned and wishing to test him, she spoke the first verse:

123.

123.

“Koyaṃ majjhe samuddasmiṃ, apassaṃ tīramāyuhe;

Kaṃ tvaṃ atthavasaṃ ñatvā, evaṃ vāyamase bhusa”nti.

"Who is this in the middle of the ocean who strives without seeing a shore? Discerning what benefit do you so greatly exert yourself?"

Tattha apassaṃ tīramāyuheti tīraṃ apassantova āyūhati vīriyaṃ karoti.

Therein, 'striving without seeing a shore' means: even while not seeing the shore, he strives and makes an effort.

Atha mahāsatto tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “ajja me sattamo divaso samuddaṃ tarantassa, na me dutiyo satto diṭṭhapubbo, ko nu maṃ vadatī”ti ākāsaṃ olokento taṃ disvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, hearing her words, thought, 'Today is the seventh day that I have been crossing the ocean, and I have not seen another being before. Who is it that speaks to me?' Looking up into the sky, he saw her and spoke the second verse:

124.

124.

“Nisamma vattaṃ lokassa, vāyāmassa ca devate;

Tasmā majjhe samuddasmiṃ, apassaṃ tīramāyuhe”ti.
