Angered, the physician went home, told his wife, and said, 'My dear, I am treating his eye disease, but now he gives me no payment. What should we do?' She too became angry and said, 'We have no need of his property. Give him a specific preparation of medicine and make his eyes blind.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and went to the man and did so. Not long after, the man became blind. Because of this kamma, the eyes of both of them became blind.

Atha mahāsatto “mama mātāpitaro [P 6.0075] aññesu divasesu imāya velāya āgacchanti, idāni tesaṃ pavattiṃ na jānāmi, paṭimaggaṃ gamissāmī”ti cintetvā maggaṃ gantvā saddamakāsi. Te tassa saddaṃ sañjānitvā paṭisaddaṃ karitvā puttasinehena “tāta suvaṇṇasāma, idha paripantho atthi, mā āgamī”ti vadiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ “tena hi imaṃ laṭṭhikoṭiṃ gahetvā mama santikaṃ ethā”ti dīghalaṭṭhiṃ adāsi. Te laṭṭhikoṭiṃ gahetvā tassa santikaṃ āgamiṃsu. Atha ne “kena kāraṇena vo cakkhūni vinaṭṭhānī”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro āhaṃsu “tāta, mayaṃ deve vassante idha rukkhamūle vammikamatthake ṭhitā, tena kāraṇenā”ti. So mātāpitūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvāva aññāsi “tattha āsīvisena bhavitabbaṃ, tena kuddhena nāsāvāto vissaṭṭho bhavissatī”ti. So mātāpitaro disvā rodi ceva hasi ca. Atha naṃ te pucchiṃsu “kasmā, tāta, rodasi ceva hasasi cā”ti? Ammatātā, “tumhākaṃ daharakāleyeva evaṃ cakkhūni vinaṭṭhānī”ti rodiṃ, “idāni paṭijaggituṃ labhissāmī”ti hasiṃ. Ammatātā, tumhe mā cintayittha, ahaṃ vo paṭijaggissāmīti.

Then the Great Being thought, 'On other days, my parents come at this time, but now I do not know what has become of them; I will go to meet them on the path.' He went along the path and made a sound. Recognizing his voice, they called back, and out of love for their son, they said, 'Dear Suvaṇṇasāma, there is danger here; do not come!' Then he gave them the end of a long staff, saying, 'In that case, take hold of this end of the staff and come to me.' Taking hold of the end of the staff, they came to him. Then he asked them, 'For what reason have your eyes been destroyed?' His parents replied, 'Dear one, while it was raining, we stood here at the foot of a tree upon an anthill; that is the reason.' Hearing his parents' account, he understood at once, 'There must have been a venomous snake there, and being angered, it must have released its nasal breath.' Seeing his parents, he both wept and laughed. Then they asked him, 'Why, dear one, do you both weep and laugh?' 'Mother and father, I wept thinking, "Your eyes were destroyed while you were still young," and I laughed thinking, "Now I will have the opportunity to care for you." Mother and father, do not worry; I will look after you.'

So mātāpitaro assāsetvā assamapadaṃ ānetvā tesaṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu caṅkame paṇṇasālāyaṃ vaccaṭṭhāne passāvaṭṭhāne cāti [M 6.0093] sabbaṭṭhānesu rajjuke bandhi, tato paṭṭhāya te assamapade ṭhapetvā sayaṃ vanamūlaphalādīni āharitvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ ṭhapetvā pātova tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā ghaṭaṃ ādāya migasammatānadiṃ gantvā pānīyaparibhojanīyaṃ āharitvā upaṭṭhāpeti, dantakaṭṭhamukhodakādīni datvā madhuraphalāphalaṃ deti, tehi bhuñjitvā mukhe vikkhālite sayaṃ khāditvā mātāpitaro vanditvā migagaṇaparivuto phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ pāvisi. Pabbatapāde kinnaraparivāro phalāphalaṃ gahetvā sāyanhasamaye āgantvā ghaṭena udakaṃ āharitvā uṇhodakena tesaṃ yathāruci nhāpanaṃ pādadhovanaṃ vā katvā aṅgārakapallaṃ upanetvā hatthapāde sedetvā tesaṃ nisinnānaṃ phalāphalaṃ datvā khādāpetvā pariyosāne sayaṃ khāditvā sesakaṃ ṭhapesi. Iminā niyāmeneva mātāpitaro paṭijaggi.

Having comforted his parents, he led them to the hermitage. He tied guide-ropes for them in all places: their resting places by night and day, the walking path, the leaf-hut, and the places for defecation and urination. From then on, having settled them in the hermitage, he himself would bring wild roots and fruits and place them in the leaf-hut. Early in the morning, he would sweep their dwelling place, pay respects to his parents, take a water pot, and go to the Migasammatā River to fetch water for drinking and use. He would attend to them, giving them tooth-sticks and water for washing their mouths, and offer sweet fruits. After they had eaten and rinsed their mouths, he himself would eat, pay respects to his parents, and, surrounded by a herd of deer, enter the forest to gather fruits. At the foot of the mountain, with a retinue of kinnaras, he would gather fruits and return in the evening. Bringing water in a pot, he would bathe them with warm water according to their wish, or wash their feet. He would bring a charcoal brazier to warm their hands and feet, and give them fruits to eat as they sat. When they had finished, he himself would eat and set aside the remainder. In this very manner, he cared for his parents.

Tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasiyaṃ pīḷiyakkho nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. So migamaṃsalobhena mātaraṃ [V 6.0090] rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā sannaddhapañcāvudho himavantaṃ pavisitvā mige vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādanto [P 6.0076] migasammatānadiṃ patvā anupubbena sāmassa pānīyaggahaṇatitthaṃ sampatto migapadavalañjaṃ disvā maṇivaṇṇāhi sākhāhi koṭṭhakaṃ katvā dhanuṃ ādāya visapītaṃ saraṃ sannahitvā nilīnova acchi. Mahāsattopi sāyanhasamaye phalāphalaṃ āharitvā assamapade ṭhapetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā “pānīyaṃ āharissāmī”ti ghaṭaṃ gahetvā migagaṇaparivuto dvepi mige ekato katvā tesaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ pānīyaghaṭaṃ ṭhapetvā hatthena gahetvā nadītitthaṃ agamāsi. Rājā koṭṭhake ṭhitova taṃ tathā āgacchantaṃ disvā “mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ vicarantenapi manusso nāma na diṭṭhapubbo, devo nu kho esa nāgo nu kho, sace panāhaṃ etaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāmi. Devo ce bhavissati, ākāsaṃ uppatissati. Nāgo ce, bhūmiyaṃ pavisissati. Na kho panāhaṃ sabbakālaṃ himavanteyeva vicarissāmi, bārāṇasiṃ gamissāmi. Tatra maṃ pucchissanti ‘api nu kho te, mahārāja, himavante vasantena kiñci achariyaṃ diṭṭhapubba’nti? Tatrāhaṃ ‘evarūpo me satto diṭṭhapubbo’ti vakkhāmi. ‘Ko nāmeso’ti vutte sace ‘na jānāmī’ti vakkhāmi[M 6.0094], atha garahissanti maṃ, tasmā etaṃ vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā pucchissāmī”ti cintesi.

At that time, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Pīḷiyakkha ruled. Driven by a craving for venison, he entrusted the kingdom to his mother and, equipped with the fivefold weapons, entered the Himalayas. He hunted deer and ate their flesh, eventually reaching the Migasammatā River and coming to Sāma’s watering place. Seeing the deers' tracks, he constructed a blind with emerald-colored branches, took up his bow, fitted a poisoned arrow, and remained hidden. The Great Being, in the evening, having brought wild roots and fruits and placed them in the hermitage, paid respects to his parents. Saying, 'I will fetch water,' he took a water pot and, surrounded by a herd of deer, placed two deer side by side, set the water pot on their backs, and, holding it with his hand, went down to the riverbank. The king, standing in the blind, saw him approaching and thought, 'In all this time wandering like this, I have never seen a human being. Is this a deity or a nāga? If I approach and ask him, if he is a deity, he will fly into the sky; if a nāga, he will sink into the earth. But I will not stay in the Himalayas forever; I will return to Bārāṇasī. There, they will ask me, "Great King, while living in the Himalayas, have you seen any marvels?" Then I will say, "I have seen a creature like this." If they ask, "What is its name?" and I say, "I do not know," they will reproach me. Therefore, I will shoot him, weaken him, and then ask him.' Thus he reflected.

Atha tesu migesu paṭhamameva otaritvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā uttiṇṇesu bodhisatto uggahitavatto mahāthero viya saṇikaṃ otaritvā passaddhadaratho paccuttaritvā rattavākacīraṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ajinacammaṃ aṃse katvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ ukkhipitvā udakaṃ puñchitvā vāmaaṃsakūṭe ṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ kāle “idāni vijjhituṃ samayo”ti rājā visapītaṃ saraṃ ukkhipitvā mahāsattaṃ dakkhiṇapasse vijjhi, saro vāmapassena nikkhami. Tassa viddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā migagaṇā bhītā palāyiṃsu. Suvaṇṇasāmapaṇḍito pana viddhopi pānīyaghaṭaṃ yathā vā tathā vā anavasumbhitvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā saṇikaṃ otāretvā vālukaṃ viyūhitvā ṭhapetvā disaṃ vavatthapetvā mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānadisābhāgena sīsaṃ katvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇāya vālukāya [P 6.0077] suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya nipajjitvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā “imasmiṃ himavantappadese mama verī nāma natthi, mayhaṃ mātāpitūnañca verī nāma natthī”ti mukhena lohitaṃ chaḍḍetvā rājānaṃ adisvāva paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after the deer had first gone down, drunk water, and come up, the Bodhisatta, like a great elder well-trained in his duties, slowly went down, washed away his fatigue, and came back up. He donned one reddish bark robe and draped another over his shoulder, placed an antelope skin on his shoulder, lifted the water pot, filled it with water, and placed it on his left shoulder. At that time, thinking, 'Now is the time to shoot,' the king loosed a poisoned arrow and struck the Great Being in the right side; the arrow exited through the left side. Realizing he had been struck, the herd of deer fled in terror. However, Suvaṇṇasāma the Wise, even though wounded, did not let the water pot fall or tilt. Establishing mindfulness, he gently lowered it, cleared a space in the sand, and set it down. Having determined the direction, he lay down like a golden statue on the silver-white sand with his head toward the direction where his parents lived. Maintaining mindfulness, he thought, 'In this Himalayan region, there is no enemy of mine, nor any enemy of my mother and father.' Spitting blood from his mouth, and without seeing the king, he spoke this first verse:

296.

296.

“Ko nu maṃ usunā vijjhi, pamattaṃ udahārakaṃ;

Khattiyo brāhmaṇo vesso, ko maṃ viddhā nilīyasī”ti.

"Who has struck me with an arrow, while I was unmindful, fetching water? A kshatriya, a brahmin, or a vaishya—who is it that, having shot me, remains hidden?"

Tattha [V 6.0091] pamattanti mettābhāvanāya anupaṭṭhitasatiṃ. Idañhi so sandhāya tasmiṃ khaṇe attānaṃ pamattaṃ nāma akāsi. Viddhāti vijjhitvā.

In this context, 'unmindful' (pamattaṃ) means having mindfulness unestablished in the meditation on loving-kindness. It was with reference to this that he called himself unmindful at that moment. 'Viddhā' means 'having shot'.

Evañca pana vatvā puna attano sarīramaṃsassa abhakkhasammatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, to show that the flesh of his own body was considered inedible, he spoke the second verse:

297.

297.

“Na me maṃsāni khajjāni, cammenattho na vijjati;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, viddheyyaṃ maṃ amaññathā”ti.

"My flesh is not for eating, nor is my skin of any use; for what reason, then, did you think I should be shot?"

Dutiyagāthaṃ vatvā tameva nāmādivasena pucchanto āha –

Having spoken the second verse, he asked him about his name and so on, saying:

298.

298.

“Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ maṃ viddhā nilīyasī”ti.

"Who are you, and whose son? How are we to know you? My friend, being asked by me, please tell: why did you shoot me and then hide?"

Tattha [M 6.0095] amaññathāti ayaṃ puriso kena kāraṇena maṃ vijjhitabbanti amaññitthāti attho.

Therein, 'amaññathā' means he thought, 'For what reason should this person be shot?' This is the meaning.

Evañca pana vatvā tuṇhī ahosi. Taṃ sutvā rājā “ayaṃ mayā visapītena sallena vijjhitvā pātitopi neva maṃ akkosati na paribhāsati, mama hadayaṃ sambāhanto viya piyavacanena samudācarati, gacchissāmissa santika”nti cintetvā gantvā tassa santike ṭhitova dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken thus, he became silent. Hearing this, the king thought, 'Although he has been struck and felled by me with a poisoned arrow, he does not revile or insult me; he speaks with such pleasant words as if massaging my heart. I will go to him.' Thinking thus, he went and, standing near him, spoke two verses:

299.

299.

“Rājāhamasmi kāsīnaṃ, pīḷiyakkhoti maṃ vidū;

Lobhā raṭṭhaṃ pahitvāna, migamesaṃ carāmahaṃ.

"I am the king of the Kāsīs; they know me as Pīḷiyakkha. Having abandoned my kingdom out of greed, I wander in search of deer."

300.

300.

“Issatthe casmi kusalo, daḷhadhammoti vissuto;

Nāgopi me na mucceyya, āgato usupātana”nti.

"I am skilled in archery, renowned as a 'mighty archer'; even an elephant that has come within range of my arrow could not escape me."

Tattha rājāhamasmīti evaṃ kirassa vitakko ahosi “devāpi nāgāpi manussabhāsāya kathentiyeva, ahametaṃ devoti vā nāgoti vā manussoti vā na jānāmi. Sace kujjheyya, nāseyya [V 6.0092] maṃ, ‘rājā’ti vutte pana abhāyanto nāma natthī”ti. Tasmā attano rājabhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ paṭhamaṃ “rājāhamasmī”ti āha. Lobhāti migamaṃsalobhena. Migamesanti migaṃ esanto. Carāmahanti carāmi ahaṃ. Dutiyaṃ gāthaṃ pana attano [P 6.0078] balaṃ dīpetukāmo evamāha. Tattha issattheti dhanusippe. Daḷhadhammoti daḷhadhanuṃ sahassatthāmadhanuṃ oropetuñca āropetuñca samattho.

Herein, 'I am the king': it is said he thought, 'Deities and nāgas also speak in human language; I do not know if this is a deity, a nāga, or a human. If he were to get angry, he might destroy me; but when one says "I am a king," no one remains without fear.' Therefore, to make known his royal status, he first said, 'I am the king.' 'Lobhā' means out of greed for deer meat. 'Migamesaṃ' means searching for deer. 'Carāmahaṃ' means 'I wander.' He spoke the second verse wishing to illustrate his own power. Therein, 'issatthe' means in the art of archery. 'Daḷhadhamma' means one who is capable of stringing and unstringing a strong bow, one with the strength of a thousand men.

Iti rājā attano balaṃ vaṇṇetvā tassa nāmagottaṃ pucchanto āha –

Thus the king, having praised his own power, asked for Sāma’s name and clan, saying:

301.

301.

“Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ;

Pituno attano cāpi, nāmagottaṃ pavedayā”ti.

"Who are you, and whose son? How are we to know you? Declare the name and clan of both your father and yourself."

Tattha pavedayāti kathaya.

Herein, 'pavedayā' means 'declare'.

Taṃ [M 6.0096] sutvā mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ ‘devanāgakinnarakhattiyādīsu aññatarohamasmī’ti katheyyaṃ, saddaheyyeva esa, saccameva panassa kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā evamāha –

Hearing that, the Great Being thought, 'If I were to say, "I am one of the gods, nāgas, kinnaras, or khattiyas," he would surely believe me. However, it is fitting to tell him only the truth.' Reflecting thus, he said:

302.

302.

“Nesādaputto bhaddante, sāmo iti maṃ ñātayo;

Āmantayiṃsu jīvantaṃ, svajjevāhaṃ gato saye.

'O noble sir, I am the son of a hunter. My kinsmen called me Sāma while I was alive; but today I have come to this state and lie here [on the verge of death].'

303.

303.

“Viddhosmi puthusallena, savisena yathā migo;

Sakamhi lohite rāja, passa semi paripluto.

'O king, I am pierced by a broad, poisoned arrow, like a deer. Look at me, lying drenched in my own blood.'

304.

304.

“Paṭivāmagataṃ sallaṃ, passa dhimhāmi lohitaṃ;

Āturo tyānupucchāmi, kiṃ maṃ viddhā nilīyasi.

'See the arrow that has passed through from one side to the other; see how I spit out blood. Though in pain, I ask you: why did you shoot me and then hide?'

305.

305.

“Ajinamhi haññate dīpi, nāgo dantehi haññate;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, viddheyyaṃ maṃ amaññathā”ti.

'The leopard is killed for its skin, and the elephant for its tusks. For what reason, then, did you think I should be shot?'

Tattha jīvantanti maṃ ito pubbe jīvamānaṃ “ehi sāma, yāhi sāmā”ti ñātayo āmantayiṃsu. Svajjevāhaṃ gatoti so ahaṃ ajja evaṃ gato maraṇamukhe sampatto, paviṭṭhoti attho[V 6.0093]. Sayeti sayāmi. Pariplutoti nimuggo. Paṭivāmagatanti dakkhiṇapassena pavisitvā vāmapassena niggatanti attho. Passāti olokehi maṃ. Dhimhāmīti niṭṭhubhāmi, idaṃ so satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā avikampamānova lohitaṃ mukhena chaḍḍetvā āha. Āturo tyānupucchāmī”ti bāḷhagilāno hutvā ahaṃ taṃ anupucchāmi. Nilīyasīti etasmiṃ vanagumbe nilīno acchasi. Viddheyyanti vijjhitabbaṃ. Amaññathāti amaññittha.

In those verses, 'jīvantaṃ' means that before this, while I was alive, my relatives addressed me, saying, 'Come, Sāma, go, Sāma.' 'Svajjevāhaṃ gato' means 'I have come to this state today,' that is, 'I have reached the mouth of death.' 'Saye' means 'I lie down.' 'Paripluto' means 'submerged.' 'Paṭivāmagataṃ' means having entered from the right side and exited from the left side. 'Passa' means 'look at me.' 'Dhimhāmi' means 'I spit out.' He said this while maintaining mindfulness, without wavering, spitting out blood from his mouth. 'Āturo tyānupucchāmi' means 'being in great pain, I ask you.' 'Nilīyasi' means 'you remain hidden in this forest thicket.' 'Viddheyyaṃ' means 'worthy of being shot.' 'Amaññathā' means 'you thought.'

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā yathābhūtaṃ anācikkhitvā musāvādaṃ kathento āha –

Hearing his words, the king, not telling the truth but wishing to speak a falsehood, said:

306.

306.

“Migo upaṭṭhito āsi, āgato usupātanaṃ;

Taṃ disvā ubbijī sāma, tena kodho mamāvisī”ti.

'Sāma, a deer was nearby, having come within range of my arrow. Seeing you, it was startled; because of that, anger overcame me.'

Tattha āvisīti ajjhotthari. Tena kāraṇena me kodho uppannoti dīpeti.

Here, 'āvisī' means 'overwhelmed.' This indicates that for that reason anger arose in me.

Atha [M 6.0097][P 6.0079] naṃ mahāsatto “kiṃ vadesi, mahārāja, imasmiṃ himavante maṃ disvā palāyanamigo nāma natthī”ti vatvā āha –

Then the Great Being said to him, 'What are you saying, great king? In this Himālaya, there is no such thing as a deer that flees upon seeing me!' And he said:

307.

307.

“Yato sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ;

Na maṃ migā uttasanti, araññe sāpadānipi.

'Great king, since I can remember myself, and since I reached the age of discretion, the deer are not frightened of me, nor are even the beasts of prey in the forest.'

308.

308.

“Yato nidhiṃ parihariṃ, yato pattosmi yobbanaṃ;

Na maṃ migā uttasanti, araññe sāpadānipi.

'Great king, since I have worn the bark-fiber robe and since I reached maturity, the deer are not frightened of me, nor are even the beasts of prey in the forest.'

309.

309.

“Bhīrū kimpurisā rāja, pabbate gandhamādane;

Sammodamānā gacchāma, pabbatāni vanāni ca.

'O king, the kinnaras on Mount Gandhamādana are timid by nature; yet they wander with me, rejoicing together through the mountains and forests.'

310.

310.

“Na maṃ migā uttasanti, araññe sāpadānipi;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, utrāsanti migā mama”nti.

'The deer are not frightened of me, nor are even the beasts of prey in the forest; for what reason, then, would the deer be frightened of me?'

Tattha na maṃ migāti bho mahārāja, yato kālato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ attānaṃ sarāmi, yato kālato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ viññubhāvaṃ patto asmi bhavāmi, tato kālato paṭṭhāya maṃ disvā migā [V 6.0094] nāma na uttasanti. Sāpadānipīti vāḷamigāpi. Yato nidhinti yato kālato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ vākacīraṃ parihariṃ. Bhīrū kimpurisāti mahārāja, migā tāva tiṭṭhantu, kimpurisā nāma atibhīrukā honti. Ye imasmiṃ gandhamādanapabbate viharanti, tepi maṃ disvā na uttasanti, atha kho mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ sammodamānā gacchāma. Utrāsanti migā mamanti mamaṃ disvā migā utrāseyyuṃ, kena kāraṇena tvaṃ maṃ saddahāpessasīti dīpeti.

Here, 'na maṃ migā' means: O great king, from the time I remember myself, from the time I attained the state of understanding, from that time onward, no deer are frightened upon seeing me. 'Sāpadānipi' means even wild beasts. 'Yato nidhiṃ' means from the time I have worn the bark garment. 'Bhīrū kimpurisā' means: O great king, let the deer be, for the kiṃpurisas are extremely timid. Even those who dwell on this Mount Gandhamādana are not frightened upon seeing me; rather, we go rejoicing with one another. 'Utrāsanti migā mama' indicates: 'Upon seeing me, deer would be frightened—by what reason would you make me believe this?'

Taṃ sutvā rājā “mayā imaṃ niraparādhaṃ vijjhitvā musāvādo kathito, saccameva kathayissāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

Hearing this, the king thought, 'I have shot this innocent Sāma and spoken a falsehood. Now, it is only right to speak the truth,' and he said:

311.

311.

“Na taṃ tasa migo sāma, kiṃ tāhaṃ alikaṃ bhaṇe;

Kodhalobhābhibhūtāhaṃ, usuṃ te taṃ avassaji”nti.

'Sāma, the deer was not frightened of you. Why should I speak a lie to you? Overcome by anger and greed, I released that arrow at you.'

Tattha na taṃ tasāti na taṃ disvā migo tasa, na bhītoti attho. Kiṃ tāhanti kiṃ te evaṃ kalyāṇadassanassa santike ahaṃ alikaṃ bhaṇissāmi[M 6.0098]. Kodhalobhābhibhūtāhanti kodhena ca lobhena ca abhibhūto hutvā ahaṃ. So hi paṭhamameva migesu uppannena kodhena “mige vijjhissāmī”ti dhanuṃ āropetvā ṭhito pacchā bodhisattaṃ disvā tassa devatādīsu aññatarabhāvaṃ ajānanto “pucchissāmi na”nti lobhaṃ uppādesi, tasmā evamāha.

Here, 'na taṃ tasa' means no deer was frightened upon seeing you; that is, it was not afraid. 'Kiṃ tāhaṃ' means why should I speak a lie to you, in the presence of one so fair to behold? 'Kodhalobhābhibhūtāhaṃ' means I was overcome by both anger and greed. For at first, with anger having arisen towards the deer, he stood with his bow drawn, thinking, "I will shoot the deer." Afterwards, seeing the Bodhisatta and not knowing him to be a deva or some other such being, he developed greed, thinking, "I will ask him." Therefore, he spoke thus.

Evañca pana vatvā “nāyaṃ suvaṇṇasāmo imasmiṃ araññe ekakova vasissati, ñātakehipissa bhavitabbaṃ, pucchissāmi na”nti cintetvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, he thought, 'This Suvaṇṇasāma would not be living all alone in this forest; he must have parents or relatives. I will ask him again,' and he spoke the next verse:

312.

312.

“Kuto nu sāma āgamma, kassa vā pahito tuvaṃ;

‘Udahāro nadiṃ gaccha’, āgato migasammata”nti.

'Sāma, from where have you come? By whom were you sent, saying, "Go to the river to fetch water"? Why have you come to the Migasammata River?'

Tattha sāmāti mahāsattaṃ ālapati. Āgammāti kuto desā imaṃ vanaṃ āgamitvā “amhākaṃ udahāro udakaṃ āharituṃ nadiṃ gacchā”ti kassa vā pahitokena puggalena pesito hutvā tuvaṃ imaṃ migasammataṃ āgatoti attho.

In that verse, 'Sāma' is an address to the Great Being. 'Āgamma' means from what region did you come to this forest? 'Kassa vā pahito' means by what person were you sent, with the command, 'Go to the river to fetch water for us as our water-carrier,' and so have come here to this Migasammata? This is the meaning.

So [P 6.0080] tassa kathaṃ sutvā mahantaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ adhivāsetvā mukhena lohitaṃ chaḍḍetvā gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the Great Being endured the great, painful sensation, and spitting out blood from his mouth, he spoke this verse:

313.

313.

“Andhā [V 6.0095] mātāpitā mayhaṃ, te bharāmi brahāvane;

Tesāhaṃ udakāhāro, āgato migasammata”nti.

'My mother and father are blind; I support them in this vast forest. I am their water-carrier and have come to the Migasammata River for their sake.'

Tattha bharāmīti mūlaphalādīni āharitvā posemi.

In that verse, 'bharāmi' means I support them by bringing roots, fruits, and other things.

Evañca pana vatvā mahāsatto mātāpitaro ārabbha vilapanto āha –

Having said this, the Great Being, wishing to lament on account of the great virtues of his parents, said:

314.

314.

“Atthi nesaṃ usāmattaṃ, atha sāhassa jīvitaṃ;

Udakassa alābhena, maññe andhā marissare.

'They have only a small measure of food and life for only six more days. Without water, I think my blind parents will die.'

315.

315.

“Na me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, labbhā hi pumunā idaṃ;

Yañca ammaṃ na passāmi, taṃ me dukkhataraṃ ito.

'This [wound] is not so great a pain to me, for such pain must be borne by a man. But that I do not see my mother—that is a greater pain to me than this.'

316.

316.

“Na [M 6.0099] me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, labbhā hi pumunā idaṃ;

Yañca tātaṃ na passāmi, taṃ me dukkhataraṃ ito.

'This [wound] is not so great a pain to me, for such pain must be borne by a man. But that I do not see my father—that is a greater pain to me than this.'

317.

317.

“Sā nūna kapaṇā ammā, cirarattāya rucchati;

Aḍḍharatteva ratte vā, nadīva avasucchati.

'Surely now my poor mother will weep for a long time; like a river that dries up, she will waste away at midnight or in the last watch of the night.'

318.

318.

“So nūna kapaṇo tāto, cirarattāya rucchati;

Aḍḍharatteva ratte vā, nadīva avasucchati.

'Surely now my poor father will weep for a long time; like a river that dries up, he will waste away at midnight or in the last watch of the night.'

319.

319.

“Uṭṭhānapādacariyāya, pādasambāhanassa ca;

Sāma tātavilapantā, hiṇḍissanti brahāvane.

'Lacking the service of my rising to attend to them and the massaging of their feet, they will wander in the vast forest, lamenting, "O Sāma! O dear one!"'

320.

320.

Idampi dutiyaṃ sallaṃ, kampeti hadayaṃ mamaṃ;

Yañca andhe na passāmi, maññe hissāmi jīvita”nti.

'This is a second arrow that makes my heart tremble: that I cannot see my blind parents. Because of this, I think I shall lose my life.'

Tattha usāmattanti bhojanamattaṃ. “Usā”ti hi bhojanassa nāmaṃ tassa ca atthitāya. Sāhassa jīvitanti chadivasamattaṃ jīvitanti attho. Idaṃ āharitvā ṭhapitaṃ phalāphalaṃ sandhāyāha[V 6.0096]. Atha vā usāti usmā. Tenetaṃ dasseti – tesaṃ sarīre usmāmattaṃ atthi, atha mayā ābhatena phalāphalena sāhassa jīvitaṃ atthīti. Marissareti marissantīti maññāmi. Pumunāti purisena, evarūpañhi dukkhaṃ purisena labhitabbamevāti attho. Cirarattāya rucchatīti cirarattaṃ rodissati. Aḍḍharatte vāti majjhimaratte vā. Ratte vāti pacchimaratte vā. Avasucchatīti kunnadī viya sussissatīti attho. Uṭṭhānapādacariyāyāti mahārāja, ahaṃ rattimpi divāpi dve tayo vāre uṭṭhāya attano uṭṭhānavīriyena tesaṃ pādacariyaṃ karomi, hatthapāde sambāhāmi, idāni maṃ adisvā mamatthāya te parihīnacakkhukā “sāmatātā”ti vilapantā kaṇṭakehi vijjhiyamānā viya imasmiṃ [P 6.0081] vanappadese hiṇḍissanti vicarissantīti attho. Dutiyaṃ sallanti paṭhamaviddhavisapītasallato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena dukkhataraṃ idaṃ dutiyaṃ tesaṃ adassanasokasallaṃ.

Here, 'usāmattaṃ' means a measure of food. 'Usā' is indeed a name for food, and it refers to its presence there. 'Sāhassa jīvitaṃ' means life for a measure of six days. This is said with reference to the fruits and edibles that had been brought and stored. Alternatively, 'usā' means warmth. By this he shows: there is only a measure of warmth in their bodies, but with the fruits and edibles brought by me, there is life for six days. 'Marissare' means 'they will die,' I think. 'Pumunā' means by a man; for such pain is indeed to be experienced by a man. This is the meaning. 'Cirarattāya rucchati' means 'will weep for a long time.' 'Aḍḍharatte vā' means in the middle of the night. 'Ratte vā' means in the latter part of the night. 'Avasucchati' means will dry up like a small river. This is the meaning. 'Uṭṭhānapādacariyāya' means: O great king, day and night I rise two or three times and with my own effort I perform the service of attending to them; I massage their hands and feet. Now, not seeing me, for my sake, they with their failing eyesight, lamenting 'Dear Sāma!', will wander and roam about in this forest region as if pierced by thorns. This is the meaning. 'The second dart' means: this second dart, the arrow of grief from not seeing them, is a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times more painful than the first poison-smeared arrow.

Rājā [M 6.0100] tassa vilāpaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ accantaṃ brahmacārī dhamme ṭhito mātāpitaro bharati, idāni evaṃ dukkhappattopi tesaṃyeva vilapati, evaṃ guṇasampanne nāma mayā aparādho kato, kathaṃ nu kho imaṃ samassāseyya”nti cintetvā “niraye paccanakāle rajjaṃ kiṃ karissati, iminā paṭijaggitaniyāmenevassa mātāpitaro paṭijaggissāmi, imassa maraṇampi amaraṇaṃ viya bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā āha –

Hearing his lament, King Piliyakkha thought, 'This Sāma is indeed established in the Dhamma of the virtuous, which is the noble life, and supports his parents. Even now, having reached such suffering, he laments only for the sake of those parents. I have committed an offense against one so endowed with virtue. Therefore, I should comfort him.' Reflecting, 'What use is my kingship while I am suffering in hell? I will support his parents in the very same way that he did. If I support them thus, even if he dies, it will be as if he had not died.' Having made this resolution, he said:

321.

321.

“Mā bāḷhaṃ paridevesi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissaṃ te brahāvane.

‘Do not lament excessively, Sāma, fair to behold; I will become a servant and support them in the great forest.’

322.

322.

“Issatthe casmi kusalo, daḷhadhammoti vissuto;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissaṃ te brahāvane.

‘I am skilled in archery and renowned for my strong bow; I will become a servant and support them in the great forest.’

323.

323.

“Migānaṃ vighāsamanvesaṃ, vanamūlaphalāni ca;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissaṃ te brahāvane.

‘Searching for the leftovers of beasts, and the roots and fruits of the forest, I will become a servant and support them in the great forest.’

324.

324.

“Katamaṃ taṃ vanaṃ sāma, yattha mātāpitā tava;

Ahaṃ te tathā bharissaṃ, yathā te abharī tuva”nti.

‘Which forest is it, Sāma, where your parents are? I will support them in the same way that you supported them.’

Tattha bharissaṃ teti te tava mātāpitaro bharissāmi. Migānanti sīhādīnaṃ migānaṃ vighāsaṃ [V 6.0097] anvesanto. Idaṃ so “issatthe casmi kusaloti thūlathūle mige vadhitvā madhuramaṃsena tava mātāpitaro bharissāmī”ti vatvā “mā, mahārāja, amhe nissāya pāṇavadhaṃ karī”ti vutte evamāha. Yathā teti yathā tvaṃ te abhari, tathevāhampi bharissāmīti.

There, 'I will support them' means I will support your parents. 'Of beasts' means searching for the leftovers of beasts such as lions. He said this after having said, 'I am skilled in archery, and having killed large, stout animals, I will support your parents with sweet meat,' and upon being told, 'Great king, do not commit the taking of life for our sake.' 'Just as you' means just as you supported them, so too will I support them.

Athassa mahāsatto “sādhu, mahārāja, tena hi me mātāpitaro bharassū”ti vatvā maggaṃ ācikkhanto āha –

Hearing these words of King Piliyakkha, the Great Being said, ‘Good, great king, in that case, please support my parents.’ And wishing to indicate the path to him, he said:

325.

325.

“Ayaṃ ekapadī rāja, yoyaṃ ussīsake mama;

Ito gantvā aḍḍhakosaṃ, tattha nesaṃ agārakaṃ;

Yattha mātāpitā mayhaṃ, te bharassu ito gato”ti.

‘Here, O king, is a single-file path at my head. Go half a kosa from here, and there is their dwelling. Go from here to where my mother and father are and support them.’

Tattha ekapadīti ekapadamaggo. Ussīsaketi yo esa mama matthakaṭṭhāne. Aḍḍhakosanti aḍḍhakosantare.

There, 'ekapadī' means a single-file path. 'Ussīsake' means at the place of my head. 'Aḍḍhakosaṃ' means at a distance of half a league.

Evaṃ [M 6.0101] so tassa maggaṃ ācikkhitvā mātāpitūsu balavasinehena [P 6.0082] tathārūpaṃ vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā tesaṃ bharaṇatthāya añjaliṃ paggayha yācanto puna evamāha –

Having thus shown him the path, and enduring the painful feeling caused by the arrow due to his strong affection for his parents, he wished to beg him to support them with hands raised in reverence and spoke again thus:

326.

326.

“Namo te kāsirājatthu, namo te kāsivaḍḍhana;

Andhā mātāpitā mayhaṃ, te bharassu brahāvane.

‘Homage to you, O King of Kasi, homage to you, O Increaser of the Kasi realm; my mother and father are blind, support them in the great forest.’

327.

327.

“Añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi, kāsirāja namatthu te;

Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ mayhaṃ, vutto vajjāsi vandana”nti.

‘I raise my hands in reverence to you, O King of Kasi, homage to you! Having been requested by me, please convey my homage to my mother and father.’

Tattha vutto vajjāsīti “putto vo suvaṇṇasāmo nadītīrevisapītena sallena viddho rajatapaṭṭasadise vālukāpuline dakkhiṇapassena nipanno añjaliṃ paggayha tumhākaṃ pāde vandatī”ti evaṃ mahārāja, mayā vutto hutvā mātāpitūnaṃ me vandanaṃ vadeyyāsīti attho.

Here, 'vutto vajjāsi' means: 'Your son Suvaᅇᅇasāma, struck by a poisoned arrow on the bank of the Migasammatā river, lies on a sandbank resembling a silver slab, fallen on his right side, and with hands raised in reverence, pays homage to your feet.' Thus, O great king, having been requested by me, you should convey my homage to my parents—this is the meaning.

Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Mahāsattopi mātāpitūnaṃ vandanaṃ pesetvā visaññitaṃ pāpuṇi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

The king assented, saying, ‘Good, Suvaᅇᅇasāma, I will speak to your parents as you have requested.’ The Great Being, having sent his homage to his parents, then fell into unconsciousness. The Teacher, making this matter clear, said:

328.

328.

“Idaṃ [V 6.0098] vatvāna so sāmo, yuvā kalyāṇadassano;

Mucchito visavegena, visaññī samapajjathā”ti.

‘Having said this, that Sāma, a youth fair to behold, overcome by the force of the poison, became unconscious.’

Tattha samapajjathāti visaññī jāto.

There, 'samapajjatha' means he became unconscious.

So hi heṭṭhā ettakaṃ kathento nirassāso viya ahosi. Idāni panassa visavegena madditā bhavaṅgacittasantati hadayarūpaṃ nissāya pavatti, kathā pacchijji, mukhaṃ pihitaṃ, akkhīni nimīlitāni, hatthapādā thaddhabhāvaṃ pattā, sakalasarīraṃ lohitena makkhitaṃ. Rājā “ayaṃ idāneva mayā saddhiṃ kathesi, kiṃ nu kho”ti tassa assāsapassāse upadhāresi. Te pana niruddhā, sarīraṃ thaddhaṃ jātaṃ. So taṃ disvā “niruddho dāni sāmo”ti sokaṃ saddhāretuṃ asakkonto ubho hatthe matthake ṭhapetvā mahāsaddena paridevi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

For previously, while saying all this, he had become as if breathless. But now, crushed by the force of the poison, the stream of his life-continuum consciousness, which occurs dependent on the heart-base, [seemed to] cease; his speech was cut off, his mouth closed, his eyes shut, his hands and feet became rigid, and his entire body was smeared with blood. The king, thinking, 'Just now he was speaking with me—what has happened?' checked his in-and-out breathing. But it had ceased, and his body had become rigid. Seeing that Sāma's breathing had stopped, the king, unable to endure his grief, placed both hands on his head and lamented loudly, making the forest echo. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

329.

329.

“Sa rājā paridevesi, bahuṃ kāruññasañhitaṃ;

Ajarāmarohaṃ āsiṃ, ajjetaṃ ñāmi no pure;

Sāmaṃ kālaṅkataṃ disvā, natthi maccussa nāgamo.

‘That king lamented much, with great compassion: ‘Formerly, I thought I was ageless and deathless; but today I know—not before—seeing Sāma dead, that there is no such thing as the non-coming of death.’

330.

330.

“Yassu [M 6.0102] maṃ paṭimanteti, savisena samappito;

Svajja [P 6.0083] evaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsati.

‘He who was just now addressing me, though afflicted by the poisoned arrow—now, at this time, he says not a word to me.’

331.

331.

“Nirayaṃ nūna gacchāmi, ettha me natthi saṃsayo;

Tadā hi pakataṃ pāpaṃ, cirarattāya kibbisaṃ.

‘Surely I shall go to hell, of this I have no doubt; for I have committed a cruel evil deed, a misdeed that will last for a long time.’

332.

332.

“Bhavanti tassa vattāro, gāme kibbisakārako;

Araññe nimmanussamhi, ko maṃ vattumarahati.

‘In a village, there are those who would reproach a wrongdoer; but in this uninhabited forest, who is there to reproach me?’

333.

333.

“Sārayanti hi kammāni, gāme saṃgaccha māṇavā;

Araññe nimmanussamhi, ko nu maṃ sārayissatī”ti.

‘In a village, people gathered together would remind one of his deeds; but in this uninhabited forest, who indeed will remind me of my deeds?’

Tattha āsinti ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ ajarāmaromhīti saññī ahosiṃ. Ajjetanti ajja ahaṃ imaṃ sāmaṃ kālakataṃ disvā mamañceva aññesañca natthi maccussa nāgamoti taṃ maccussa āgamanaṃ [V 6.0099] ajja jānāmi, ito pubbe na jānāmīti vilapati. Svajja evaṃ gate kāleti yo savisena sallena samappito idāneva maṃ paṭimanteti, so ajja evaṃ gate kāle evaṃ maraṇakāle sampatte kiñci appamattakampi na bhāsati. Tadā hīti tasmiṃ khaṇe sāmaṃ vijjhantena mayā pāpaṃ kataṃ. Cirarattāya kibbisanti taṃ pana cirarattaṃ vipaccanasamatthaṃ dāruṇaṃ pharusaṃ.

Here, ‘āsiṃ’ means ‘I was of the view that I was ageless and deathless for so long.’ ‘Ajjetanti’ means he laments, 'Today, seeing this Sāma dead, I know the arrival of death—that for me and for others there is no escape from it—but before I did not know it.' ‘Svajja evaṃ gate kāle’ means he who just now spoke to me, though afflicted by the poisoned arrow, now, at this very hour when the time of death has arrived, says not even the slightest word. ‘Tadā hi’ means at that moment, an evil deed was done by me in shooting Sāma. ‘Cirarattāya kibbisaṃ’ means that cruel, harsh misdeed, capable of ripening for a long time.

Tassāti tassa evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ katvā vicarantassa. Vattāroti ninditāro bhavanti “kuhiṃ gāme kinti kibbisakārako”ti. Imasmiṃ pana araññe nimmanussamhi ko maṃ vattumarahati, sace hi bhaveyya, vadeyyāti vilapati. Sārayantīti gāme vā nigamādīsu vā saṃgaccha māṇavā tattha tattha bahū purisā sannipatitvā “ambho purisaghātaka, dāruṇaṃ te kammaṃ kataṃ, asukadaṇḍaṃ patto nāma tva”nti evaṃ kammāni sārenti codenti. Imasmiṃ pana nimmanusse araññe maṃ ko sārayissatīti attānaṃ codento vilapati.

‘Tassa’ means of one who wanders about after having committed such an evil deed. ‘Vattāro’ means there are those who censure him, saying, ‘Where in the village is that wrongdoer?’ But in this wilderness, devoid of humans, who is there to speak to me? If there were someone, they would speak—thus he laments. ‘Sārayanti’ means in a village or town, many people gather, and assembled there, they remind and accuse him of his deeds, saying, ‘Hey, murderer! You have done a cruel deed; you deserve such-and-such punishment!’ But in this wilderness, devoid of humans, who will remind me?—thus he accuses himself and laments.

Tadā bahusundarī nāma devadhītā gandhamādanavāsinī mahāsattassa sattame attabhāve mātubhūtapubbā. Sā puttasinehena bodhisattaṃ niccaṃ āvajjeti, taṃ divasaṃ pana dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamānā na taṃ āvajjeti. “Devasamāgamaṃ gatā”tipi vadantiyeva. Sā tassa visaññibhūtakāle “kiṃ [M 6.0103] nu kho me puttassa pavattī”ti āvajjamānā addasa “ayaṃ pīḷiyakkho nāma rājā mama puttaṃ visapītena sallena vijjhitvā migasammatānadītīre vālukāpuline ghātetvā mahantena saddena paridevati. Sacāhaṃ na gamissāmi, mama putto suvaṇṇasāmo ettheva marissati, raññopi hadayaṃ phalissati, sāmassa mātāpitaropi nirāhārā pānīyampi alabhantā sussitvā marissanti. Mayi pana gatāya rājā pānīyaghaṭaṃ ādāya tassa mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ gamissati, gantvā ca pana “putto vo mayā hato’ti kathessati. Evañca vatvā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā [P 6.0084] te puttassa santikaṃ ānayissati. Atha kho te ca ahañca saccakiriyaṃ karissāma, saccabalena sāmassa visaṃ vinassissati. Evaṃ me putto jīvitaṃ labhissati, mātāpitaro ca cakkhūni labhissanti, rājā ca sāmassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nagaraṃ gantvā mahādānaṃ datvā saggaparāyaṇo bhavissati, tasmā gacchāmahaṃ tatthā”ti. Sā gantvā migasammatānadītīre adissamānena kāyena ākāse ṭhatvā raññā saddhiṃ kathesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then there was a goddess named Bahusundarī, dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana, who had been the mother of the Great Being in his seventh existence. Out of love for her son, she constantly watched over the Bodhisatta. But on that day, enjoying divine bliss, she did not think of him. Some say she had gone to the assembly of the gods. When he was unconscious, she thought, “What is happening to my son?” Reflecting, she saw: “This King Pīḷiyakkha has struck my son with a poisoned arrow and, after shooting him on the sandbank by the Migasammatā River, he is wailing loudly. If I do not go, my son Suvaṇṇasāma will die right here, the king’s heart will break, and Sāma’s parents, deprived of food and water, will wither away and perish. But if I go, the king will take a water pot and go to his parents. Having gone, he will say, ‘I have killed your son.’ And having heard their words, he will bring them to his son. Then, they and I will perform an act of truth, and by the power of truth, Sāma’s poison will be destroyed. Thus, my son will recover his life, his parents will regain their sight, and the king, hearing Sāma’s Dhamma teaching, will return to the city, give great alms, and be destined for heaven. Therefore, I must go there.” She went and, with her body invisible, stood in the sky above the bank of the Migasammatā River and spoke with the king. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

334.

334.

“Sā devatā antarahitā, pabbate gandhamādane;

Raññova anukampāya, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

That deity, invisible, on Mount Gandhamādana, out of compassion for the king, spoke these verses:

335.

335.

“Āguṃ [V 6.0100] kira mahārāja, akari kammadukkaṭaṃ;

Adūsakā pitāputtā, tayo ekūsunā hatā.

“Indeed, great king, you have committed a wrong, a terrible deed; the innocent parents and son, three were slain by a single arrow.”

336.

336.

“Ehi taṃ anusikkhāmi, yathā te sugatī siyā;

Dhammenandhe vane posa, maññehaṃ sugatī tayā”ti.

“Come, let me instruct you, so that you may have a happy destiny; righteously nourish the blind ones in the forest, and I think you will attain a happy destiny.”

Tattha raññovāti raññoyeva. Āguṃ kirāti mahārāja, tvaṃ mahāparādhaṃ mahāpāpaṃ akari. Dukkaṭanti yaṃ kataṃ dukkaṭaṃ hoti, taṃ lāmakakammaṃ akari. Adūsakāti niddosā. Pitāputtāti mātā ca pitā ca putto ca ime tayo janā ekausunā hatā. Tasmiñhi hate tappaṭibaddhā tassa mātāpitaropi hatāva honti. Anusikkhāmīti sikkhāpemi anusāsāmi. Posāti sāmassa ṭhāne ṭhatvā sinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā sāmo viya te ubho andhe posehi. Maññehaṃ sugatī tayāti evaṃ tayā sugatiyeva gantabbā bhavissatīti ahaṃ maññāmi.

Herein, 'raññova' means 'rañño eva' (for the king). 'Āguṃ kira' means: 'Great king, you have committed a great offense, a great evil.' 'Dukkaṭaṃ' means: 'What is done is a misdeed; you have done a wicked deed.' 'Adūsakā' means blameless. 'Pitāputtā' means: mother, father, and son—these three people were slain by a single arrow. For when he is killed, his parents, who are dependent on him, are as good as killed. 'Anusikkhāmi' means: I teach, I instruct. 'Posa' means: 'Standing in Sāma's place, establishing affection, nourish both those blind ones as Sāma did.' 'Maññehaṃ sugatī tayā' means: 'I think that in this way a happy destiny will be reached by you.'

So [M 6.0104] devatāya vacanaṃ sutvā “ahaṃ kira tassa mātāpitaro posetvā saggaṃ gamissāmī”ti saddahitvā “kiṃ me rajjena, teyeva posessāmī”ti daḷhaṃ adhiṭṭhāya balavaparidevaṃ paridevanto sokaṃ tanukaṃ katvā “suvaṇṇasāmo mato bhavissatī”ti nānāpupphehi tassa sarīraṃ pūjetvā udakena siñcitvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā tena pūritaṃ udakaghaṭaṃ ādāya domanassappatto dakkhiṇadisābhimukho agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having heard the deity's words, believing, “Indeed, I will support his parents and go to heaven,” and firmly resolving, “What use is the kingdom to me? I myself will support them,” he wailed loudly, then lessened his grief. Thinking, “Suvaṇṇasāma must be dead,” he honored his body with various flowers, sprinkled it with water, circumambulated it three times, paid homage at the four places, took the water pot filled by him, and, overcome with sorrow, set off toward the south. The Teacher, revealing this matter, said:

337.

337.

“Sa rājā paridevitvā, bahuṃ kāruññasañhitaṃ;

Udakakumbhamādāya, pakkāmi dakkhiṇāmukho”ti.

“That king, having lamented much and piteously, taking a water pot, departed facing south.”

Pakatiyāpi [P 6.0085] mahāthāmo rājā pānīyaghaṭaṃ ādāya gacchanto assamapadaṃ koṭṭento viya pavisitvā dukūlapaṇḍitassa paṇṇasālādvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Dukūlapaṇḍito anto nisinnova tassa padasaddaṃ sutvā “nāyaṃ sāmassa padasaddo, kassa nu kho”ti pucchanto gāthādvayamāha –

The king, who was mighty by nature, carrying the water pot, entered the hermitage grounds with heavy steps and reached the door of the wise Dukūla's leaf hut. Dukūla, sitting inside, heard the sound of his footsteps and, realizing, “This is not the sound of Sāma's footsteps, whose could it be?” he spoke these two verses:

338.

338.

“Kassa nu eso padasaddo, manussasseva āgato;

Neso sāmassa nigghoso, ko nu tvamasi mārisa.

“Whose footstep sound is this, of a human being who has come? This is not Sāma’s sound; who are you, good sir?”

339.

339.

“Santañhi [V 6.0101] sāmo vajati, santaṃ pādāni neyati;

Neso sāmassa nigghoso, ko nu tvamasi mārisā”ti.

“For Sāma walks gently, he places his feet gently; this is not Sāma’s sound; who are you, good sir?”

Tattha manussassevāti nāyaṃ sīhabyagghadīpiyakkhanāgakinnarānaṃ, āgacchato pana manussassevāyaṃ padasaddo, neso sāmassāti. Santaṃ hīti upasamayuttaṃ eva. Vajatīti caṅkamati. Neyatīti patiṭṭhāpeti.

Herein, ‘manussasseva’ means: this is not the sound of a lion, tiger, leopard, yakkha, nāga, or kinnara; rather, this footstep sound is of an approaching human being. ‘Neso sāmassā’ means: this is not Sāma’s. ‘Santaṃ hi’ means: indeed, endowed with tranquility. ‘Vajati’ means: he walks. ‘Neyati’ means: he places [his feet].

Taṃ sutvā rājā “sacāhaṃ attano rājabhāvaṃ akathetvā ‘mayā tumhākaṃ putto mārito’ti vakkhāmi, ime kujjhitvā mayā saddhiṃ pharusaṃ kathessanti. Evaṃ me tesu kodho uppajjissati, atha ne viheṭhessāmi, taṃ mama akusalaṃ bhavissati, ‘rājā’ti pana vutte abhāyantā nāma natthi, tasmā rājabhāvaṃ tāva kathessāmī”ti cintetvā pānīyamāḷake pānīyaghaṭaṃ ṭhapetvā paṇṇasālādvāre ṭhatvā āha –

Hearing this, the king thought: 'If, without declaring my status as king, I say, "Your son has been killed by me," they will become angry and speak harshly to me. Then anger towards them will arise in me, and I might harm them; that would be unwholesome for me. But when "king" is spoken, there is no one who is not afraid; therefore, I will first declare my status as king.' Having thought thus, he placed the water pot on the water-stand, stood at the door of the leaf hut, and said:

340.

340.

“Rājāhamasmi [M 6.0105] kāsīnaṃ, pīḷiyakkhoti maṃ vidū;

Lobhā raṭṭhaṃ pahitvāna, migamesaṃ carāmahaṃ.

“I am the king of the Kasis; they know me as Pīḷiyakkha. Having left my kingdom out of greed [for venison], I wander seeking deer.”

341.

341.

“Issatthe casmi kusalo, daḷhadhammoti vissuto;

Nāgopi me na mucceyya, āgato usupātana”nti.

“I am skilled in archery, known as ‘Strong-bow.’ Even an elephant would not escape me once it comes within the range of my arrow.”

Dukūlapaṇḍitopi tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto āha –

Dukūla the Wise, exchanging friendly greetings with him, said:

342.

342.

“Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yaṃ idhatthi pavedaya.

“Welcome to you, great king; your coming is a happy one. You have arrived as a lord; make known whatever is here [that you desire].”

343.

343.

“Tindukāni piyālāni, madhuke kāsumāriyo;

Phalāni khuddakappāni, bhuñja rāja varaṃ varaṃ.

“Tinduka, piyāla, madhuka, and kāsumāri fruits—these small fruits are sweet as honey; enjoy them, O king, choosing the best ones.”

344.

344.

“Idampi pānīyaṃ sītaṃ, ābhataṃ girigabbharā;

Tato piva mahārāja, sace tvaṃ abhikaṅkhasī”ti;

“Here also is cool water, brought from a mountain gorge; drink from it, great king, if you so desire.”

Tassattho [V 6.0102][P 6.0086] sattigumbajātake (jā. 1.15.159 ādayo) kathito. Idha pana “girigabbharā”ti migasammataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sā hi nadī girigabbharā nikkhantattā “girigabbharā” tveva jātā.

The meaning of that is explained in the Sattigumba Jātaka (Jā. 1.15.159, etc.). But here, `girigabbharā` is said with reference to the Migasammatā river. For that river, having emerged from a mountain gorge, came to be known as `girigabbharā`.

Evaṃ tena paṭisanthāre kate rājā “putto vo mayā mārito”ti paṭhamameva vattuṃ ayuttaṃ, ajānanto viya kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā kathessāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

When a friendly welcome was thus offered by him, the king thought: 'It is not fitting to say at the very beginning, "Your son has been killed by me." I will start a conversation as if I do not know, and then I will speak.' And he said:

345.

345.

“Nālaṃ andhā vane daṭṭhuṃ, ko nu vo phalamāhari;

Anandhassevayaṃ sammā, nivāpo mayha khāyatī”ti.

“Being blind, you are unable to see anything in the forest; who then brought you fruit? This provision, properly gathered, appears to me to be the work of one who is not blind.”

Tattha nālanti tumhe andhā imasmiṃ vane kiñci daṭṭhuṃ na samatthā. Ko nu vo phalamāharīti ko nu tumhākaṃ imāni phalāphalāni āhari. Nivāpoti ayaṃ sammā nayena upāyena kāraṇena kato khāditabbayuttakānaṃ parisuddhānaṃ phalāphalānaṃ nivāpo sannicayo anandhassa viya mayhaṃ khāyati paññāyati upaṭṭhāti.

Herein, ‘nālaṃ’ means: you, being blind, are not able to see anything in this forest. ‘Ko nu vo phalamāhari’ means: who then brought you these various fruits? ‘Nivāpo’ means: this provision, a collection of pure and edible fruits, made properly by the right method, means, and reason, appears, is manifest, and presents itself to me as if [gathered] by one who is not blind.

Taṃ sutvā dukūlapaṇḍito “mahārāja, na mayaṃ phalāphalāni āharāma, putto pana no āharatī”ti dassento gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, Dukūla the Wise, showing: 'Great king, we do not bring these various fruits, but our son does,' spoke two verses:

346.

346.

“Daharo [M 6.0106] yuvā nātibrahā, sāmo kalyāṇadassano;

Dīghassa kesā asitā, atho sūnaggavellitā.

“A lad, a youth, not too tall, Sāma of lovely appearance; his hair is long and black, and curled at the tips.”

347.

347.

“So have phalamāharitvā, ito ādāya kamaṇḍaluṃ;

Nadiṃ gato udahāro, maññe na dūramāgato”ti.

“Indeed, having brought the fruit and taken the water pot from here, he has gone to the river to fetch water; I think he is not far off [from returning].”

Tattha nātibrahāti nātidīgho nātirasso. Sūnaggavellitāti sūnasaṅkhātāya maṃsakoṭṭanapotthaniyā aggaṃ viya vinatā. Kamaṇḍalunti ghaṭaṃ. Na dūramāgatoti idāni na dūraṃ āgato, āsannaṭṭhānaṃ āgato bhavissatīti maññāmīti attho.

Herein, ‘nātibrahā’ means not too tall, not too short. ‘Sūnaggavellitā’ means bent like the tip of a meat-chopping block called a ‘sūna’. ‘Kamaṇḍalu’ means a pot. ‘Na dūramāgato’ means: he has not gone far now; I think he will have come to a nearby place—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā rājā āha –

Hearing that, the king said:

348.

348.

“Ahaṃ [V 6.0103] taṃ avadhiṃ sāmaṃ, yo tuyhaṃ paricārako;

Yaṃ kumāraṃ pavedetha, sāmaṃ kalyāṇadassanaṃ.

“I am the one who killed Sāma, your attendant; the youth whom you describe, Sāma of lovely appearance.”

349.

349.

“Dīghassa kesā asitā, atho sūnaggavellitā;

Tesu lohitalittesu, seti sāmo mahā hato”ti.

“His hair is long and black, with the ends well-curled; with his body smeared with blood, Sāma lies there, slain by me.”

Tattha avadhinti visapītena sarena vijjhitvā māresiṃ. Pavedethāti kathetha. Setīti migasammatānadītīre vālukāpuline sayati.

Herein, ‘avadhiṃ’ means: I killed him by piercing him with a poison-tipped arrow. ‘Pavedetha’ means: you speak of. ‘Seti’ means: he lies on a sandbank on the bank of the Migasammatā river.

Dukūlapaṇḍitassa pana avidūre pārikāya paṇṇasālā hoti. Sā tattha nisinnāva rañño vacanaṃ sutvā taṃ pavattiṃ sotukāmā [P 6.0087] attano paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā rajjukasaññāya dukūlapaṇḍitassa santikaṃ gantvā āha –

Now, not far from Dukūla the Wise was the leaf hut of Pārikā. While sitting there, she heard the king’s words and, desiring to hear the news, came out from her leaf hut. Guided by a cord, she approached Dukūla the Wise and said:

350.

350.

“Kena dukūla mantesi, ‘hato sāmo’ti vādinā;

‘Hato sāmo’ti sutvāna, hadayaṃ me pavedhati.

“With whom, Dukūla, are you conversing, with one who says, ‘Sāma is slain’? Hearing that Sāma is slain, my heart trembles.”

351.

351.

“Assatthasseva taruṇaṃ, pavāḷaṃ māluteritaṃ;

‘Hato sāmo’ti sutvāna, hadayaṃ me pavedhatī”ti.

“Like a tender shoot of the Assattha tree stirred by the wind, my heart trembles on hearing that Sāma is slain.”

Tattha vādināti “mayā sāmo hato”ti vadantena. Pavāḷanti pallavaṃ. Māluteritanti vātena pahaṭaṃ.

Herein, ‘vādinā’ means: by one who says, ‘Sāma has been killed by me.’ ‘Pavāḷa’ means: a sprout. ‘Māluterita’ means: struck by the wind.

Dukūlapaṇḍito [M 6.0107] ovadanto āha –

Dukūla the Wise, advising her, said:

352.

352.

“Pārike kāsirājāyaṃ, so sāmaṃ migasammate;

Kodhasā usunā vijjhi, tassa mā pāpamicchimhā”ti.

“O Pārikā, this is the king of Kāsi. He pierced Sāma with an arrow by the Migasammatā, out of anger [at the deer]. Let us not wish him any evil.”

Tattha migasammateti migasammatānadītīre. Kodhasāti migesu uppannena kodhena. Mā pāpamicchimhāti tassa mayaṃ ubhopi pāpaṃ mā icchimhā.

Herein, ‘migasammate’ means: on the bank of the Migasammatā river. ‘Kodhasā’ means: with anger that arose on account of the deer. ‘Mā pāpamicchimhā’ means: let neither of us wish evil for him.

Puna [V 6.0104] pārikā āha –

Again, Pārikā said:

353.

353.

“Kicchā laddho piyo putto, yo andhe abharī vane;

Taṃ ekaputtaṃ ghātimhi, kathaṃ cittaṃ na kopaye”ti.

“Our beloved son, obtained with difficulty, who supported us blind ones in the forest; with that only son slain, how could the heart not be enraged?”

Tattha ghātimhīti ghātake.

Herein, ‘ghātimhi’ means: towards the killer.

Dukūlapaṇḍito āha –

Dukūla the Wise said:

354.

354.

“Kicchā laddho piyo putto, yo andhe abharī vane;

Taṃ ekaputtaṃ ghātimhi, akkodhaṃ āhu paṇḍitā”ti.

“A beloved son, obtained with difficulty, who supported us blind ones in the forest; towards the killer of that only son, the wise recommend non-anger.”

Tattha akkodhanti kodho nāma nirayasaṃvattaniko, tasmā taṃ kodhaṃ akatvā puttaghātakamhi akkodho eva kattabboti paṇḍitā āhu kathenti.

Herein, the word ‘akkodha’ means: anger is indeed conducive to rebirth in hell; therefore, the wise say and declare that, without giving rise to such anger, one should practice non-anger even toward the slayer of one's own son.

Evañca pana vatvā te ubhohi hatthehi uraṃ paharitvā mahāsattassa guṇe vaṇṇetvā bhusaṃ parideviṃsu. Atha ne rājā samassāsento āha –

Having spoken thus, both of them struck their breasts with their hands and, praising the virtues of the Great Being, they lamented and wailed intensely. Then the king, wishing to console them, spoke these verses:

355.

355.

“Mā bāḷhaṃ paridevetha, ‘hato sāmo’ti vādinā;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissāmi brahāvane.

“Do not lament so excessively to me, the one who says, ‘Sāma is slain.’ I will become your servant and support you in this great forest.

356.

356.

“Issatthe casmi kusalo, daḷhadhammoti vissuto;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissāmi brahāvane.

“I am skilled in archery and renowned as a powerful bowman. I will become your servant and support you in this great forest.

357.

357.

“Migānaṃ vighāsamanvesaṃ, vanamūlaphalāni ca;

Ahaṃ kammakaro hutvā, bharissāmi brahāvane”ti.

“Seeking out the food of wild beasts and the roots and fruits of the forest, I will become your servant and support you in this great forest.”

Tattha [P 6.0088] vādināti tumhe “sāmo hato”ti vadantena mayā saddhiṃ “tayā no evaṃ guṇasampanno putto mārito, idāni ko amhe bharissatī”tiādīni [M 6.0108] vatvā mā bāḷhaṃ paridevetha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ kammakaro hutvā sāmo viya tumhe bharissāmīti.

Herein, the word ‘vādinā’ means: do not lament so greatly toward me—the one who speaks thus, ‘Sāma is slain’—by saying such things as, ‘Our son, so endowed with virtue, has been killed by you; now who will support us?’ I will become your servant and support you just as Sāma did.

Evaṃ [V 6.0105] rājā “tumhe mā cintayittha, na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, ahaṃ vo yāvajīvaṃ bharissāmī”ti te assāsesi. Te tena saddhiṃ sallapantā āhaṃsu –

Thus the king reassured them, saying, “Do not worry. I have no need for my kingdom. I will support you for as long as you live.” Conversing with him, they said:

358.

358.

“Nesa dhammo mahārāja, netaṃ amhesu kappati;

Rājā tvamasi amhākaṃ, pāde vandāma te maya”nti.

“This is not the proper way, O great king; this is not suitable for us. You are our king; we bow at your feet.”

Tattha dhammoti sabhāvo kāraṇaṃ vā. Netaṃ amhesu kappatīti etaṃ tava kammakaraṇaṃ amhesu na kappati na sobhati. “Pāde vandāma te maya”nti idaṃ pana te pabbajitaliṅge ṭhitāpi puttasokena samabbhāhatāya ceva nihatamānatāya ca vadiṃsu. “Rañño vissāsaṃ uppādetuṃ evamāhaṃsū”tipi vadanti.

Herein, ‘dhamma’ refers to nature or reason. ‘Netaṃ amhesu kappati’ means: this service of yours toward us is not fitting, nor is it appropriate. As for ‘Pāde vandāma te mayaṃ,’ they spoke thus—even though established in the state of renouncers—because they were overwhelmed by grief for their son and because their pride was completely humbled. Some teachers also say they spoke thus to inspire trust in the king.

Taṃ sutvā rājā ativiya tussitvā “aho acchariyaṃ, evaṃ dosakārake nāma mayi pharusavacanamattampi natthi, paggaṇhantiyeva mama”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king was exceedingly delighted and, reflecting, “Oh, how wonderful! Toward me, who has committed such a wrong, they do not speak even a single harsh word; they only speak in praise of me,” he spoke this verse:

359.

359.

“Dhammaṃ nesādā bhaṇatha, katā apacitī tayā;

Pitā tvamasi amhākaṃ, mātā tvamasi pārike”ti.

“You speak righteously, O forest-dwellers; reverence has been shown by you. You, O sage, are my father, and you, Pārikā, are my mother.”

Tattha tayāti ekekaṃ vadanto evamāha. Pitāti dukūlapaṇḍita, ajja paṭṭhāya tvaṃ mayhaṃ pituṭṭhāne tiṭṭha, amma pārike, tvampi me mātuṭṭhāne tiṭṭha, ahaṃ pana vo puttassa sāmassa ṭhāne ṭhatvā pādadhovanādīni sabbakiccāni karissāmi, maṃ rājāti asallakkhetvā sāmoti sallakkhethāti.

Herein, ‘tayā’ is said while addressing each one individually. ‘Pitā’ refers to the wise Dukūla: ‘From this day forward, you shall stand in the place of my father.’ ‘Amma Pārike’: ‘You too shall stand in the place of my mother.’ ‘I, for my part, will stand in the place of your son Sāma and perform all your needs, such as washing your feet. Do not regard me as a king, but regard me only as Sāma.’

Te añjaliṃ paggayha vanditvā “mahārāja, tava amhākaṃ kammakaraṇakiccaṃ natthi, apica kho pana laṭṭhikoṭiyā no gahetvā ānetvā sāmaṃ dassehī”ti yācantā gāthādvayamāhaṃsu –

They raised their joined hands in reverence and, bowing, said: “Great king, there is no need for you to serve us. However, please take us by the tip of a staff and, leading us there, show us Sāma.” Pleading thus, they spoke two verses:

360.

360.

“Namo te kāsirājatthu, namo te kāsivaḍḍhana;

Añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāma, yāva sāmānupāpaya.

“Homage to you, O King of Kāsi; homage to you, O Increaser of the Kāsi realm. We raise our joined hands to you; please lead us to Sāma.

361.

361.

“Tassa [V 6.0106][M 6.0109] pāde samajjantā, mukhañca bhujadassanaṃ;

Saṃsumbhamānā attānaṃ, kālamāgamayāmase”ti.

“Stroking his feet, his face, and his beautiful arms, and striking our own bodies in grief, we shall await the time of our death.”

Tattha yāva sāmānupāpayāti yāva sāmo yattha, tattha amhe anupāpaya. Bhujadassananti [P 6.0089] kalyāṇadassanaṃ abhirūpaṃ. Saṃsumbhamānāti pothentā. Kālamāgamayāmaseti kālakiriyaṃ āgamessāma.

Herein, ‘yāva sāmānupāpaya’ means ‘bring us to wherever Sāma is.’ ‘Bhujadassanaṃ’ means ‘of beautiful and handsome appearance.’ ‘Saṃsumbhamānā’ means ‘striking or beating.’ ‘Kālamāgamayāmase’ means ‘we will await the end of our lives.’

Tesaṃ evaṃ kathentānaññeva sūriyo atthaṅgato. Atha rājā “sacāhaṃ idāneva ime tattha nessāmi, taṃ disvāva nesaṃ hadayaṃ phalissati, iti tiṇṇampi etesaṃ matakāle ahaṃ niraye uppajjantoyeva nāma, tasmā tesaṃ gantuṃ na dassāmī”ti cintetvā catasso gāthāyo ajjhabhāsi –

While they were conversing in this manner, the sun set. Then the king thought: “If I take them there at this very moment, their hearts will surely break upon seeing him. If these three should die, I will certainly be reborn in hell. Therefore, I will not allow them to go now.” Reflecting thus, he spoke four verses:

362.

362.

“Brahā vāḷamigākiṇṇaṃ, ākāsantaṃva dissati;

Yattha sāmo hato seti, candova patito chamā.

“Vast and teeming with wild beasts, the forest appears like the very end of the sky; where Sāma lies slain, like the moon fallen to the earth.

363.

363.

“Brahā vāḷamigākiṇṇaṃ, ākāsantaṃva dissati;

Yattha sāmo hato seti, sūriyova patito chamā.

“Vast and teeming with wild beasts, it appears like the very end of the sky; where Sāma lies slain, like the sun fallen to the earth.

364.

364.

“Brahā vāḷamigākiṇṇaṃ, ākāsantaṃva dissati;

Yattha sāmo hato seti, paṃsunā patikunthito.

“Vast and teeming with wild beasts, it appears like the end of the sky; where Sāma lies slain, covered all over with dust.

365.

365.

“Brahā vāḷamigākiṇṇaṃ, ākāsantaṃva dissati;

Yattha sāmo hato seti, idheva vasathassame”ti.

“Vast and teeming with wild beasts, it appears like the end of the sky; where Sāma lies slain. Therefore, stay right here in this hermitage.”

Tattha brahāti accuggataṃ. Ākāsantaṃvāti etaṃ vanaṃ ākāsassa anto viya hutvā dissati. Atha vā ākāsantanti ākāsamānaṃ, pakāsamānanti attho. Chamāti chamāyaṃ, pathaviyanti attho. “Chama”ntipi pāṭho, pathaviṃ patito viyāti attho. Patikunthitoti parikiṇṇo, paliveṭhitoti attho.

Here, 'brahā' means 'exceedingly high.' 'Ākāsantaṃva' means 'this forest appears as if it were the limit of the sky.' Alternatively, 'ākāsantaṃ' means 'shining,' that is, 'radiant.' 'Chamā' means 'on the earth,' that is, 'on the ground.' There is also the reading 'chama,' meaning 'as if fallen to the earth.' 'Patikunthito' means 'strewn over,' that is, 'enveloped.'

Atha [M 6.0110] te attano vāḷamigabhayābhāvaṃ dassetuṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then, to demonstrate their total lack of fear toward wild beasts, they spoke this verse:

366.

366.

“Yadi [V 6.0107] tattha sahassāni, satāni niyutāni ca;

Nevamhākaṃ bhayaṃ koci, vane vāḷesu vijjatī”ti.

“Even if there were thousands, hundreds, or myriads of them, no fear whatsoever of wild beasts exists for us in this forest.”

Tattha kocīti imasmiṃ vane katthaci ekasmiṃ padesepi amhākaṃ vāḷesu bhayaṃ nāma natthi.

Herein, ‘koci’ means ‘even in any single part of this forest, we have no fear of wild beasts.’

Rājā te paṭibāhituṃ asakkonto hatthesu gahetvā tattha nesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

The king, being unable to prevent them, took them by their hands and led them there. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

367.

367.

“Tato andhānamādāya, kāsirājā brahāvane;

Hatthe gahetvā pakkāmi, yattha sāmo hato ahū”ti.

“Then the King of Kāsi, taking the blind ones by the hand in that great forest, proceeded to where Sāma had been slain.”

Tattha [P 6.0090] tatoti tadā. Andhānanti andhe. Ahūti ahosi. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne so nipanno, tattha nesīti attho.

Herein, ‘tato’ means ‘at that time.’ ‘Andhānaṃ’ means ‘the blind ones.’ ‘Ahū’ means ‘was.’ ‘Yattha’ means ‘to the place where he lay; he led them there.’

So ānetvā ca pana sāmassa santike ṭhapetvā “ayaṃ vo putto”ti ācikkhi. Athassa pitā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā mātā pāde gahetvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā nisīditvā vilapiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having brought them and placed them near Sāma, the king announced, “This is your son.” Then his father lifted the boy's head, and his mother took hold of his feet, placed them on her lap, and as they sat there, they lamented. To reveal this matter, the Teacher said:

368.

368.

“Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Apaviddhaṃ brahāraññe, candaṃva patitaṃ chamā.

“Seeing Sāma fallen, their dear son covered in dust, cast away in the great forest like the moon fallen to the earth—

369.

369.

“Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Apaviddhaṃ brahāraññe, sūriyaṃva patitaṃ chamā.

“Seeing Sāma fallen, their dear son covered in dust, cast away in the great forest like the sun fallen to the earth, they wailed with a loud voice.”

370.

370.

“Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Apaviddhaṃ brahāraññe, kalūnaṃ paridevayuṃ.

Seeing Sāma fallen, their dear son smeared with dust, cast away in the great forest, they lamented piteously.

371.

371.

“Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Bāhā paggayha pakkanduṃ, ‘adhammo kira bho’iti.

"Seeing Sāma fallen, their dear son covered in dust, they stretched out their arms and cried out, 'Surely this is unrighteous, indeed!'

372.

372.

“Bāḷhaṃ [V 6.0108] kho tvaṃ pamattosi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Yo ajjevaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsasi.

Surely you are very heedless, Sāma, fair to behold, that at such a time as this, you speak not a word to me.

373.

373.

“Bāḷhaṃ [M 6.0111] kho tvaṃ padittosi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Yo ajjevaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsasi.

Surely you are greatly inflamed, Sāma, fair to behold, who at such a time as this speak not a word to me.

374.

374.

“Bāḷhaṃ kho tvaṃ pakuddhosi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Yo ajjevaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsati.

"Surely you are very angry, Sāma, fair to behold, that when things have come to this, he speaks not a word to me.

375.

375.

“Bāḷhaṃ kho tvaṃ pasuttosi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Yo ajjevaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsasi.

"Surely you are deeply asleep, Sāma, fair to behold, who at such a time as this speak not a word to me.

376.

376.

“Bāḷhaṃ kho tvaṃ vimanosi, sāma kalyāṇadassana;

Yo ajjevaṃ gate kāle, na kiñci mabhibhāsasi.

"Surely you are greatly distressed, Sāma, fair to behold, who at such a time as this speak not a word to me.

377.

377.

“Jaṭaṃ valinaṃ paṃsugataṃ, kodāni saṇṭhapessati;

Sāmo ayaṃ kālakato, andhānaṃ paricārako.

Who now will arrange our matted, tangled, and dust-covered hair? This Sāma is dead, the attendant of the blind.

378.

378.

“Ko me sammajjamādāya, sammajjissati assamaṃ;

Sāmo ayaṃ kālakato, andhānaṃ paricārako.

Who, taking a broom, will sweep the hermitage for me? This Sāma is dead, the attendant of the blind.

379.

379.

“Kodāni nhāpayissati, sītenuṇhodakena ca;

Sāmo ayaṃ kālakato, andhānaṃ paricārako.

Who now will wash us with cool and warm water? This Sāma has passed away, the attendant of the blind.

380.

380.

“Kodāni [P 6.0091] bhojayissati, vanamūlaphalāni ca;

Sāmo ayaṃ kālakato, andhānaṃ paricārako”ti.

Who now will feed us with forest roots and fruits? This Sāma is dead, the attendant of the blind.

Tattha apaviddhanti raññā niratthakaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Adhammo kira bho itīti ayuttaṃ kira bho, ajja imasmiṃ loke vattati. Pamattoti tikhiṇasuraṃ pivitvā viya matto pamatto pamādaṃ āpanno. Padittoti dappito. “Pakuddhosi vimanosī”ti sabbaṃ vilāpavasena bhaṇanti. Jaṭanti tāta[V 6.0109], amhākaṃ jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ. Valinaṃ paṃsugatanti yadā ākulaṃ malaggahitaṃ bhavissati. Kodānīti idāni ko saṇṭhapessati, sodhetvā ujuṃ karissatīti.

Here, 'abandoned' means discarded by the king as useless. 'This is unjust, O lord!' means, 'O lord, what is improper now prevails in this world.' 'Heedless' means heedless, having fallen into negligence, as if intoxicated from drinking strong liquor. 'Inflamed' means proud. 'Agitated' and 'distressed'—all this is spoken in the manner of lamentation. 'Matted hair'—O dear, our matted cluster of hair. 'Wrinkled and covered in dust'—when it becomes tangled and seized by dirt. 'Now who'—who will now set it in order, clean and straighten it?

Athassa mātā bahuṃ vilapitvā tassa ure hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā santāpaṃ upadhārentī “puttassa me santāpo pavattatiyeva, visavegena visaññitaṃ āpanno bhavissati, nibbisabhāvatthāya cassa saccakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā saccakiriyamakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then his mother, after much lamentation, placed her hand on his chest and, feeling for warmth, thought, "The warmth of my son still remains; he must have been rendered unconscious by the power of the poison. For his sake, to make him free from poison, I shall perform an act of truth." Thinking thus, she performed an act of truth. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

381.

381.

“Disvāna [M 6.0112] patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Aṭṭitā puttasokena, mātā saccaṃ abhāsatha.

Seeing Sāma fallen, her dear son smeared with dust, distraught with grief for her son, the mother spoke the truth.

382.

382.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, dhammacārī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly one who lived righteously; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

383.

383.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, brahmacārī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly one who lived a holy life; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

384.

384.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, saccavādī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly a speaker of truth; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

385.

385.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, mātāpettibharo ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was one who supported his mother and father; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

386.

386.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyiko;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma revered the elders in his family; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

387.

387.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, pāṇā piyataro mama;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma is dearer to me than life itself; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

388.

388.

“Yaṃ kiñcitthi kataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañceva pitucca te;

Sabbena tena kusalena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatū”ti.

Whatever merit has been performed by me and by your father, by all that wholesome deed, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

Tattha [V 6.0110] yena saccenāti yena bhūtena sabhāvena. Dhammacārīti dasakusalakammapathadhammacārī. Saccavādīti hasitavasenapi musāvādaṃ na vadati. Mātāpettibharoti [P 6.0092] analaso hutvā rattindivaṃ mātāpitaro bhari. Kule jeṭṭhāpacāyikoti jeṭṭhānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ sakkārakārako hoti.

Here, 'by the truth' means by the actual nature. 'Righteous in conduct' refers to practicing the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Speaker of truth' means not speaking falsehood even in jest. 'Supporting his parents' means tirelessly supporting his parents day and night. 'Revered the elders in his family' means honoring his elder parents.

Evaṃ mātarā sattahi gāthāhi saccakiriyāya katāya sāmo parivattitvā nipajji. Athassa pitā “jīvati me putto, ahampissa saccakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti tatheva saccakiriyamakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

When his mother had thus performed the act of truth with seven verses, Sāma turned over and lay down. Then his father thought, "My son lives; I too shall perform an act of truth for him," and he did so in the same way. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

389.

389.

“Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ;

Aṭṭito puttasokena, pitā saccaṃ abhāsatha.

Seeing Sāma fallen, his dear son smeared with dust, tormented by grief for his son, the father spoke the truth.

390.

390.

“Yena [M 6.0113] saccenayaṃ sāmo, dhammacārī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly one who lived righteously; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

391.

391.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, brahmacārī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly one who lived a holy life; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

392.

392.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, saccavādī pure ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly a speaker of truth; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

393.

393.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, mātāpettibharo ahu;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma was one who supported his mother and father; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

394.

394.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyiko;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma revered the elders in his family; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

395.

395.

“Yena saccenayaṃ sāmo, pāṇā piyataro mama;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

By the truth that this Sāma is dearer to me than life itself; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

396.

396.

“Yaṃ [V 6.0111] kiñcitthi kataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañceva mātucca te;

Sabbena tena kusalena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatū”ti.

Whatever merit has been performed by me and your mother, by all that wholesome deed, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

Evaṃ pitari saccakiriyaṃ karonte mahāsatto parivattitvā itarena passena nipajji. Athassa tatiyaṃ saccakiriyaṃ devatā akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā aha –

While his father was thus performing the act of truth, the Great Being turned over and lay on his other side. Then a deity performed a third act of truth for him. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

397.

397.

“Sā devatā antarahitā, pabbate gandhamādane;

Sāmassa anukampāya, imaṃ saccaṃ abhāsatha.

That deity, invisible on Mount Gandhamādana, out of compassion for Sāma, spoke this truth:

398.

398.

“Pabbatyāhaṃ gandhamādane, cirarattanivāsinī;

Na me piyataro koci, añño sāmena vijjati;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

I have long been a dweller on Mount Gandhamādana; no one is dearer to me than Sāma; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

399.

399.

“Sabbe vanā gandhamayā, pabbate gandhamādane;

Etena saccavajjena, visaṃ sāmassa haññatu.

All the forests are fragrant on Mount Gandhamādana; by this utterance of truth, may the poison in Sāma be destroyed.

400.

400.

“Tesaṃ lālappamānānaṃ, bahuṃ kāruññasañhitaṃ;

Khippaṃ sāmo samuṭṭhāsi, yuvā kalyāṇadassano”ti.

As they lamented with much compassion, at the conclusion of the deity's act of truth, Sāma quickly arose, a youth of beautiful appearance.

Tattha [M 6.0114] pabbatyāhanti pabbate ahaṃ. Sabbe vanā gandhamayāti sabbe rukkhā gandhamayā. Na hi tattha agandho nāma koci rukkho atthi. Tesanti bhikkhave, tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ lālappamānānaññeva devatāya saccakiriyāya pariyosāne khippaṃ sāmo uṭṭhāsi, padumapattato udakaṃ viyassa visaṃ vinivattetvā ābādho vigato, idha nu kho viddho, ettha nu kho viddhoti viddhaṭṭhānampi na paññāyi.

Here, 'pabbatyāhaṃ' means 'I am on the mountain.' 'All the forests are fragrant' means all the trees are fragrant, for no tree there is without fragrance. 'As they lamented'—monks, at the end of the deity's asseveration of truth, while those two were lamenting, Sāma quickly arose. Like water from a lotus leaf, the poison receded from him and the affliction vanished, and even the place where he was struck could not be discerned, as they wondered, 'Was he struck here? Was he struck here?'

Iti mahāsattassa nirogabhāvo, mātāpitūnañca cakkhupaṭilābho, aruṇuggamanañca, devatānubhāvena tesaṃ catunnaṃ assameyeva pākaṭabhāvo [P 6.0093] cāti sabbaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Mātāpitaro “cakkhūni no laddhāni, suvaṇṇasāmo ca arogo jāto”ti atirekataraṃ tussiṃsu. Atha ne sāmapaṇḍito gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Thus, the Great Being's freedom from illness, his parents' regaining of sight, the rising of the sun at dawn, and the manifestation of all four of them in the hermitage by the power of the deity—all this occurred in a single moment. His parents rejoiced exceedingly, exclaiming, 'We have regained our sight, and Suvaṇṇasāma is free from illness!' Then the wise Sāma spoke this verse to them:

401.

401.

“Sāmohamasmi [V 6.0112] bhaddaṃ vo, sotthināmhi samuṭṭhito;

Mā bāḷhaṃ paridevetha, mañcunābhivadetha ma”nti.

“I am Sāma; may it be well with you. I have arisen in safety. Do not lament excessively; greet me with a pleasant voice.”

Tattha sotthināmhi samuṭṭhitoti sotthinā sukhena uṭṭhito amhi bhavāmi. Mañjunāti madhurassarena maṃ abhivadetha.

Here, 'I have arisen in safety' means 'I have arisen happily, with well-being.' 'With a pleasant voice' means 'greet me with a sweet voice.'

Atha so rājānaṃ disvā paṭisanthāraṃ karonto āha –

Then, seeing the king and wishing to engage in friendly conversation, he said:

402.

402.

“Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yaṃ idhatthi pavedaya.

“Welcome to you, great king; your coming is a welcome one. You have arrived as the lord; declare what is your desire here.”

403.

403.

“Tindukāni piyālāni, madhuke kāsumāriyo;

Phalāni khuddakappāni, bhuñja rāja varaṃ varaṃ.

“Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhuka, and kāsumārī fruits—fruits as sweet as honey; enjoy them, O king, the best of the best.”

404.

404.

“Atthi me pānīyaṃ sītaṃ, ābhataṃ girigabbharā;

Tato piva mahārāja, sace tvaṃ abhikaṅkhasī”ti.

“I have cool drinking water brought from a mountain cave. Drink from it, great king, if you so desire.”

Rājāpi taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā āha –

The king, too, seeing that marvel of Suvaṇṇasāma restored to life after having died, and wishing to question him, said:

405.

405.

“Sammuyhāmi pamuyhāmi, sabbā muyhanti me disā;

Petaṃ taṃ sāma maddakkhiṃ, ko nu tvaṃ sāma jīvasī”ti.

“I am utterly bewildered, I am confused; all directions are a blur to me. I saw you dead, Sāma; how is it that you live, Sāma?”

Tattha [M 6.0115] petanti sāma ahaṃ taṃ mataṃ addasaṃ. Ko nu tvanti kathaṃ nu tvaṃ jīvitaṃ paṭilabhasīti pucchi.

Herein, ‘dead’ (petaṃ) means, ‘Sāma, I saw you dead.’ By ‘how is it that you live,’ he asked, ‘How have you regained your life?’

Mahāsatto “ayaṃ rājā maṃ ‘mato’ti sallakkhesi, amatabhāvamassa pakāsessāmī”ti cintetvā āha –

The Great Being, thinking, “This king perceives me as dead; I will show him that I am alive,” said:

406.

406.

“Api jīvaṃ mahārāja, purisaṃ gāḷhavedanaṃ;

Upanītamanasaṅkappaṃ, jīvantaṃ maññate mataṃ.

“Even though living, O great king, a person in severe pain, whose mental states have descended into the life-continuum, is considered dead, though he is still living.”

407.

407.

“Api [V 6.0113] jīvaṃ mahārāja, purisaṃ gāḷhavedanaṃ;

Taṃ nirodhagataṃ santaṃ, jīvantaṃ maññate mata”nti.

“Even though living, O great king, a person in severe pain who has attained the cessation of breath is considered dead by the world, though he is still living.”

Tattha api jīvanti jīvamānaṃ api. Upanītamanasaṅkappanti bhavaṅgaotiṇṇacittācāraṃ. Jīvantanti jīvamānameva “eso mato”ti maññati. Nirodhagatanti assāsapassāsanirodhaṃ samāpannaṃ santaṃ vijjamānaṃ maṃ evaṃ loko mataṃ viya jīvantameva maññati.

Herein, ‘api jīvaṃ’ means ‘even while still living.’ ‘Upanītamanasaṅkappaṃ’ means the conduct of a mind that has descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). ‘Jīvantaṃ’ means that even while living, people think, ‘He is dead.’ ‘Nirodhagataṃ’ means having attained the cessation of in-breaths and out-breaths; although living and existing, the world considers such a one to be dead.

Evañca pana vatvā mahāsatto rājānaṃ atthe yojetukāmo dhammaṃ desento puna dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken thus, the Great Being, wishing to lead the king toward his welfare and to teach the Dhamma, spoke two more verses:

408.

408.

“Yo [P 6.0094] mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā, macco dhammena posati;

Devāpi naṃ tikicchanti, mātāpettibharaṃ naraṃ.

“A mortal who righteously supports his mother or father—even the devas heal him, that person who supports his parents.”

409.

409.

“Yo mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā, macco dhammena posati;

Idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti.

“A mortal who righteously supports his mother or father—they praise him even here in this life, and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā “acchariyaṃ vata, bho, mātāpettibharassa jantuno uppannarogaṃ devatāpi tikicchanti, ativiya ayaṃ sāmo sobhatī”ti añjaliṃ paggayha yācanto āha –
