When Mahosadha enters tomorrow, kill him with this sword.' He handed Senaka his own royal sword. The four ministers, hearing this, said, 'Lord, if it is about the householder's son, we are here; do not fear.' They left the palace, rejoicing, 'We have seen the back of our enemy,' and sat together on the dining-platform. Then Senaka asked, 'Sirs, who will kill the householder's son?' The others replied, 'Teacher, you are the one the king commanded; you should kill him,' thus placing the burden on him.

Atha ne senako pucchi “tumhe ‘rahassaṃ nāma asukassa asukassa kathetabba’nti vadatha, kiṃ vo etaṃ kataṃ, udāhu diṭṭhaṃ suta”nti? “Kataṃ etaṃ, ācariyā”ti. Tumhe “rahassaṃ nāma sahāyakassa kathetabba”nti vadatha, “kiṃ vo etaṃ kataṃ, udāhu diṭṭhaṃ suta”nti? “Kataṃ etaṃ mayā”ti? “Kathetha, ācariyā”ti. “Imasmiṃ rahasse raññā ñāte jīvitaṃ me natthī”ti. “Mā bhāyatha ācariya, idha tumhākaṃ rahassabhedako natthi, kathethā”ti. So nakhena ambaṇaṃ koṭṭetvā “atthi nu kho imassa heṭṭhā gahapatiputto”ti āha. “Ācariya, gahapatiputto attano issariyena evarūpaṃ ṭhānaṃ na pavisissati, idāni yasena matto bhavissati, kathetha [M 6.0227][P 6.0383] tumhe”ti. Senako tāva attano rahassaṃ kathento āha – “tumhe imasmiṃ nagare asukaṃ nāma vesiṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma, ācariyā”ti. “Idāni sā paññāyatī”ti. “Na paññāyati, ācariyā”ti. “Ahaṃ sālavanuyyāne tāya saddhiṃ purisakiccaṃ katvā tassā piḷandhanesu lobhena taṃ māretvā tassāyeva sāṭakena bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā āharitvā amhākaṃ ghare asukabhūmikāya asuke nāma gabbhe nāgadantake laggesiṃ, vaḷañjetuṃ 3 visahāmi, purāṇabhāvamassa olokemi, evarūpaṃ aparādhakammaṃ katvā mayā ekassa sahāyakassa kathitaṃ, na tena kassaci kathitapubbaṃ, iminā kāraṇena ‘sahāyakassa guyhaṃ kathetabba’nti mayā kathita”nti. Paṇḍito tassa rahassaṃ sādhukaṃ vavatthapetvā sallakkhesi.

Then Senaka asked them, 'You each said that a secret should be told to such and such a person. Did you say that because you have actually done so, or was it from your own wisdom, or did you hear it from others?' They replied, 'Teacher, it was from our own direct experience.' Then they asked, 'Teacher, you also said a secret should be told to a friend. Did you say that without reason, or from direct experience like us?' Senaka replied, 'What benefit is there for you to hear what I told the king?' They said, 'Whether there is benefit or not, we wish to know. Please tell us.' Senaka said, 'It is not that I wish to hide it, but if the king hears of it, I will not live. Therefore, do not ask me.' They replied, 'Teacher, even if it is a crime, there is no one here but us. The householder’s son would not enter under this platform to listen. It is only us; how can you be punished? Please speak.' Tapping the platform with his fingernail, Senaka asked, 'Could the householder’s son be under here?' They replied, 'Teacher, the householder’s son, with all his wealth, would not enter such a place. He must be drunk with his own fame. You may speak.' Then Senaka revealed his secret: 'Sirs, do you know a certain courtesan in this city?' 'Yes, teacher.' 'Is she seen anymore?' 'No, teacher.' Senaka said, 'In the Sala grove, after having relations with her, I desired her ornaments. I killed her, stripped off her jewels, wrapped them in her own cloth, and hung the bundle on an ivory peg in a certain room of my house. Only one close friend knows. No one else, not even my family, knows. The king does not know either. I have not dared to use those jewels to this day, but only look at them as they age. Because my friend is tight-lipped, the matter has not spread. That is why I said a secret should be told to a friend.' The Bodhisatta, listening from under the platform, heard everything and recorded it word for word.

Pukkusopi attano rahassaṃ kathento āha – “mama ūruyā kuṭṭhaṃ atthi, kaniṭṭho me pātova kañci ajānāpetvā taṃ dhovitvā bhesajjena makkhetvā upari pilotikaṃ datvā bandhati. Rājā mayi muducitto ‘ehi pukkusā’ti maṃ pakkositvā yebhuyyena mama ūruyāyeva sayati[V 6.0213], sace pana etaṃ rājā jāneyya, maṃ māreyya. Taṃ mama kaniṭṭhaṃ ṭhapetvā añño jānanto nāma natthi, tena kāraṇena ‘rahassaṃ nāma bhātu kathetabba’nti mayā vutta”nti. Kāmindopi attano rahassaṃ kathento āha – “maṃ kāḷapakkhe uposathadivase naradevo nāma yakkho gaṇhāti, ahaṃ ummattakasunakho viya viravāmi, svāhaṃ tamatthaṃ puttassa kathesiṃ. So mama yakkhena gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā maṃ antogehagabbhe nipajjāpetvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā nikkhamitvā mama saddaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ dvāre samajjaṃ kāresi, iminā kāraṇena ‘rahassaṃ nāma puttassa kathetabba’nti mayā vutta”nti. Tato tayopi devindaṃ pucchiṃsu. So attano rahassaṃ kathento āha – “mayā maṇipahaṃsanakammaṃ karontena rañño santakaṃ sakkena kusarañño dinnaṃ, siripavesanaṃ maṅgalamaṇiratanaṃ thenetvā mātuyā dinnaṃ. Sā kañci ajānāpetvā mama rājakulaṃ pavisanakāle taṃ mayhaṃ deti, ahaṃ tena maṇinā siriṃ pavesetvā rājanivesanaṃ gacchāmi. Rājā tumhehi saddhiṃ akathetvā paṭhamataraṃ mayā saddhiṃ kathesi. Devasikaṃ aṭṭha, soḷasa, dvattiṃsa, catusaṭṭhi kahāpaṇe mama paribbayatthāya deti[M 6.0228]. Sace tassa maṇiratanassa channabhāvaṃ rājā jāneyya, mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi, iminā kāraṇena ‘rahassaṃ nāma mātu kathetabba’nti mayā vutta”nti.

Pukkusa also, revealing his secret, said: "I have a skin disease on my thigh. Every morning, my younger brother, without letting anyone know, washes it, applies medicine, and bandages it with a cloth. The king, being fond of me, calls me, saying, 'Come, Pukkusa,' and usually rests his head on my thigh to sleep. If the king were to learn of this, I would not be able to live. No one knows this except for my younger brother, who keeps it well-hidden. For this reason, I told the king, 'A secret should be told to a brother.'" Kāminda also, revealing his secret, said: "On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, a yakkha named Naradeva seizes me. When the yakkha seizes me, I do not want to stay in one place; I howl and wander about like a mad dog. I told this matter to my son. Knowing this, on every Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, when it is time for the affliction to appear, he puts me in an inner chamber and closes the door. He also arranges music and a festival outside the door to prevent others from hearing my cries. Because of this, no one but my son knows of my affliction. For this reason, I told the king, 'A secret should be told to a son.'" Then the three of them asked Devinda. He, revealing his secret, said: "While I was engaged in the work of polishing gems, I stole the king’s auspicious gem—which brings glory and fortune and was given by Sakka to King Kusa—without the king's knowledge and gave it to my mother. My mother keeps it hidden so that no one knows, and she gives it to me when I enter the palace. I attend upon the king while carrying that gem. Because of the power of the gem, the king calls and consults me first before speaking to any of you. Every day, for my maintenance, he gives me eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four kahāpaṇas. If the king knew it was because of the power of that gem, I would not be able to live. Because my mother keeps it so well-hidden, no one knows to this day. For this reason, I told the king, 'A secret should be told to a mother.'" Mahosadha the wise noted the words of Devinda as well.

Mahāsatto sabbesampi guyhaṃ attano paccakkhaṃ akāsi[P 6.0384]. Te pana attano udaraṃ phāletvā antaṃ bāhiraṃ karontā viya rahassaṃ aññamaññaṃ kathetvā “tumhe appamattā pātova āgacchatha, gahapatiputtaṃ māressāmā”ti uṭṭhāya pakkamiṃsu. Tesaṃ gatakāle paṇḍitassa purisā āgantvā ambaṇaṃ ukkhipitvā mahāsattaṃ ādāya pakkamiṃsu. So gharaṃ gantvā nhatvā alaṅkaritvā subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā “ajja me bhaginī udumbaradevī rājagehato sāsanaṃ pesessatī”ti ñatvā dvāre paccāyikaṃ purisaṃ ṭhapesi “rājagehato āgataṃ sīghaṃ pavesetvā mama dasseyyāsī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā sayanapiṭṭhe nipajji. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājāpi sayanapiṭṭhe nipannova paṇḍitassa guṇaṃ saritvā “mahosadhapaṇḍito sattavassikakālato paṭṭhāya maṃ upaṭṭhahanto na kiñci mayhaṃ anatthaṃ akāsi, devatāya pucchitapañhepi paṇḍite asati jīvitaṃ me laddhaṃ na siyā. Veripaccāmittānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā ‘asamadhuraṃ paṇḍitaṃ mārethā’ti khaggaṃ dentena ayuttaṃ mayā kataṃ, sve dāni naṃ passituṃ na labhissāmī”ti sokaṃ uppādesi. Sarīrato sedā mucciṃsu. So sokasamappito cittassādaṃ na labhi. Udumbaradevīpi tena saddhiṃ ekasayanagatā taṃ ākāraṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho mayhaṃ koci aparādho atthi, udāhu devassa kiñci sokakāraṇaṃ uppannaṃ, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being witnessed all their secrets for himself. As if tearing open their own bellies and turning them inside out, they spoke their secrets to one another, saying, "Be diligent and come early to the palace gate in the morning; we have the task of killing the householder’s son. Do not forget!" Having thus consulted and urged one another, they rose from the dining table and went home. After they had gone, Mahosadha’s attendants arrived, lifted the table, and brought the Great Being out, then escorted him home. Upon reaching home, Mahosadha bathed, dressed, and ate a fine meal. Sitting in a noble place, he thought, "Today the four advisors have slandered me to the king with an evil plot to destroy me. My sister, Queen Udumbarā, will surely know the king's mind and will undoubtedly send word to me." He called a trusted servant and sent him to the palace gate, saying, "Keep watch at the gate tonight. If you see someone coming from the palace, bring them to me immediately." Then he lay down on his noble bed. King Videha, having entered his bedchamber, lay there recalling the virtues of the Great Being: "Mahosadha has served me since the age of seven and has never done me any harm. He has served my interests in many ways. Even in the matter of the deity's riddle, had Mahosadha not been there, I would surely have died. I only live because of him. It was wrong of me to listen to those who spoke out of malice and to give the sword to kill such a benefactor. Tomorrow morning, I shall no longer see him." He was overcome with intense regret and sorrow, and sweat poured from his body. Distressed in body and mind, the king could not sleep as usual and lay there in a daze. Queen Udumbarā, lying on the same bed, noticed his demeanor and thought, "The king seems troubled. Is it because of some fault of mine, or is there some other cause for his anxiety? I will ask him to find out." She then spoke this verse:

“Kiṃ [V 6.0214] tvaṃ vimanosi rājaseṭṭha, dvipadajaninda vacanaṃ suṇoma metaṃ;

Kiṃ cintayamāno dummanosi, nūna deva aparādho atthi mayha”nti. (jā. 1.15.323);

"Why are you dejected, O best of kings? O lord of men, let us hear the reason. What are you pondering that makes you sad? Surely, my lord, is there some fault of mine?"

Atha rājā kathento gāthamāha –

Then the king, wishing to explain the cause of his sorrow, spoke this verse:

“Paṇhe vajjho mahosadhoti, āṇatto me vamāya bhūripañño;

Taṃ cintayamāno dummanosmi, na hi devī aparādho atthi tuyha”nti. (jā. 1.15.324);

"I gave the order that Mahosadha should be executed; I commanded the death of the one of vast wisdom. Pondering this, I am sad; indeed, O queen, there is no fault of yours."

Tattha [M 6.0229] āṇattoti bhadde, cattāro paṇḍitā “mahosadho mama paccatthiko”ti kathayiṃsu. Mayā tathato avicinitvā “vadhetha na”nti bhūripañño vadhāya āṇatto. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ cintayamāno dummanosmīti.

The meaning is: "O auspicious queen, it is not because of any failure in your duties that I am sad, nor for any other reason. It is because tonight, when the four advisors spoke out of a desire to destroy Mahosadha, I failed to reflect. In a fit of haste and anger, I wrongly accepted their words and gave my personal sword to Senaka to kill my son Mahosadha, who is as wise as the earth is wide. Recalling this now, I am in great distress." Thus he spoke.

Tassā [P 6.0385] tassa vacanaṃ sutvāva mahāsatte sinehena pabbatamatto soko uppajji. Tato sā cintesi “ekena upāyena rājānaṃ assāsetvā rañño niddaṃ okkamanakāle mama kaniṭṭhassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇissāmī”ti. Atha sā “mahārāja, tayāvetaṃ kataṃ gahapatiputtaṃ mahante issariye patiṭṭhāpentena, tumhehi so senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapito, idāni kira so tumhākaṃyeva paccatthiko jāto, na kho pana paccatthiko khuddako nāma atthi, māretabbova, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti rājānaṃ assāsesi. So tanubhūtasoko niddaṃ okkami. Devī uṭṭhāya gabbhaṃ pavisitvā “tāta mahosadha, cattāro paṇḍitā taṃ paribhindiṃsu, rājā kuddho sve dvārantare taṃ vadhāya āṇāpesi, sve rājakulaṃ mā āgaccheyyāsi, āgacchanto pana nagaraṃ hatthagataṃ katvā samattho hutvā āgaccheyyāsī”ti paṇṇaṃ likhitvā modakassa anto pakkhipitvā modakaṃ suttena veṭhetvā navabhājane katvā chādetvā lañchetvā atthacārikāya dāsiyā adāsi “imaṃ modakaṃ gahetvā mama kaniṭṭhassa dehī”ti. Sā tathā akāsi. “Rattiṃ kathaṃ nikkhantā”ti na cintetabbaṃ. Raññā paṭhamameva deviyā varo dinno, tena na naṃ koci nivāresi. Bodhisatto paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā naṃ uyyojesi. Sā puna āgantvā dinnabhāvaṃ ārocesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe devī āgantvā raññā saddhiṃ nipajji. Mahāsattopi modakaṃ bhinditvā paṇṇaṃ vācetvā tamatthaṃ ñatvā kattabbakiccaṃ vicāretvā sayane nipajji.

Upon hearing his words, a sorrow as great as a mountain arose in her out of affection for the Great Being. Then she thought, "By some means, I will console the king and, when the king has fallen asleep, I will send a message to my younger brother." Then she consoled the king, saying, "Great king, it was you who established that householder’s son in great power. You appointed him to the position of commander-in-chief. Now, it seems he has become your enemy. But no enemy is insignificant—he must be killed. Do not worry." With his sorrow thus lessened, the king fell asleep. The queen rose, entered her chamber, and wrote on a leaf: "Dear Mahosadha, the four wise men have conspired against you. The king is angry and has ordered your execution at the gate tomorrow. Do not come to the royal court tomorrow. If you are to come, however, come only after having brought the city under your control and being fully capable." She then placed the leaf inside a sweet cake, wrapped it with a string, placed it in a new dish, covered it, sealed it, and gave it to a trusted maidservant, saying, "Take this cake and give it to my younger brother." The maid did so. One should not wonder, "How did she leave at night?" For the king had previously granted the queen a boon, so no one stopped her. The Bodhisatta took the gift and dismissed her. She returned and reported that she had delivered it. At that moment, the queen came and lay down with the king. The Great Being, having broken open the cake, read the leaf, understood the matter, considered what was to be done, and then lay down on his bed.

Itarepi [V 6.0215] cattāro janā pātova khaggaṃ gahetvā dvārantare ṭhatvā paṇḍitaṃ apassantā dummanā hutvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ paṇḍitā mārito vo gahapatiputto”ti vutte “na passāma, devā”ti āhaṃsu. Mahāsattopi aruṇuggamaneyeva nagaraṃ attano hatthagataṃ katvā tattha tattha ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā mahājanaparivuto rathaṃ āruyha mahantena parivārena rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā bahi olokento aṭṭhāsi. Atha mahāsatto rathā otaritvā rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā cintesi “sace ayaṃ mama paccatthiko bhaveyya[P 6.0386][M 6.0230], na maṃ vandeyyā”ti. Atha naṃ pakkosāpetvā rājā āsane nisīdi. Mahāsattopi ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Cattāropi paṇḍitā tattheva nisīdiṃsu. Atha naṃ rājā kiñci ajānanto viya “tāta, tvaṃ hiyyo gantvā idāni āgacchasi, kiṃ maṃ pariccajasī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The other four men, taking up their swords early in the morning, stood at the gate. Not seeing the wise man, they became distressed and went to the king. When asked, "Wise sirs, has your householder's son been killed?" they replied, "We do not see him, Your Majesty." The Great Being, at the rising of the dawn, brought the city under his control. Setting guards here and there, surrounded by a great crowd, he mounted a chariot and approached the royal gate with a large retinue. The king, opening the lion-window, stood looking out. Then the Great Being descended from the chariot, paid homage to the king, and stood there. Seeing him, the king thought, "If this man were my enemy, he would not pay homage to me." Then, having summoned him, the king sat on his seat. The Great Being also sat to one side. The four wise men also sat right there. Then the king, as if knowing nothing, said to him, "Dear one, you went yesterday and have come back now. Are you abandoning me?" and spoke this verse:

“Abhidosagato dāni ehisi, kiṃ sutvā kiṃ saṅkate mano te;

Ko te kimavoca bhūripañña, iṅgha vacanaṃ suṇoma brūhi meta”nti. (jā. 1.15.325);

"Having gone in the early night, now you come. What have you heard? What does your mind suspect? Who told you what, O greatly wise one? Come, let us hear your words; speak them to me."

Tattha abhidosagatoti hiyyo paṭhamayāme gato idāni āgato. Kiṃ saṅkateti kiṃ āsaṅkate. Kimavocāti kiṃ rañño santikaṃ mā gamīti taṃ koci avoca.

Therein, 'abhidosagato' means: having gone yesterday in the first watch, he has now come. 'Kiṃ saṅkate' means: what does he suspect. 'Kimavoca' means: did someone tell him, "Do not go into the king's presence?"

Atha naṃ mahāsatto “mahārāja, tayā me catunnaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā vadho āṇatto, tenāhaṃ na emī”ti codento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, rebuking him by saying, "Great King, having accepted the word of the four wise men, you ordered my execution; for that reason I did not come," spoke this verse:

“Paṇhe vajjho mahosadhoti, yadi te mantayitaṃ janinda dosaṃ;

Bhariyāya rahogato asaṃsi, guyhaṃ pātukataṃ sutaṃ mameta”nti. (jā. 1.15.326);

"'Mahosadha is to be executed on account of the question'—that you consulted at night, O lord of men, and spoke to your wife in private—that secret was made known, and this was heard by me."

Tattha yadi teti yasmā tayā. Mantayitanti kathitaṃ. Dosanti abhidosaṃ, rattibhāgeti attho. Kassa kathitanti? Bhariyāya. Tvañhi hiyyo tassā imamatthaṃ rahogato asaṃsi. Guyhaṃ pātukatanti tassā evarūpaṃ attano rahassaṃ pātukataṃ. Sutaṃ mametanti mayā panetaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇeyeva sutaṃ.

Therein, 'yadi te' means 'because you'. 'Mantayitaṃ' means 'it was spoken'. 'Dosaṃ' means 'abhidosaṃ', which means 'in the night-time'. To whom was it spoken? To the wife. For yesterday, you privately declared this matter to her. 'Guyhaṃ pātukataṃ' means 'such a secret of your own was made known to her'. 'Sutaṃ mametaṃ' means 'but this was heard by me at that very moment.'

Rājā [V 6.0216] taṃ sutvā “imāya taṅkhaṇaññeva sāsanaṃ pahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti kuddho deviṃ olokesi. Taṃ ñatvā mahāsatto “kiṃ, deva, deviyā kujjhatha, ahaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ jānāmi. Deva, tumhākaṃ tāva rahassaṃ deviyā kathitaṃ hotu, ācariyasenakassa pukkusādīnaṃ vā rahassaṃ mama kena kathitaṃ, ahaṃ etesampi rahassaṃ jānāmiyevā”ti [M 6.0231] senakassa tāva rahassaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, enraged, thinking, "A message must have been sent by her at that very moment," glared at the queen. Knowing this, the Great Being said, "Why, Your Majesty, are you angry with the queen? I know all things past, future, and present. Your Majesty, let it be that your secret was told by the queen; but the secret of Teacher Senaka, Pukkusa, and the others—by whom was it told to me? I know their secrets as well." Then, revealing Senaka's secret first, he spoke this verse:

“Yaṃ sālavanasmiṃ senako, pāpakammaṃ akāsi asabbhirūpaṃ;

Sakhinova [P 6.0387] rahogato asaṃsi, guyhaṃ pātukataṃ sutaṃ mameta”nti. (jā. 1.15.327);

“In the Sala forest, Senaka, you committed an evil deed, an unseemly act. You confessed it in private as if to a friend; the secret was made manifest, and this was heard by me.”

Tattha asabbhirūpanti asādhujātikaṃ lāmakaṃ akusalakammaṃ akāsi. Imasmiṃyeva hi nagare asukaṃ nāma vesiṃ sālavanuyyāne purisakiccaṃ katvā taṃ māretvā alaṅkāraṃ gahetvā tassāyeva sāṭakena bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā attano ghare asukaṭṭhāne nāgadantake laggetvā ṭhapesi. Sakhinovāti atha naṃ, mahārāja, ekassa sahāyakassa rahogato hutvā akkhāsi, tampi mayā sutaṃ. Nāhaṃ devassa paccatthiko, senakoyeva. Yadi te paccatthikena kammaṃ atthi, senakaṃ gaṇhāpehīti.

Herein, ‘asabbhirūpaṃ’ means he committed a base, vile, unwholesome deed. For in this very city, in the Sāla grove park, he had sexual intercourse with a certain courtesan, then killed her, took her ornaments, made a bundle with her garment, and hung it on an ivory peg in a certain place in his own house. ‘Sakhinova’ means, O great king, he privately confessed it to a companion, and that too was heard by me. I am not your opponent, O king; Senaka is. If you have any business with an opponent, have Senaka seized.

Rājā senakaṃ oloketvā “saccaṃ, senakā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, devā”ti vutte tassa bandhanāgārappavesanaṃ āṇāpesi. Paṇḍito pukkusassa rahassaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, looking at Senaka, asked, “Is it true, Senaka?” When he replied, “It is true, Your Majesty,” the king ordered him to be put in prison. The Bodhisatta, revealing Pukkusa’s secret, spoke this verse:

“Pukkusapurisassa te janinda, uppanno rogo arājayutto;

Bhātucca rahogato asaṃsi, guyhaṃ pātukataṃ sutaṃ mameta”nti. (jā. 1.15.328);

“O lord of men, a disease has arisen in the man Pukkusa, one unsuitable for a king. He confessed it in private to his brother; the secret was made manifest, and this was heard by me.”

Tattha arājayuttoti mahārāja, etassa kuṭṭharogo uppanno, so rājānaṃ pattuṃ ayutto, chupanānucchaviko na hoti. Tumhe ca “pukkusassa ūru muduko”ti yebhuyyena tassa ūrumhi nipajjatha. So panesa vaṇabandhapilotikāya phasso, devāti.

Herein, ‘arājayutto’ means, O great king, that leprosy has arisen in him. He is unfit to approach the king and is unsuitable for being in close attendance. And you often lie upon his thigh, thinking, “Pukkusa’s thigh is soft.” But that touch is from the cloth bandaging a wound, Your Majesty.

Rājā tampi oloketvā “saccaṃ pukkusā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ devā”ti vutte tampi bandhanāgāraṃ pavesāpesi. Paṇḍito kāmindassapi rahassaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, looking at him too, asked, “Is it true, Pukkusa?” When he replied, “It is true, Your Majesty,” the king had him also sent to prison. The Bodhisatta, then revealing Kāminda’s secret, spoke this verse:

“Ābādhoyaṃ [V 6.0217][M 6.0232] asabbhirūpo, kāmindo naradevena phuṭṭho;

Puttassa rahogato asaṃsi, guyhaṃ pātukataṃ sutaṃ mameta”nti. (jā. 1.15.329);

“This affliction is unseemly, Kāminda, being struck by a human-deity. You confessed it to your son in private; the secret was made manifest, and this was heard by me.”

Tattha asabbhirūpoti yena so ābādhena phuṭṭho ummattakasunakho viya viravati, so naradevayakkhābādho asabbhijātiko lāmako, rājakulaṃ pavisituṃ na yutto, mahārājāti vadati.

Herein, ‘asabbhirūpo’ means that affliction by which he is struck, causing him to howl like a mad dog. That affliction from a human-deity spirit is of an unseemly kind, base, and unfit for entering the royal household, O great king.

Rājā [P 6.0388] tampi oloketvā “saccaṃ kāmindā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ devā”ti vutte tampi bandhanāgāraṃ pavesāpesi. Paṇḍito devindassapi rahassaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, looking also at him, asked, “Is it true, Kāminda?” When he replied, “It is true, Your Majesty,” the king had him also sent to prison. The wise one, revealing Devinda’s secret as well, spoke this verse:

“Aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ maṇiratanaṃ uḷāraṃ, sakko te adadā pitāmahassa;

Devindassa gataṃ tadajja hatthaṃ, mātucca rahogato asaṃsi;

Guyhaṃ pātukataṃ sutaṃ mameta”nti. (jā. 1.15.330);

“An eight-faceted jewel, splendid, Sakka gave to your grandfather. Today it has come into Devinda’s hand, and he told his mother in private. The secret was made manifest, and this was heard by me.”

Tattha pitāmahassāti tava pitāmahassa kusarājassa. Tadajja hatthanti taṃ maṅgalasammataṃ maṇiratanaṃ ajja devindassa hatthagataṃ, mahārājāti.

Herein, ‘to the grandfather’ means to your paternal grandfather, King Kusa. ‘Today to the hand’ means that jewel-treasure, considered auspicious, has today come into Devinda’s possession, O great king.

Rājā tampi oloketvā “saccaṃ devindā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ devā”ti vutte tampi bandhanāgāraṃ pavesāpesi. Evaṃ “bodhisattaṃ vadhissāmā”ti cintetvā sabbepi te bandhanāgāraṃ paviṭṭhā. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ ‘attano guyhaṃ parassa na kathetabba’nti vadāmi, vadantā pana mahāvināsaṃ pattā”ti vatvā uttari dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

The king, looking also at him, asked, “Is it true, Devinda?” When he replied, “It is true, Your Majesty,” the king had him also sent to prison. Thus, having thought, “We will kill the Bodhisatta,” all of them entered the prison. The Bodhisatta said, “Great king, for this reason I say, ‘One’s own secret should not be told to another,’ for those who tell it have met with great ruin.” Then, teaching the Dhamma further, he spoke these verses:

“Guyhassa hi guyhameva sādhu, na guyhassa pasatthamāvikammaṃ;

Anipphannatā saheyya dhīro, nipphannova yathāsukhaṃ bhaṇeyya.

“Indeed, for a secret, it is good that it remains secret; the disclosure of a secret is not praised. A wise man should endure as long as his purpose is unaccomplished; when it is accomplished, he may speak as he pleases.”

“Na [M 6.0233] guyhamatthaṃ vivareyya, rakkheyya naṃ yathā nidhiṃ;

Na hi pātukato sādhu, guyho attho pajānatā.

“One should not reveal a secret matter; one should guard it like a treasure. For a secret matter, when made manifest, is not good for one who knows it.”

“Thiyā [V 6.0218] guyhaṃ na saṃseyya, amittassa ca paṇḍito;

Yo cāmisena saṃhīro, hadayattheno ca yo naro.

“A wise man should not confide a secret to a woman, nor to an enemy, nor to one who is enticed by material gain, nor to a man who is a thief of hearts.”

“Guyhamatthaṃ asambuddhaṃ, sambodhayati yo naro;

Mantabhedabhayā tassa, dāsabhūto titikkhati.

“The man who reveals a secret matter that is not yet known must endure like a slave, out of fear that his secret will be disclosed.”

“Yāvanto purisassatthaṃ, guyhaṃ jānanti mantinaṃ;

Tāvanto tassa ubbegā, tasmā guyhaṃ na vissaje.

“However many counselors know a man’s secret purpose, so many are his anxieties; therefore, one should not disclose a secret.”

“Vivicca bhāseyya divā rahassaṃ, rattiṃ giraṃ nātivelaṃ pamuñce;

Upassutikā [P 6.0389] hi suṇanti mantaṃ, tasmā manto khippamupeti bheda”nti. (jā. 1.15.331-336);

“One should speak a secret by day in solitude; at night, one should not raise one’s voice too much. For eavesdroppers hear the counsel; therefore, the secret is quickly revealed.”

Tattha amittassa cāti itthiyā ca paccatthikassa ca na katheyya. Saṃhīroti yo ca yena kenaci āmisena saṃhīrati upalāpati saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tassapi na saṃseyya. Hadayatthenoti yo ca amitto mittapatirūpako mukhena aññaṃ katheti, hadayena aññaṃ cinteti, tassapi na saṃseyya. Asambuddhanti parehi aññātaṃ. “Asambodha”ntipi pāṭho, paresaṃ bodhetuṃ ayuttanti attho. Titikkhatīti tassa akkosampi paribhāsampi pahārampi dāso viya hutvā adhivāseti. Mantinanti mantitaṃ, mantīnaṃ vā antare yāvanto jānantīti attho. Tāvantoti te guyhajānanake paṭicca tattakā tassa ubbegā santāsā uppajjanti. Na vissajeti na vissajjeyya paraṃ na jānāpeyya. Viviccāti sace divā rahassaṃ mantetukāmo hoti, vivittaṃ okāsaṃ kāretvā suppaṭicchannaṭṭhāne manteyya. Nātivelanti rattiṃ rahassaṃ kathento pana ativelaṃ mariyādātikkantaṃ mahāsaddaṃ karonto giraṃ nappamuñceyya. Upassutikā hīti mantanaṭṭhānaṃ upagantvā tirokuṭṭādīsu ṭhatvā sotāro. Tasmāti mahārāja, tena kāraṇena so manto khippameva bhedamupāgamīti.

Herein, ‘and to an enemy’ means one should not speak to a woman or to an adversary. ‘Saṃhīro’ refers to one who is enticed by some material gain, is flattered, and becomes attached; one should not confide in such a person either. ‘Hadayattheno’ means one who, an enemy in the guise of a friend, speaks one thing with their mouth but thinks another in their heart; one should not confide in them either. ‘Asambuddhaṃ’ means ‘not known by others.’ There is also the reading ‘asambodha,’ meaning ‘it is unsuitable to make known to others.’ ‘Titikkhati’ means ‘he endures’ their insults, abuse, and even blows, having become like a servant. ‘Mantinaṃ’ refers to ‘counsel,’ or ‘as many as know among the counselors.’ ‘Tāvanto’ means that, on account of those who know the secret, so many anxieties and fears arise for him. ‘Na vissaje’ means ‘one should not disclose,’ ‘one should not make known to another.’ ‘Vivicca’ means that if one wishes to discuss a secret during the day, one should arrange for a secluded place and speak in a well-concealed spot. ‘Nātivelaṃ’ means that when speaking a secret at night, one should not utter speech making a great sound that transgresses the limit. ‘Upassutikā’ refers to eavesdroppers who, having approached the place of counsel, stand and listen from behind walls and so forth. ‘Tasmā’ means, O great king, for that reason, that counsel quickly came to be broken.

Rājā [M 6.0234] mahāsattassa kathaṃ sutvā “ete sayaṃ rājaverino hutvā paṇḍitaṃ mama veriṃ karontī”ti kujjhitvā “gacchatha ne nagarā nikkhamāpetvā sūlesu vā uttāsetha, sīsāni vā tesaṃ chindathā”ti āṇāpesi. Tesu pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā catukke catukke kasāhi pahārasahassaṃ datvā nīyamānesu paṇḍito “deva, ime tumhākaṃ porāṇakā amaccā, khamatha nesaṃ aparādha”nti [V 6.0219] rājānaṃ khamāpesi. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sādhū”ti te pakkosāpetvā tasseva dāse katvā adāsi. So pana te tattheva bhujisse akāsi. Rājā “tena hi mama vijite mā vasantū”ti pabbājanīyakammaṃ āṇāpesi. Paṇḍito “khamatha, deva, etesaṃ andhabālānaṃ dosa”nti khamāpetvā tesaṃ ṭhānantarāni puna pākatikāni kāresi. Rājā “paccāmittesupi tāvassa evarūpā mettā bhavati, aññesu janesu kathaṃ na bhavissatī”ti paṇḍitassa ativiya pasanno ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya cattāro paṇḍitā uddhatadāṭhā viya sappā nibbisā hutvā kiñci kathetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

Upon hearing the Great Being’s words, the king became angry, thinking, “These men, being themselves enemies of the king, are trying to make the wise one my enemy,” and ordered, “Go, drive them out of the city, impale them on stakes, or cut off their heads!” As they were being bound with their hands behind their backs and led away, after receiving a thousand lashes with whips at every crossroad, the wise one pleaded with the king, “Your Majesty, these are your ancient ministers; forgive their offense.” Hearing his words, the king said, “Very well,” summoned them back, and gave them to him as slaves. He, however, freed them right there. The king then ordered their banishment, saying, “Then let them not dwell in my realm.” The wise one again interceded, “Forgive, Your Majesty, the fault of these blind fools,” and had them restored to their former positions. The king, thinking, “If he has such loving-kindness even for his enemies, how much more will he have for other people?” became exceedingly pleased with the wise one. From then on, the four counselors, like snakes with their fangs pulled out, having become harmless, were unable to say anything.

Pañcapaṇḍitapañho niṭṭhito.

The Question of the Five Wise Men is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca paribhindakathā.

And the discourse on sowing dissension is concluded.

Yuddhaparājayakaṇḍaṃ

The Section on Defeat in Battle.

Tato [V 6.0220] paṭṭhāya paṇḍitova rañño atthañca dhammañca anusāsati. So cintesi “rañño setachattamattameva, rajjaṃ pana ahameva vicāremi[P 6.0390], mayā appamattena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So nagare mahāpākāraṃ nāma kāresi, tathā anupākārañca dvāraṭṭālake antaraṭṭālake udakaparikhaṃ kaddamaparikhaṃ sukkhaparikhanti tisso parikhāyo kāresi, antonagare jiṇṇagehāni paṭisaṅkharāpesi, mahāpokkharaṇiyo kāretvā tāsu udakanidhānaṃ kāresi, nagare sabbakoṭṭhāgārāni dhaññassa pūrāpesi, himavantappadesato kulupakatāpasehi kudrūsakumudabījāni āharāpesi, udakaniddhamanāni sodhāpetvā tattha ropāpesi, bahinagarepi jiṇṇasālāpaṭisaṅkharaṇakammaṃ kāresi. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Anāgatabhayapaṭibāhanatthaṃ. Tato tato āgatavāṇijakepi “sammā, tumhe kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchitvā “asukaṭṭhānato”ti vutte “tumhākaṃ raññā kiṃ piya”nti pucchitvā “asukaṃ nāmā”ti vutte tesaṃ sammānaṃ kāretvā uyyojetvā [M 6.0235] attano ekasate yodhe pakkosāpetvā “sammā, mayā dinne paṇṇākāre gahetvā ekasatarājadhāniyo gantvā ime paṇṇākāre attano piyakāmatāya tesaṃ rājūnaṃ datvā teyeva upaṭṭhahantā tesaṃ kiriyaṃ vā mantaṃ vā ñatvā mayhaṃ sāsanaṃ pesentā tattheva vasatha, ahaṃ vo puttadāraṃ posessāmī”ti vatvā kesañci kuṇḍale, kesañci pādukāyo, kesañci khagge, kesañci suvaṇṇamālāyo akkharāni chinditvā “yadā mama kiccaṃ atthi, tadā paññāyantū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ hatthe datvā pesesi. Te tattha tattha gantvā tesaṃ tesaṃ rājūnaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ datvā “kenatthenāgatā”ti vutte “tumheva upaṭṭhātuṃ āgatamhā”ti vatvā “kuto āgatatthā”ti puṭṭhā āgataṭṭhānaṃ avatvā aññāni ṭhānāni ācikkhitvā “tena hi sādhū”ti sampaṭicchite upaṭṭhahantā tesaṃ abbhantarikā ahesuṃ.

From that time onward, the wise Mahosadha alone advised the king on matters of both state and righteousness. He thought, 'The king possesses only the white parasol; I alone shall manage the kingdom's affairs. I must be vigilant.' He constructed a great rampart for the city, as well as an inner wall, gate towers, intermediate towers, and three types of moats: a water moat, a mud moat, and a dry moat. Within the city, he had dilapidated houses repaired, great lotus ponds constructed, and water stored in them. He filled all the city's granaries with grain. He had hermits, his supporters from the Himalayan region, bring seeds of kodo millet and water-lilies, and after clearing the drainage channels, he had them planted there. He also oversaw the repair of old halls outside the city. Why? To ward off future dangers. Furthermore, whenever merchants arrived from various places, he would ask them, 'Friends, from where have you come?' When they replied, 'From such and such a place,' he would ask, 'What does your king favor?' When they answered, 'Such and such a thing,' he would honor them and send them on their way. Then, summoning one hundred of his own warriors, he said, 'Friends, take these gifts provided by me and go to one hundred royal cities. Present these gifts to those kings as a token of goodwill. Stay there serving them, observe their actions and plans, and send word to me. I will support your wives and children.' He then gave some of them earrings, some sandals, some swords, and some golden garlands, having engraved letters on them, and resolved, 'When I have a task to perform, let these be recognized.' Placing the gifts in their hands, he sent them forth. They traveled to various places, presented the gifts to the respective kings, and when asked, 'For what purpose have you come?' they replied, 'We have come to serve you.' When asked about their origin, they did not disclose their true home but named other places instead. Being accepted with the words, 'Very well then,' they became intimate attendants to those kings.

Tadā kapilaraṭṭhe saṅkhabalako nāma rājā āvudhāni sajjāpesi, senaṃ saṅkaḍḍhi. Tassa santike upanikkhittakapuriso paṇḍitassa sāsanaṃ pesesi “sāmi, mayaṃ idha pavattiṃ ‘idaṃ nāma karissatī’ti na jānāma, āvudhāni sajjāpeti, senaṃ saṅkaḍḍhati, tumhe purisavisese pesetvā idaṃ pavattiṃ tathato jānāthā”ti. Atha mahāsatto suvapotakaṃ āmantetvā “samma, kapilaraṭṭhe saṅkhabalako nāma rājā āvudhāni sajjāpesi, tvaṃ tattha gantvā ‘imaṃ nāma karotī’ti tathato ñatvā sakalajambudīpaṃ [P 6.0391] āhiṇḍitvā mayhaṃ pavattiṃ āharāhī”ti vatvā madhulāje khādāpetvā madhupānīyaṃ pāyetvā satapākasahassapākehi telehi pakkhantaraṃ makkhetvā pācīnasīhapañjare [V 6.0221] ṭhatvā vissajjesi. Sopi tattha gantvā tassa purisassa santikā tassa rañño pavattiṃ tathato ñatvā sakalajambudīpaṃ pariggaṇhanto kapilaraṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā tattha cūḷanibrahmadatto nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa kevaṭṭo nāma brāhmaṇo atthañca dhammañca anusāsati, paṇḍito byatto. So paccūsakāle pabujjhitvā dīpālokena alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ sirigabbhaṃ olokento attano mahantaṃ yasaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mama yaso, kassa santako”ti cintetvā “na aññassa santako cūḷanibrahmadattassa[M 6.0236], evarūpaṃ pana yasadāyakaṃ rājānaṃ sakalajambudīpe aggarājānaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, ahañca aggapurohito bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā pātova nhatvā bhuñjitvā alaṅkaritvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “mahārāja, sukhaṃ sayathā”ti sukhaseyyaṃ pucchitvā “āma, paṇḍitā”ti vutte rājānaṃ “deva, mantetabbaṃ atthī”ti āha. “Vada, ācariyā”ti. “Deva, antonagare raho nāma na sakkā laddhuṃ, uyyānaṃ gacchāmā”ti. “Sādhu, ācariyā”ti rājā tena saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā balakāyaṃ bahi ṭhapetvā ārakkhaṃ kāretvā brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ pavisitvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīdi.

At that time, in the kingdom of Kapila, a king named Saṅkhabalaka prepared his weapons and mustered his army. A spy stationed near him sent a message to the wise Mahosadha: 'Lord, we do not yet know the purpose of these activities, but he is preparing weapons and gathering an army. You should send special agents to find out the truth of this matter.' Then the Great Being summoned a young parrot and said, 'Friend, in the kingdom of Kapila, a king named Saṅkhabalaka is preparing weapons. Go there, find out exactly what he intends to do, then wander throughout all of Jambudīpa and bring news to me.' After saying this, he fed the parrot honeyed parched grain, gave it honeyed water to drink, anointed its wings with oil refined a hundred and a thousand times, and released it from the eastern lion-window. The parrot went there, learned the truth of the king's activities from the spy, and while surveying all of Jambudīpa, arrived at the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila. At that time, King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta was ruling there. A Brahmin named Kevaṭṭa, wise and eloquent, was his advisor on matters of state and righteousness. Waking at dawn and looking at his splendidly adorned inner chamber illuminated by lamps, Kevaṭṭa observed his own great glory and thought, 'This glory of mine—to whom does it belong?' He reflected, 'It belongs to none other than Cūḷani-Brahmadatta. It is fitting that I make such a king, who bestows such glory, the supreme ruler of all Jambudīpa, and I shall become his chief chaplain.' Early in the morning, after bathing, eating, and dressing, he went to the king and inquired if he had slept well. When the king replied, 'Yes, wise one,' the Brahmin said, 'Great King, there is a matter to be discussed.' 'Speak, teacher,' the king replied. 'Great King, it is impossible to find privacy within the city; let us go to the garden.' 'Very well, teacher,' said the king. He went to the garden with him, stationed his troops outside, arranged for guards, and entering the garden with the Brahmin, sat down on the auspicious stone slab.

Tadā suvapotakopi taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā “bhavitabbamettha kāraṇena, ajja paṇḍitassa ācikkhitabbayuttakaṃ kiñci suṇissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ pavisitvā maṅgalasālarukkhassa pattantare nilīyitvā nisīdi. Rājā “kathetha, ācariyā”ti āha. “Mahārāja, tava kaṇṇe ito karohi, catukkaṇṇova manto bhavissati. Sace, mahārāja, mama vacanaṃ kareyyāsi, sakalajambudīpe taṃ aggarājānaṃ karomī”ti. So mahātaṇhatāya tassa vacanaṃ sutvā somanassappatto hutvā “kathetha, ācariya, karissāmi te vacana”nti āha. “Deva, mayaṃ senaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā paṭhamaṃ khuddakanagaraṃ rumbhitvā gaṇhissāma, ahañhi cūḷadvārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājānaṃ vakkhāmi – mahārāja, tava yuddhena kiccaṃ natthi, kevalaṃ amhākaṃ rañño santako hohi, tava rajjaṃ taveva bhavissati, yujjhanto pana amhākaṃ balavāhanassa mahantatāya [P 6.0392] ekantena parājissasī”ti. “Sace me vacanaṃ karissati, saṅgaṇhissāma naṃ. No ce, yujjhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā dve senā gahetvā aññaṃ nagaraṃ gaṇhissāma, tato aññanti etenupāyena sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā ‘jayapānaṃ pivissāmā’ti vatvā ekasatarājāno amhākaṃ nagaraṃ ānetvā uyyāne āpānamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā tattha nisinne visamissakaṃ suraṃ pāyetvā sabbepi te rājāno jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ekasatarājadhānīsu rajjaṃ amhākaṃ hatthagataṃ karissāma. Evaṃ tvaṃ sakalajambudīpe aggarājā bhavissasī”ti. Sopi “sādhu, ācariya, evaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati. “Mahārāja, catukkaṇṇo manto nāma, ayañhi manto [V 6.0222] na sakkā aññena jānituṃ, tasmā [M 6.0237] papañcaṃ akatvā sīghaṃ nikkhamathā”ti. Rājā tussitvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

Then the young parrot, seeing that action, thought, 'There must be some reason for this. Today I shall hear something worth telling to the wise one.' So he entered the park and hid among the leaves of the auspicious sāl tree, perching right above the king and his minister. The king said, 'Speak, teacher.' Kevaṭṭa replied, 'Great king, lend me your ear; let this counsel be between the four ears of the two of us alone. If, great king, you follow my words, I will surely make you the supreme ruler over all the one hundred kings of Jambudīpa.' Hearing his words, the king, being very greedy for sensual pleasures, became delighted and said, 'Speak, teacher, I will follow your words. Why would I not follow what is for my own benefit?' Kevaṭṭa then proposed his plan: 'Sire, we will set out with a great army and first besiege and capture the small cities. When the people are terrified, I will enter the city through a side gate and, without using weapons, persuade the kings to submit through skillful words of diplomacy. Thus, they will surely come to your feet. After making the minor kings your subjects without destroying their wealth or lives, we will likewise surround the great kings and bring all one hundred kings of Jambudīpa to our capital. We will then hold a victory celebration in the park, seat the kings there, and give them liquor mixed with poison. When they have all perished, we will cast their bodies into the Ganges and you will be consecrated as the unrivaled emperor over all Jambudīpa.' The king replied, 'Good, teacher, I will follow your plan.' Kevaṭṭa said, 'Great king, this is a secret counsel; none should know but the two of us. There is no point in further talk here. Let us depart from the park.' Then the king and his minister prepared to leave the stone seat.

Suvapotako taṃ sutvā tesaṃ mantapariyosāne sākhāyaṃ olambakaṃ otārento viya kevaṭṭassa sīse chakaṇapiṇḍaṃ pātetvā “kimeta”nti mukhaṃ vivaritvā uddhaṃ olokentassa aparampi mukhe pātetvā “kiri kirī”ti saddaṃ viravanto sākhato uppatitvā “kevaṭṭa, tvaṃ catukkaṇṇamantoti maññasi, idāneva chakkaṇṇo jāto, puna aṭṭhakaṇṇo bhavitvā anekasatakaṇṇopi bhavissatī”ti vatvā “gaṇhatha, gaṇhathā”ti vadantānaññeva vātavegena mithilaṃ gantvā paṇḍitassa nivesanaṃ pāvisi. Tassa pana idaṃ vattaṃ – sace kutoci ābhatasāsanaṃ paṇḍitasseva kathetabbaṃ hoti, athassa aṃsakūṭe otarati, sace amarādeviyāpi sotuṃ vaṭṭati, ucchaṅge otarati, sace mahājanena sotabbaṃ, bhūmiyaṃ otarati. Tadā so paṇḍitassa aṃsakūṭe otari. Tāya saññāya “rahassena bhavitabba”nti mahājano paṭikkami. Paṇḍito taṃ gahetvā uparipāsādatalaṃ abhiruyha “kiṃ te, tāta, diṭṭhaṃ suta”nti pucchi. Athassa so “ahaṃ, deva, sakalajambudīpe vicaranto aññassa rañño santike kiñci guyhaṃ na passāmi, uttarapañcālanagare pana cūḷanibrahmadattassa purohito kevaṭṭo nāma brāhmaṇo rājānaṃ uyyānaṃ netvā catukkaṇṇamantaṃ gaṇhi. Athāhaṃ sākhantare nisīditvā tesaṃ mantaṃ suṇitvā mantapariyosāne tassa sīse ca mukhe ca chakaṇapiṇḍaṃ pātetvā āgatomhī”ti vatvā sabbaṃ kathesi. ‘Raññā sampaṭicchita”nti [P 6.0393] vutte “sampaṭicchi, devā”ti āha.

The young parrot, having heard the entire conversation, waited until the conclusion of their counsel. As he was about to depart, he dangled from the branch above Kevaṭṭa’s head and dropped a lump of dung on it. Kevaṭṭa, wondering what had happened, opened his mouth and looked up, and the parrot dropped another lump directly into his mouth. The parrot then cried “Kiri! Kirī!” in his animal voice and, flying out from the branches into the sky, spoke in human language: “O Brahmin Kevaṭṭa, you thought this was a four-eared counsel—now it has become six-eared with my hearing it! When I tell my master, it will be eight-eared, and as it spreads, it will have hundreds and thousands of ears!” Even as the others shouted, “Catch this wretched parrot! Shoot him!” the bird flew with the speed of the wind toward Mithilā. King Cūḷanibrahmadatta then returned to his palace. When the parrot reached Mahosadha’s house, he perched on the wise man's shoulder to ensure no one else would hear. Mahosadha, recognizing the parrot's behavior, thought, 'He must have a secret meant for me alone.' He dismissed his attendants, took the bird to the upper terrace of the palace, and asked, 'Dear parrot, what have you seen and heard?' The parrot related everything: 'Lord, I traveled through all the one hundred kingdoms as ordered, but I found no cause for alarm elsewhere. However, in Uttarapañcāla, Kevaṭṭa, the minister of King Cūḷanibrahmadatta, took the king to a park to hold a secret four-eared counsel. I hid among the leaves of a sāl tree and heard Kevaṭṭa’s entire plan. After dropping dung on his head and in his mouth, I flew here to inform you.' He then detailed the whole plot. Mahosadha asked, 'Did the king agree to Kevaṭṭa’s plan?' The parrot answered, 'Yes, my lord, King Cūḷanibrahmadatta joyfully accepted it.'

Athassa paṇḍito kattabbayuttakaṃ sakkāraṃ karitvā taṃ mudupaccattharaṇe suvaṇṇapañjare suṭṭhu sayāpetvā “kevaṭṭo mama mahosadhassa paṇḍitabhāvaṃ na jānāti maññe, ahaṃ na dānissa mantassa matthakaṃ pāpuṇituṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā nagarato duggatakulāni nīharāpetvā bahi nivāsāpesi, raṭṭhajanapadadvāragāmesu samiddhāni issariyakulāni āharitvā antonagare nivāsāpesi, bahuṃ dhanadhaññaṃ kāresi. Cūḷanibrahmadattopi kevaṭṭassa vacanaṃ gahetvā senaṅgaparivuto gantvā ekaṃ khuddakanagaraṃ parikkhipi. Kevaṭṭopi vuttanayeneva tattha [M 6.0238] pavisitvā taṃ rājānaṃ saññāpetvā attano santakamakāsi. Dve senā ekato katvā tato aññaṃ nagaraṃ rumbhati. Etenupāyena paṭipāṭiyā sabbāni tāni nagarāni gaṇhi. Evaṃ cūḷanibrahmadatto kevaṭṭassa ovāde ṭhito, ṭhapetvā vedeharājānaṃ sesarājāno sakalajambudīpe attano santake akāsi. Bodhisattassa pana upanikkhittakapurisā “cūḷanibrahmadattena ettakāni nagarāni gahitāni[V 6.0223], appamatto hotū”ti niccaṃ sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Sopi tesaṃ “ahaṃ idha appamatto vasāmi, tumhepi anukkaṇṭhantā appamatto hutvā vasathā”ti paṭipesesi.

Mahosadha, having carefully considered the parrot's words, provided him with proper hospitality, feeding him parched rice mixed with honey and syrup, and placed him in a golden cage on a bed made of soft cloths. He thought, 'Kevaṭṭa, the minister of Cūḷanibrahmadatta, seems unaware that I, Mahosadha, am the wise counselor of King Vedeha. If he comes to attack our city with the one hundred kings, I shall use my wisdom to ensure their plan fails.' He then ordered all the poor people to move outside the city to where they preferred, while bringing prosperous and powerful families from the countryside, small towns, and villages to reside within the city. He also had all the granaries filled to capacity. Meanwhile, King Cūḷanibrahmadatta, following Kevaṭṭa’s advice, marched with a vast army and besieged a small city. Kevaṭṭa entered through a side gate and persuaded the king to submit through his skillful words of intimidation and flattery, making him a subject. In this manner, Cūḷanibrahmadatta spent seven years, seven months, and seven days capturing all one hundred kingdoms of Jambudīpa, except for the kingdom of Videha. The spy whom Mahosadha had placed in the service of the Pañcāla king sent a message: 'Lord Mahosadha, King Cūḷanibrahmadatta has now conquered all the kings of Jambudīpa. Only the kingdom of Videha remains. Please be diligent and heedful.' Mahosadha sent back a reply to his trusted spy: 'You have done well to inform me. I am staying vigilant day and night. You too, remain loyal and continue to be heedful and diligent.'

Cūḷanibrahmadatto sattadivasasattamāsādhikehi sattasaṃvaccharehi videharajjaṃ vajjetvā sesaṃ sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā kevaṭṭaṃ āha – “ācariya, mithilāyaṃ videharajjaṃ gaṇhāmā”ti. “Mahārāja, mahosadhapaṇḍitassa vasananagare rajjaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkhissāma. So hi evaṃ ñāṇasampanno evaṃ upāyakusalo”ti so vitthāretvā candamaṇḍalaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya mahosadhassa guṇe kathesi. Ayañhi sayampi upāyakusalova, tasmā “mithilanagaraṃ nāma deva appamattakaṃ, sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ amhākaṃ pahoti, kiṃ no etenā”ti upāyeneva rājānaṃ sallakkhāpesi. Sesarājānopi “mayaṃ mithilarajjaṃ gahetvāva jayapānaṃ pivissāmā”ti vadanti. Kevaṭṭo tepi nivāretvā “videharajjaṃ gahetvā kiṃ karissāma, sopi rājā amhākaṃ santakova, tasmā nivattathā”ti te upāyeneva bodhesi. Te tassa vacanaṃ sutvā nivattiṃsu. Mahāsattassa upanikkhittakapurisā sāsanaṃ pesayiṃsu “brahmadatto ekasatarājaparivuto mithilaṃ āgacchantova nivattitvā attano nagarameva [P 6.0394] gato”ti. Sopi tesaṃ “ito paṭṭhāya tassa kiriyaṃ jānantū”ti paṭipesesi. Brahmadattopi kevaṭṭena saddhiṃ “idāni kiṃ karissāmī”ti mantetvā “jayapānaṃ pivissāmā”ti vutte uyyānaṃ alaṅkaritvā cāṭisatesu cāṭisahassesu suraṃ ṭhapetha, nānāvidhāni ca macchamaṃsādīni upanethā”ti sevake āṇāpesi. Upanikkhittakapurisā taṃ pavattiṃ paṇḍitassa ārocesuṃ. Te pana “visena suraṃ yojetvā rājāno māretukāmo”ti na jāniṃsu. Mahāsatto pana suvapotakassa santikā sutattā [M 6.0239] tathato jānitvā “nesaṃ surāpānadivasaṃ tathato jānitvā mama pesethā”ti paṭisāsanaṃ pesesi. Te tathā kariṃsu.

Cūḷanibrahmadatta, after seven years, seven months, and seven days, having taken sovereignty over all of Jambudīpa except for the kingdom of Videha, said to Kevaṭṭa: "Teacher, let us seize the kingdom of Videha in Mithilā." "Great king, we will not be able to seize the kingdom in the city where the wise Mahosadha resides. For he is so accomplished in wisdom and so skilled in means," Kevaṭṭa explained at length, extolling Mahosadha’s virtues as if raising the disc of the moon. Since Kevaṭṭa himself was skilled in strategy, he persuaded the king by saying, "The city of Mithilā, sire, is a small matter. The sovereignty of the entire Jambudīpa is sufficient for us; what need have we for this?" The other kings also said, "We will drink the victory wine only after capturing the kingdom of Mithilā." Kevaṭṭa restrained them as well, advising them through strategy: "What will we gain by seizing the kingdom of Videha? That king also belongs to us; therefore, turn back." Hearing his words, they withdrew. The Great Being’s spies sent a message: "Brahmadatta, surrounded by a hundred and one kings, turned back while on the way to Mithilā and returned to his own city." He sent word back to them: "From now on, monitor his actions." Brahmadatta then consulted with Kevaṭṭa: "What shall I do now?" When it was said, "Let us drink the victory wine," he ordered his servants: "Adorn the park, set out liquor in hundreds and thousands of jars, and bring various kinds of fish, meat, and other delicacies." The spies reported these developments to the wise one. However, they did not realize, "The king intends to kill the kings by mixing poison in the wine." But the Great Being, having heard the truth from the young parrot, sent word back to them: "Ascertain the exact day of their wine-drinking and inform me." They did as instructed.

Paṇḍito “mādise dharamāne ettakānaṃ rājūnaṃ maraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, avassayo nesaṃ bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā sahajātaṃ yodhasahassaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sammā, cūḷanibrahmadatto kira uyyānaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā ekasatarājaparivuto suraṃ pātukāmo, tumhe tattha gantvā rājūnaṃ āsanesu paññattesu kismiñci anisinneyeva ‘cūḷanibrahmadattassa anantaraṃ mahārahaṃ āsanaṃ amhākaṃ raññova dethā’ti vadantā gahetvā tesaṃ purisehi ‘tumhe kassa purisā’ti vutte ‘videharājassā’ti vadeyyātha. Te tumhehi saddhiṃ ‘mayaṃ sattadivasasattamāsādhikāni sattavassāni rajjaṃ gaṇhantā ekadivasampi videharājānaṃ na passāma, kiṃ rājā nāmesa, gacchatha pariyante āsanaṃ gaṇhathā’ti vadantā kalahaṃ karissanti. Atha tumhe ‘ṭhapetvā brahmadattaṃ añño amhākaṃ rañño uttaritaro idha natthī’ti kalahaṃ vaḍḍhetvā amhākaṃ rañño āsanamattampi alabhantā ‘na dāni [V 6.0224] vo suraṃ pātuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khādituṃ dassāmā’ti nadantā vaggantā mahāghosaṃ karontā tesaṃ santāsaṃ janentā mahantehi leḍḍudaṇḍehi sabbacāṭiyo bhinditvā macchamaṃsaṃ vippakiritvā aparibhogaṃ katvā javena senāya antaraṃ pavisitvā devanagaraṃ paviṭṭhā asurā viya ulloḷaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā ‘mayaṃ mithilanagare mahosadhapaṇḍitassa purisā, sakkontā amhe gaṇhathā’ti tumhākaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā āgacchathā”ti pesesi. Te “sādhū”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā [P 6.0395] vanditvā sannaddhapañcāvudhā nikkhamitvā tattha gantvā nandanavanamiva alaṅkatauyyānaṃ pavisitvā samussitasetacchatte ekasatarājapallaṅke ādiṃ katvā alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ sirivibhavaṃ disvā mahāsattena vuttaniyāmeneva sabbaṃ katvā mahājanaṃ saṅkhobhetvā mithilābhimukhā pakkamiṃsu. Rājapurisāpi taṃ pavattiṃ tesaṃ rājūnaṃ ārocesuṃ. Cūḷanibrahmadattopi “evarūpassa nāma me visayogassa antarāyo kato”ti kujjhi. Rājānopi “amhākaṃ jayapānaṃ pātuṃ nādāsī”ti kujjhiṃsu. Balakāyāpi “mayaṃ amūlakaṃ suraṃ pātuṃ na labhimhā”ti kujjhiṃsu.

The wise one thought, "While someone like me is alive, it is not right for so many kings to die; I shall be their refuge." Having summoned the thousand warriors born on the same day as himself, he instructed them: "Friends, it is said that Cūḷanibrahmadatta has had the park decorated and, surrounded by a hundred and one kings, intends to drink wine. Go there, and when the seats are arranged for the kings but before anyone has sat down, say: 'Give the most magnificent seat next to Cūḷanibrahmadatta to our king alone!' When their men ask, 'Whose men are you?' reply, 'We are King Videha's.' They will argue with you, saying, 'While we have been seizing kingdoms for seven years, seven months, and seven days, we have not seen King Videha even once. What kind of king is he? Go and take a seat at the edge!' Then, escalating the quarrel, you should say, 'Except for Brahmadatta, there is no one here superior to our king!' If you do not obtain even a seat for our king, shouting and leaping about, make a great uproar to terrify them. Then, with large stones and clubs, smash all the jars, scatter the fish and meat to make them unusable, and quickly enter the midst of the army. Like asuras entering the city of the devas, raise a tumult and announce: 'We are the men of the wise Mahosadha from the city of Mithilā. If you can, capture us!' After making your arrival known, return here." Saying "Very well," they accepted his words, paid homage, and departed armed with the five weapons. Arriving there, they entered the park, adorned like the Nandana Grove. Seeing the splendidly prepared royal glory, including the one hundred and one royal couches under raised white umbrellas, they did everything exactly as the Great Being had instructed. Having agitated the multitude, they set out towards Mithilā. The royal attendants reported the matter to the kings. Cūḷanibrahmadatta grew angry, thinking, "An obstacle has been created for this plan of mine to use poison!" The kings also grew angry, saying, "He did not let us drink the victory wine!" The soldiers too were furious, exclaiming, "We did not get to drink the free wine!"

Cūḷanibrahmadatto [M 6.0240] te rājāno āmantetvā “etha, bho, mithilaṃ gantvā videharājassa khaggena sīsaṃ chinditvā pādehi akkamitvā nisinnā jayapānaṃ pivissāma, senaṃ gamanasajjaṃ karothā”ti vatvā puna rahogato kevaṭṭassapi etamatthaṃ kathetvā “amhākaṃ evarūpassa mantassa antarāyakaraṃ paccāmittaṃ gaṇhissāma, ekasatarājūnaṃ aṭṭhārasaakkhobhaṇisaṅkhāya senāya parivutā gacchāma, etha, ācariyā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo attano paṇḍitabhāvena cintesi “mahosadhapaṇḍitaṃ jinituṃ nāma na sakkā, amhākaṃyeva lajjitabbaṃ bhavissati, nivattāpessāmi na”nti. Atha naṃ evamāha – “mahārāja, na esa videharājassa thāmo, mahosadhapaṇḍitassa saṃvidhānametaṃ, mahānubhāvo panesa, tena rakkhitā mithilā sīharakkhitaguhā viya na sakkā kenaci gahetuṃ, kevalaṃ amhākaṃ lajjanakaṃ bhavissati, alaṃ tattha gamanenā”ti. Rājā pana khattiyamānena issariyamadena matto hutvā “kiṃ so karissatī”ti vatvā ekasatarājaparivuto aṭṭhārasaakkhobhaṇisaṅkhāya senāya saddhiṃ nikkhami. Kevaṭṭopi attano kathaṃ gaṇhāpetuṃ asakkonto “rañño paccanīkavutti nāma ayuttā”ti tena saddhiṃyeva nikkhami. Tepi yodhā ekaratteneva mithilaṃ patvā attanā katakiccaṃ paṇḍitassa kathayiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ upanikkhittakapurisāpissa sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. “Cūḷanibrahmadatto ‘videharājānaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti ekasatarājaparivuto āgacchati, paṇḍito appamatto hotu, ajja asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma āgato, ajja [P 6.0396] asukaṭṭhānaṃ, ajja nagaraṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti paṇḍitassa nibaddhaṃ pesentiyeva. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto appamatto ahosi. Videharājā pana “brahmadatto kira imaṃ nagaraṃ gahetuṃ āgacchatī”ti paramparaghosena assosi.

King Cūḷanībrahmadatta summoned those kings and said, 'Come, sirs, let us go to Mithila, cut off King Videha's head with a sword, and trampling upon him, sit down and drink the victory draught. Prepare the army for the march.' Then, in private, he also told the counselor Kevaṭṭa about this matter, saying, 'We will capture the enemy who obstructed such a plan of ours. Let us go, surrounded by one hundred and one kings and an army numbering eighteen akkhobhinīs. Come, teacher.' The brahmin, considering his own wisdom, thought, 'It is impossible to conquer the wise Mahosadha. It will only result in our own shame. I must turn him back.' Then he said to him, 'Great king, this is not the power of King Videha; it is the strategy of the wise Mahosadha. He is immensely powerful. Mithila, protected by him, is like a cave guarded by a lion—impossible for anyone to capture. It will only be a cause for our shame. Enough of going there.' But the king, intoxicated with the pride of a warrior and the arrogance of power, said, 'What can he do?' and rejecting Kevaṭṭa's words, he set out surrounded by one hundred and one kings and a vast army numbering eighteen akkhobhinīs. Kevaṭṭa, unable to make his advice accepted, thought, 'It is improper to oppose the king,' and so he too departed with him. Those thousand warriors reached Mithila in a single night and reported what they had done to the Great Being. The spies placed beforehand also sent messages: 'Cūḷanībrahmadatta is coming, surrounded by one hundred and one kings, to capture King Videha. Let the wise one be vigilant. Today he has arrived at such-and-such a place, today at such-and-such a place, today he will reach the city.' They kept sending continuous reports to the wise one. Hearing this, the Great Being remained vigilant. Meanwhile, King Videha heard through successive reports, 'Brahmadatta is coming with a vast army to seize this city.'

Atha [V 6.0225] brahmadatto aggapadoseyeva ukkāsatasahassena dhāriyamānena āgantvā sakalanagaraṃ parivāresi. Atha naṃ hatthipākārarathapākārādīhi parikkhipāpetvā tesu tesu ṭhānesu balagumbaṃ ṭhapesi. Manussā unnādentā apphoṭentā seḷentā naccantā gajjantā tajjentā mahāghosaṃ karontā aṭṭhaṃsu. Dīpobhāsena ceva alaṅkārobhāsena ca sakalasattayojanikā mithilā ekobhāsā ahosi. Hatthiassarathatūriyānaṃ [M 6.0241] saddena pathaviyā bhijjanakālo viya ahosi. Cattāro paṇḍitā ulloḷasaddaṃ sutvā ajānantā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “mahārāja, ulloḷasaddo jāto, na kho pana mayaṃ jānāma, kiṃ nāmetaṃ, vīmaṃsituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. Taṃ sutvā rājā “cūḷanibrahmadatto nu kho āgato bhaveyyā”ti sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokento tassāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhītatasito “natthi amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ, sabbe no jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessatī”ti tehi saddhiṃ sallapanto nisīdi. Mahāsatto pana tassāgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā sīho viya achambhito sakalanagare ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahitvā “rājānaṃ assāsessāmī”ti rājanivesanaṃ abhiruhitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvāva paṭiladdhassāso hutvā “ṭhapetvā mama puttaṃ mahosadhapaṇḍitaṃ añño maṃ imamhā dukkhā mocetuṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti cintetvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto āha –

Then Brahmadatta arrived at the very onset of the evening, with a hundred thousand torches held aloft, and surrounded the entire city. He then had it encircled with elephant-ramparts, chariot-ramparts, and so on, placing battalions in various positions. The soldiers stood shouting, applauding, snapping their fingers, dancing, roaring, and threatening, making a great noise. With the radiance of the torches and the brilliance of the soldiers' ornaments, the entire seven-league Mithila was illuminated at once. With the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, and the music of countless drums, it was as if this great earth were about to break apart. Hearing the tumultuous and terrifying noise, the four counselors, not knowing the cause, went to King Videha and said, 'Great king, a tumultuous noise has arisen around the city; we do not know what it is. It is fitting to investigate to find out its cause.' Hearing this, the king, thinking, 'Could it be that Cūḷanībrahmadatta has arrived?' opened the lion-window and looked out. Seeing the vast army surrounding the city, he realized Brahmadatta's arrival and was struck with great fear. 'Counselors, when morning comes, we and our citizens will surely fall into the hands of the enemy and perish,' he said, and unable to think of any way to resist, they sat in dejected silence. The Great Being, however, knowing of Brahmadatta's arrival, remained unshaken like a lion emerging from a golden cave. After arranging defenses throughout the entire city with many troops and commanders so that no enemy would dare approach, he thought, 'I will reassure the king.' He entered the palace, paid homage to King Videha, and sat in a suitable place. The king, seeing the wise Mahosadha, felt relieved and thought, 'No one else is capable of freeing me from this present distress except my son Mahosadha.' Desiring to speak with him, he spoke these eight verses beginning with "Pañcālo sabbasenāya" from the Mahosadha Paṇḍita Jātaka, adorned with a thousand verses.

590.

590.

“Pañcālo sabbasenāya, brahmadattoyamāgato;

Sāyaṃ pañcāliyā senā, appameyyo mahosadha.

My son Mahosadha, the Pañcāla king has come with all his forces and now surrounds our city. I have heard that the number of the Pañcāla king's forces is eighteen akkhobhinīs. In that army, it is filled with craftsmen, architects, masons, blacksmiths, and carpenters.

591.

591.

“Vīthimatī pattimatī, sabbasaṅgāmakovidā;

Ohārinī saddavatī, bherisaṅkhappabodhanā.

It is filled with heroes who are skilled and brave on the battlefield, who can enter the enemy's ranks unseen and strike at their very heart. It is also filled with the ten types of sounds, such as the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots.

592.

592.

“Lohavijjālaṅkārābhā, dhajinī vāmarohinī;

Sippiyehi susampannā, sūrehi suppatiṭṭhitā.

They are constantly alerted by the sounds of drums, gongs, bells, conches, lutes, flutes, and various instruments, as well as by the cries of "Strike! Kill!" The kings, counselors, and commanders are adorned with ornaments made of the seven jewels and wear magnificent mail, helmets, and crowns. The brilliance of the golden and jeweled armor of these heroic kings and counselors shines intensely. The victory banners fixed on the fronts of numerous chariots flutter and gleam. Between the elephants, horses, and chariots, heroes clad in dark mail and carrying spears, swords, bows, and shields march in formation on the left and right. Those skilled in riding elephants and horses display their prowess with weapons, playing and rejoicing in their skill.

593.

593.

“Dasettha paṇḍitā āhu, bhūripaññā rahogamā;

Mātā ekādasī rañño, pañcāliyaṃ pasāsati.

I have heard that in Cūḷanībrahmadatta's army, there are ten wise counselors whose wisdom is as vast as the earth. These ten wise men are accustomed to consulting in private and managing all affairs. With the king's mother, Queen Salākadevī, there are eleven wise ones.

594.

594.

“Athetthekasataṃ [P 6.0397]khatyā, anuyantā yasassino;

Acchinnaraṭṭhā byathitā, pañcāliyaṃ vasaṃ gatā.

Being thus endowed with the strength of wise heroes, one hundred kings, not daring to resist, follow the will of the Pañcāla king.

595.

595.

“Yaṃvadā [V 6.0226] takkarā rañño, akāmā piyabhāṇino;

Pañcālamanuyāyanti, akāmā vasino gatā.

Though they themselves have no such desire, they speak pleasant words to the Pañcāla king to please him and follow him wherever he goes.

596.

596.

“Tāya senāya mithilā, tisandhiparivāritā;

Rājadhānī videhānaṃ, samantā parikhaññati.

With such a vast army, the Pañcāla king has now surrounded our city of Mithila with four divisions of troops—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—encircling it on all sides and striving to break into Mithila.

597.

597.

“Uddhaṃ [M 6.0242] tārakajātāva, samantā parivāritā;

Mahosadha vijānāhi, kathaṃ mokkho bhavissatī”ti.

Surrounded on all sides like the stars in the sky, they are making a tumultuous noise as they strive to break through and destroy. From the Avīci hell to the highest heaven, there is no wise man equal to my son. This present matter is for my son alone to handle. How will my son, the wise one, reflect upon this, manage it, and protect the country so that we may escape from this distress?

Tattha sabbasenāyāti sabbāya ekasatarājanāyikāya aṭṭhārasaakkhobhaṇisaṅkhāya senāya saddhiṃ āgato kira, tātāti vadati. Pañcāliyāti pañcālarañño santakā. Vīthimatīti vīthiyā ānīte dabbasambhāre gahetvā vicarantena vaḍḍhakigaṇena samannāgatā. Pattimatīti padasañcarena balakāyena samannāgatā. Sabbasaṅgāmakovidāti sabbasaṅgāme kusalā. Ohārinīti parasenāya antaraṃ pavisitvā apaññāyantāva parasīsaṃ āharituṃ samatthā. Saddavatīti dasahi saddehi avivittā. Bherisaṅkhappabodhanāti “etha yātha yujjhathā”tiādīni tattha vacībhedena jānāpetuṃ na sakkā, tādisāni panettha kiccāni bherisaṅkhasaddeheva bodhentīti bherisaṅkhappabodhanā. Lohavijjālaṅkārābhāti ettha lohavijjāti lohasippāni. Sattaratanapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ kavacacammajālikāsīsakareṇikādīnaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Alaṅkārāti rājamahāmattādīnaṃ alaṅkārā. Tasmā lohavijjāhi ceva alaṅkārehi ca bhāsatīti lohavijjālaṅkārābhāti ayamettha attho. Dhajinīti suvaṇṇādipaṭimaṇḍitehi nānāvatthasamujjalehi rathādīsu samussitadhajehi samannāgatā. Vāmarohinīti hatthī ca asse ca ārohantā vāmapassena ārohanti, tena “vāmarohinī”ti vuccanti, tehi samannāgatā, aparimitahatthiassasamākiṇṇāti attho. Sippiyehīti hatthisippaassasippādīsu aṭṭhārasasu sippesu nipphattiṃ pattehi suṭṭhu samannāgatā susamākiṇṇā. Sūrehīti tāta, esā kira senā sīhasamānaparakkamehi sūrayodhehi suppatiṭṭhitā.

There, 'sabbasenāyāti' means he came, it is said, with the whole army consisting of eighteen akkhobhaṇis led by one hundred and one kings; he says, 'Dear one.' 'Pañcāliyāti' means belonging to the king of Pañcāla. 'Vīthimatīti' means provided with a group of carpenters who wander about taking building materials brought on the street. 'Pattimatīti' means provided with a body of foot soldiers. 'Sabbasaṅgāmakovidāti' means skilled in all battles. 'Ohārinīti' means capable of entering into the midst of the enemy's army and bringing back the enemy's head without being recognized. 'Saddavatīti' means not devoid of the ten sounds. 'Bherisaṅkhappabodhanāti' means it is not possible to make things known there through the distinct parts of speech such as 'Come, go, fight'; instead, such duties are made known through the sounds of drums and conches; therefore, 'bherisaṅkhappabodhanā.' 'Lohavijjālaṅkārābhāti'—here, 'lohavijjā' refers to metal crafts. This is the name for armor, leather shields, chain mail, helmets, neck-guards, and so forth, adorned with the seven gems. 'Alaṅkārāti' refers to the ornaments of royal ministers and others. Thus the meaning here is that it shines with both metal crafts and ornaments. 'Dhajinīti' means provided with banners raised on chariots and so on, made of various brightly colored cloths and adorned with gold and so forth. 'Vāmarohinīti' means those who mount elephants and horses do so from the left side; thus they are called 'left-mounters' (vāmarohinī); provided with them, meaning crowded with countless elephants and horses. 'Sippiyehīti' means well-provided with those who have reached perfection in the eighteen crafts, such as the craft of elephants and the craft of horses. 'Sūrehīti' means, dear one, this army is well-established with heroic warriors of lion-like prowess.

Āhūti dasa kirettha senāya paṇḍitāti vadanti. Bhūripaññāti pathavisamāya vipulāya paññāya samannāgatā. Rahogamāti raho gamanasīlā raho nisīditvā mantanasīlā. Te kira ekāhadvīhaṃ cintetuṃ labhantā pathaviṃ parivattetuṃ ākāse gaṇhituṃ samatthā. Ekādasīti tehi [M 6.0243] kira [V 6.0227] paṇḍitehi atirekatarapaññā pañcālarañño mātā. Sā tesaṃ ekādasī hutvā pañcāliyaṃ senaṃ pasāsati anusāsati.

'Āhūti'—they say there are ten wise men in this army. 'Bhūripaññā' means endowed with wisdom as vast as the earth. 'Rahogamā' means having the habit of going into secret and sitting in secret to deliberate. It is said that if they get a day or two to think, they are capable of turning the earth over and grasping the sky. 'Ekādasī' (the eleventh) means the mother of the Pañcāla king, whose wisdom is even more superior than those wise men. She, becoming the eleventh among them, governs and instructs the Pañcāla army.

Ekadivasaṃ kireko puriso ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷiñca puṭakabhattañca kahāpaṇasahassañca gahetvā “nadiṃ tarissāmī”ti otiṇṇo nadimajjhaṃ patvā tarituṃ asakkonto tīre ṭhite manusse evamāha – “ambho, mama hatthe ekā taṇḍulanāḷi puṭakabhattaṃ kahāpaṇasahassañca atthi, ito yaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati, taṃ dassāmi. Yo sakkoti, so maṃ uttāretū”ti. Atheko thāmasampanno puriso gāḷhaṃ nivāsetvā nadiṃ ogāhetvā taṃ hatthe gahetvā paratīraṃ uttāretvā “dehi me dātabba”nti āha. “So taṇḍulanāḷiṃ vā puṭakabhattaṃ vā gaṇhāhī”ti[P 6.0398]. “Samma, ahaṃ jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā taṃ uttāresiṃ, na me etehi attho, kahāpaṇaṃ me dehī”ti. Ahaṃ “ito mayhaṃ yaṃ ruccati, taṃ dassāmī”ti avacaṃ, idāni mayhaṃ yaṃ ruccati, taṃ dammi, icchanto gaṇhāti. So samīpe ṭhitassa ekassa kathesi. Sopi taṃ “esa attano ruccanakaṃ tava deti, gaṇhā”ti āha. So “ahaṃ na gaṇhissāmī”ti taṃ ādāya vinicchayaṃ gantvā vinicchayāmaccānaṃ ārocesi. Tepi sabbaṃ sutvā tathevāhaṃsu. So tesaṃ vinicchayena atuṭṭho rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājāpi vinicchayāmacce pakkosāpetvā tesaṃ santike ubhinnaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā vinicchinituṃ ajānanto attano jīvitaṃ pahāya nadiṃ otiṇṇaṃ parajjāpesi.

One day, it is said, a certain man took a measure of raw rice, a packet of cooked rice, and a thousand coins and, thinking 'I will cross the river,' he entered it. Reaching the middle of the river and being unable to cross, he said to the people standing on the bank: 'Sirs, I have a measure of raw rice, a packet of cooked rice, and a thousand coins; from these, I will give whatever pleases me. Let whoever is able ferry me across.' Then a strong man, girding himself tightly, waded into the river, took him by the hand, brought him to the other side, and said: 'Give me what is to be given.' The man replied: 'Take either the measure of raw rice or the packet of cooked rice.' The rescuer said: 'Friend, I disregarded my life to ferry you across. I have no use for these; give me the coins.' The man replied: 'I said, "From these, I will give what pleases me." Now I am giving what pleases me; take it if you want.' He told this to a man standing nearby. That person also said to the rescuer: 'He is giving you what he pleases; take it.' The rescuer said, 'I will not take it,' and taking the other man, went to the court and informed the judicial ministers. They too, hearing everything, said the same. Dissatisfied with their decision, he went to the king and reported the matter. The king also summoned the judicial ministers and, having heard the words of both in their presence, being unable to decide, he ruled against the rescuer who had entered the river disregarding his life.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe rañño mātā calākadevī nāma avidūre nisinnā ahosi. Sā rañño dubbinicchitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tāta, imaṃ aḍḍaṃ ñatvāva suṭṭhu vinicchita”nti āha. “Amma, ahaṃ ettakaṃ jānāmi. Sace tumhe uttaritaraṃ jānātha, tumheva vinicchinathā”ti. Sā “evaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā taṃ purisaṃ pakkosāpetvā “ehi, tāta, tava hatthagatāni tīṇipi bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapehī”ti paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapāpetvā “tāta, tvaṃ udake vuyhamāno imassa kiṃ kathesī”ti pucchitvā “idaṃ nāmayye”ti vutte “tena hi tava ruccanakaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha. So sahassatthavikaṃ gaṇhi. Atha naṃ sā thokaṃ gatakāle pakkosāpetvā “tāta, sahassaṃ te ruccatī”ti pucchitvā “āma, ruccatī”ti vutte “tāta, tayā ‘ito [M 6.0244] yaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati, taṃ dassāmī’ti imassa vuttaṃ, na vutta”nti pucchitvā “vuttaṃ devī”ti vutte “tena hi imaṃ sahassaṃ etassa dehī”ti vatvā dāpesi. So rodanto paridevanto adāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā amaccā ca tussitvā sādhukāraṃ pavattayiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya tassā paṇḍitabhāvo sabbattha pākaṭo jāto. Taṃ sandhāya videharājā “mātā ekādasī rañño”ti āha.

At that moment, the king’s mother, named Calākadevī, was seated nearby. Knowing the king’s failure to judge correctly, she said: 'Dear, this case is properly decided only after knowing the facts.' 'Mother, I know only this much. If you know better, then you decide it yourself.' She said, 'I will do so,' and having summoned that man, she said: 'Come, dear, place all three items from your hand on the ground.' Having had them placed in a row, she asked, 'Dear, while you were being swept away in the water, what did you say to this man?' When he answered, 'This [is what I said], my lady,' she said, 'In that case, pick up what pleases you.' He picked up the purse of a thousand coins. Then, after he had gone a little way, she had him called back and asked, 'Dear, does the thousand please you?' When he replied, 'Yes, it pleases me,' she asked, 'Dear, did you or did you not say to this man, "From these, I will give what pleases me"?' When he replied, 'I did say so, O Queen,' she said, 'Then give this thousand to him,' and had it given. He gave it, weeping and lamenting. At that moment, the king and the ministers were delighted and shouted 'Sādhu!' From then on, her wisdom became known everywhere. Referring to this, King Videha said, 'The mother is the eleventh of the king's counselors.'

Khatyāti [V 6.0228] khattiyā. Acchinnaraṭṭhāti cūḷanibrahmadattena acchinditvā gahitaraṭṭhā. Byathitāti maraṇabhayabhītā aññaṃ gahetabbagahaṇaṃ apassantā. Pañcāliyaṃ vasaṃ gatāti etassa pañcālarañño vasaṃ gatāti attho. Sāmivacanatthe hi etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Yaṃvadā takkarāti yaṃ mukhena vadanti, taṃ rañño kātuṃ sakkontāva. Vasino gatāti pubbe sayaṃvasino idāni panassa vasaṃ gatāti attho. Tisandhīti paṭhamaṃ hatthipākārena parikkhittā, tato rathapākārena, tato assapākārena, tato yodhapattipākārena parikkhittāti imehi catūhi saṅkhepehi tisandhīhi parivāritā. Hatthirathānañhi antaraṃ eko sandhi, rathaassānaṃ antaraṃ eko sandhi, assapattīnaṃ antaraṃ eko sandhi. Parikhaññatīti khanīyati. Imañhi idāni uppāṭetvā gaṇhitukāmā viya samantato khananti. Uddhaṃ tārakajātāvāti tāta, yāya senāya samantā parivāritā, sā anekasatasahassadaṇḍadīpikāhi uddhaṃ tārakajātā viya khāyati. Vijānāhīti tāta mahosadhapaṇḍita, avīcito yāva bhavaggā añño tayā sadiso upāyakusalo paṇḍito nāma natthi, paṇḍitabhāvo nāma evarūpesu ṭhānesu paññāyati, tasmā tvameva jānāhi, kathaṃ amhākaṃ ito dukkhā pamokkho bhavissatīti.

'Khatyā' means Khattiyas. 'Acchinnaraṭṭhā' means those whose kingdoms were seized by Cūḷanibrahmadatta. 'Byathitā' means terrified by the fear of death, seeing no other refuge to be taken. 'Pañcāliyaṃ vasaṃ gatā' means they have come under the rule of this king of Pañcāla. This usage of the accusative case is in the sense of the genitive (master's command). 'Yaṃvadā takkarā' means whatever they say with their mouths, they are capable of doing for the king. 'Vasino gatā' means previously they were independent, but now they have come under his rule. 'Tisandhī' means surrounded by four divisions—elephants, chariots, cavalry, and infantry—which in summary have three junctions. For between the elephants and chariots is one junction, between the chariots and horses is another, and between the horses and infantry yet another. 'Parikhaññati' means being dug around; for now, as if intending to uproot and seize it, they dig all around. 'Uddhaṃ tārakajātāvā' means, dear one, the army surrounding the city on all sides appears like a field of stars above, illuminated by countless hundreds of thousands of torches. 'Vijānāhī' means, O wise Mahosadha, from the lowest hell up to the highest heaven, there is no other wise man as skilled in strategy as you. True wisdom is recognized in such situations. Therefore, you alone must know how we can be freed from this suffering.

Imaṃ rañño kathaṃ sutvā mahāsatto cintesi “ayaṃ rājā ativiya maraṇabhayabhīto, gilānassa kho pana vejjo paṭisaraṇaṃ, chātassa [P 6.0399] bhojanaṃ, pipāsitassa pānīyaṃ, imassapi maṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, assāsessāmi na”nti. Atha mahāsatto manosilātale nadanto sīho viya “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, rajjasukhaṃ anubhava, ahaṃ leḍḍuṃ

Hearing the king's words, the Great Being thought: 'This king is extremely terrified of the fear of death. Just as a doctor is the refuge for a sick person, food for the hungry, and water for the thirsty, so too there is no refuge for him other than me. I will reassure him.' Then the Great Being, like a lion roaring on a slab of red orpiment, spoke words of reassurance to the king with the verse beginning with "Pāde deva pasārehi," saying: 'Do not fear, great king! Enjoy the pleasures of kingship. I...'

Gahetvā [M 6.0245] kākaṃ viya, dhanuṃ gahetvā makkaṭaṃ viya ca, imaṃ aṭṭhārasaakkhobhaṇisaṅkhaṃ senaṃ udare bandhasāṭakānampi assāmikaṃ katvā palāpessāmī”ti vatvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

...just as one scatters a flock of crows by taking up a clod of earth, or a troop of monkeys by taking up a bow, I shall scatter this army of eighteen akkhobhinis, making them so powerless that they will not even be masters of their own waistcloths.' Having said this, he spoke the ninth verse:

598.

598.

“Pāde deva pasārehi, bhuñja kāme ramassu ca;

Hitvā pañcāliyaṃ senaṃ, brahmadatto palāyitī”ti.

“O king, stretch forth your feet, enjoy pleasures and delight yourself; abandoning the Pañcāla army, Brahmadatta will flee.”

Tassattho – “deva, tvaṃ yathāsukhaṃ attano rajjasukhasaṅkhāte te pāde pasārehi, pasārento ca saṅgāme cittaṃ akatvā bhuñja, kāme ramassu ca, esa brahmadatto imaṃ senaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyissatī”ti.

The meaning is: “O king, stretch out your feet as you please, in the happiness that is your kingdom. While stretching them out, enjoy yourself without setting your mind on battle, and revel in pleasures. This Brahmadatta will abandon this army and flee.”

Evaṃ paṇḍito rājānaṃ samassāsetvā vanditvā rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā nagare chaṇabheriṃ [V 6.0229] carāpetvā nāgare āha – “ambho, tumhe mā cintayittha, sattāhaṃ mālāgandhavilepanapānabhojanādīni sampādetvā chaṇakīḷaṃ paṭṭhapetha. Tattha tattha manussā yathārūpaṃ mahāpānaṃ pivantu, gandhabbaṃ karontu, vādentu vaggantu seḷentu nadantu naccantu gāyantu apphoṭentu, paribbayo pana vo mama santakova hotu, ahaṃ mahosadhapaṇḍito nāma, passissatha me ānubhāva”nti. Te tathā kariṃsu. Tadā gītavāditādisaddaṃ bahinagare ṭhitā suṇanti, cūḷadvārena manussā nagaraṃ pavisanti. Ṭhapetvā paṭisattuṃ diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ na gaṇhanti, tasmā sañcāro na chijjati, nagaraṃ paviṭṭhamanussā chaṇakīḷanissitaṃ janaṃ passanti.

Thus, the wise man consoled the king, paid homage, and left the palace. He had the festival drum sounded throughout the city and announced to the citizens: 'Friends, do not worry! For seven days, prepare garlands, perfumes, unguents, drinks, and food, and begin a festival. Let the people everywhere drink as they please, make music, play instruments, leap about, jest, shout, roar, dance, sing, and clap their hands. Let the expenses be mine alone! I am Mahosadha the Wise—you shall witness my power!' They did so. At that time, those outside the city heard the sounds of singing and music. People entered the city through the small gates. Except for known enemies, they did not arrest anyone; therefore, the flow of traffic was not interrupted. Those who entered the city saw the crowd devoted to the festival.
