Here, ‘dhanusekhaca’ means Dhanusekha, or Dhanusekha the young man. ‘Ettha’ means right here in this city. ‘Pañcālā’ refers to being born in the northern city of Pañcāla; hence the designation. ‘Susamāvayā’ means of very similar age. ‘Cariyā taṃ anubandhitthoti’ means as a youth, he followed you on your travels in the countryside, never leaving your side like a shadow. ‘Ussukko’ means eager in your affairs, with desire arisen day and night, always engaged. “For what fault would you give him to the water-demon?”

Athassa rājā dosaṃ kathento āha –

Then the king, stating the fault, said:

“Cariyā maṃ ayaṃ ayye, pajagghittho mayā saha;

Ajjāpi tena vaṇṇena, ativelaṃ pajagghati.

“Esteemed lady, this one used to laugh with me during our wanderings; even now, he laughs excessively in that same manner.

“Ubbariyāpihaṃ ayye, mantayāmi rahogato;

Anāmanto pavisati, pubbe appaṭivedito.

“Furthermore, esteemed lady, when I am in private with Ubbarī and consulting, he enters uninvited, without having been announced beforehand.

“Laddhadvāro katokāso, ahirikaṃ anādaraṃ;

Sahāyaṃ tena dosena, dajjāhaṃ dakarakkhino”ti. (jā. 1.16.241-243);

“Having gained entry and made an opportunity, shameless and disrespectful—for that fault, I would give this companion to the water-demon.”

Tattha [M 6.0329] ajjāpi tena vaṇṇenāti yathā cariyāya pubbe maṃ anubandhanto mayā anāthena saddhiṃ ekatova bhuñjanto sayanto hatthaṃ paharitvā mahāhasitaṃ hasi, ajjāpi tatheva hasati, duggatakāle viya maṃ maññati. Anāmantoti raho nandādeviyā saddhiṃ mantentepi mayi ajānāpetvā sahasāva pavisati. Iminā dosena taṃ ahirikaṃ anādaraṃ dakarakkhasassa dassāmīti.

Here, ‘even now with that same expression’ means: just as before, during our wanderings, while following me when I was without a protector, he would eat and sleep together with me, and striking his hand, would laugh a great laugh; even now he laughs in the very same way, thinking of me as if I were still in a time of misfortune. ‘Uninvited’ means: even when I am consulting in private with Queen Nandā, he enters suddenly without informing me. For this fault, I will give that shameless and disrespectful one to the water-demon.

Atha paribbājikā “mahārāja, tava sahāyakassa tāva eso doso hotu, purohito pana tava bahūpakāro”ti tassa guṇaṃ kathentī āha –

Then the female wanderer, praising his virtues, said, “Great king, let that be a fault of your companion, but the chaplain is of great service to you.”

“Kusalo sabbanimittānaṃ, rutaññū āgatāgamo;

Uppāte supine yutto, niyyāne ca pavesane.

“Skilled in all omens, a knower of sounds, learned in the sacred texts; adept in portents and dreams, and in departures and entrances.

“Paṭṭho [P 6.0476] bhūmantalikkhasmiṃ, nakkhattapadakovido;

Brāhmaṇaṃ kena dosena, dajjāsi dakarakkhino”ti. (jā. 1.16.244-245);

“Expert in matters of earth and sky, skilled in the paths of the constellations; for what fault would you give the brahmin to the water-demon?”

Tattha [V 6.0308] sabbanimittānanti “iminā nimittena idaṃ bhavissati, iminā ida”nti evaṃ sabbanimittesu kusalo. Rutaññūti sabbaravaṃ jānāti. Uppāteti candaggāhasūriyaggāhaukkāpātadisāḍāhādike uppāte. Supine yuttoti supine ca tassa nipphattijānanavasena yutto. Niyyāne ca pavesaneti iminā nakkhattena niyyāyitabbaṃ, iminā pavisitabbanti jānāti. Paṭṭhoti cheko paṭibalo, bhūmiyañca antalikkhe ca dosaguṇe jānituṃ samattho. Nakkhattapadakovidoti aṭṭhavīsatiyā nakkhattakoṭṭhāsesu cheko. Taṃ kena dosena dakarakkhasassa dassasīti.

Here, ‘skilled in all omens’ means one who is skilled in all omens, knowing that ‘by this omen, this will happen; by that omen, that will happen.’ ‘Knower of sounds’ means he knows all cries. ‘In portents’ refers to portents such as eclipses of the moon and sun, the falling of meteors, the glowing of the quarters, and so on. ‘Adept in dreams’ means adept by way of knowing their fulfillment. ‘In departures and entrances’ means he knows that ‘by this constellation one should depart, and by this one should enter.’ ‘Expert’ means clever and capable, able to know the faults and virtues both on earth and in the sky. ‘Skilled in the paths of the constellations’ means he is an expert in the twenty-eight divisions of the constellations. ‘For what fault would you give him to the water-demon?’

Rājā tassa dosaṃ kathento āha –

Stating his fault, the king said:

“Parisāyampi me ayye, ummīletvā udikkhati;

Tasmā accabhamuṃ luddaṃ, dajjāhaṃ dakarakkhino”ti. (jā. 1.16.246);

“Even in my assembly, esteemed lady, he stares at me with eyes wide open; therefore, this fierce one with excessive eyebrows, I would give to the water-demon.”

Tassattho – ayye, esa maṃ parisamajjhe olokentopi akkhīni ummīletvā kuddho viya udikkhati, tasmā evaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitabhamuṃ amanāpena ukkhittabhamukaṃ viya luddaṃ bhayānakaṃ taṃ ahaṃ dakarakkhasassa dassāmīti.

The meaning is: ‘O lady, even when looking at me in the midst of the assembly, this man stares with open eyes as if he were angry. Therefore, I will give that fierce and terrifying one to the water-demon, for his eyebrows stand out excessively as if raised in a displeasing manner.’

Tato [M 6.0330] paribbājikā “mahārāja, tvaṃ ‘mātaraṃ ādiṃ katvā ime pañca dakarakkhasassa dammī’ti vadasi, ‘evarūpañca sirivibhavaṃ agaṇetvā attano jīvitampi mahosadhassa dammī’ti vadasi, kaṃ tassa guṇaṃ passasī”ti pucchantī imā gāthāyo āha –

Then the female wanderer, asking, “Great king, you say, ‘Starting with my mother, I will give these five to the water-demon,’ and yet you say, ‘Disregarding such glory and prosperity, I will give even my own life for the sake of Mahosadha.’ What virtue do you see in him?” spoke these verses:

“Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ, mahiṃ sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ;

Vasundharaṃ āvasati, amaccaparivārito.

“You dwell upon this earth, the land encompassed by the ocean’s boundary, adorned with the sea as its earrings, surrounded by your ministers.

“Cāturanto mahāraṭṭho, vijitāvī mahabbalo;

Pathabyā ekarājāsi, yaso te vipulaṃ gato.

“Ruler of the four quarters, with a great realm, victorious and of great strength; you are the sole king of the earth, your fame has spread far and wide.

“Soḷasitthisahassāni, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Nānājanapadā nārī, devakaññūpamā subhā.

“Sixteen thousand women, adorned with jeweled earrings; women from various lands, lovely, like celestial maidens.

“Evaṃ [V 6.0309] sabbaṅgasampannaṃ, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Sukhitānaṃ piyaṃ dīghaṃ, jīvitaṃ āhu khattiya.

“O warrior, they say that for the happy, who are fulfilled in every desire, a life so endowed with all factors is long and dear.

“Atha tvaṃ kena vaṇṇena, kena vā pana hetunā;

Paṇḍitaṃ anurakkhanto, pāṇaṃ cajasi duccaja”nti. (jā. 1.16.247-251);

“Then for what reason, or for what cause, while protecting the wise one, do you give up your life, so hard to give up?”

Tattha [P 6.0477] sasamuddapariyāyanti samuddamariyādasaṅkhātena samuddaparikkhepena samannāgataṃ. Sāgarakuṇḍalanti parikkhipitvā ṭhitassa sāgarassa kuṇḍalabhūtaṃ. Vijitāvīti vijitasaṅgāmo. Ekarājāti aññassa attano sadisassa rañño abhāvato ekova rājā. Sabbakāmasamiddhinanti sabbesampi vatthukāmakilesakāmānaṃ samiddhiyā samannāgatānaṃ. Sukhitānanti evarūpānaṃ sukhitānaṃ sattānaṃ evaṃ sabbaṅgasampannaṃ jīvitaṃ dīghameva piyaṃ, na te appaṃ jīvitamicchantīti paṇḍitā vadanti. Pāṇanti evarūpaṃ attano jīvitaṃ kasmā paṇḍitaṃ anurakkhanto cajasīti.

Here, ‘sasamuddapariyāya’ means endowed with an ocean boundary, defined by the ocean's enclosure. ‘Sāgarakuṇḍala’ refers to being like an earring to the ocean that stands surrounding it. ‘Vijitāvī’ means one who has conquered in battle. ‘Ekarājā’ signifies being the sole king because of the absence of another king equal to himself. ‘Sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ’ denotes those endowed with the fulfillment of all desires—both material desires and the desires of defilements. ‘Sukhitānaṃ’ means: for such happy beings, a life so endowed in every way is long and dear; they do not desire a short life—thus say the wise. ‘Pāṇaṃ’ means: ‘Why do you give up such a life of your own while protecting the wise one?’

Rājā tassā kathaṃ sutvā paṇḍitassa guṇaṃ kathento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing her words, the king, recounting the virtues of the wise one, spoke these verses:

“Yatopi āgato ayye, mama hatthaṃ mahosadho;

Nābhijānāmi dhīrassa, aṇumattampi dukkaṭaṃ.

“Since the day Mahosadha came into my presence, O lady, I do not recall even the slightest misdeed of this wise one.

“Sace ca kismici kāle, maraṇaṃ me pure siyā;

So me putte paputte ca, sukhāpeyya mahosadho.

“And if at any time death should come to me first, that Mahosadha would establish my sons and grandsons in happiness.

“Anāgataṃ [M 6.0331] paccuppannaṃ, sabbamatthampi passati;

Anāparādhakammantaṃ, na dajjaṃ dakarakkhino”ti. (jā. 1.16.252-254);

“He sees every benefit, both future and present; one whose actions are faultless, I would not give to the water-demon.”

Tattha kismicīti kismiñci kāle. Sukhāpeyyāti sukhasmiṃyeva patiṭṭhāpeyya. Sabbamatthanti esa anāgatañca paccuppannañca atītañca sabbaṃ atthaṃ sabbaññubuddho viya passati. Anāparādhakammantanti kāyakammādīsu aparādharahitaṃ. Na dajjanti ayye, evaṃ asamadhuraṃ [V 6.0310] paṇḍitaṃ nāhaṃ dakarakkhasassa dassāmīti evaṃ so mahāsattassa guṇe candamaṇḍalaṃ uddharanto viya ukkhipitvā kathesi.

In this context, ‘kismici’ means at any time. ‘Sukhāpeyya’ means he would establish them in happiness alone. ‘Sabbamattham’ means he sees all benefits—future, present, and past—like an omniscient Buddha. ‘Anāparādhakammantam’ means free from fault in bodily actions and so on. ‘Na dajjaṃ’ means: ‘O lady, I will not give such an incomparable wise one to the water-demon.’ Thus he spoke, extolling the Great Being’s virtues as if raising the orb of the moon.

Iti imaṃ jātakaṃ yathānusandhippattaṃ. Atha paribbājikā cintesi “ettakenapi paṇḍitassa guṇā pākaṭā na honti, sakalanagaravāsīnaṃ majjhe sāgarapiṭṭhe āsittatelaṃ vippakirantī viya tassa guṇe pākaṭe karissāmī”ti rājānaṃ gahetvā pāsādā oruyha rājaṅgaṇe āsanaṃ paññapetvā tattha nisīdāpetvā nāgare sannipātāpetvā puna rājānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya dakarakkhasassa pañhaṃ pucchitvā tena heṭṭhā kathitaniyāmeneva kathitakāle nāgare āmantetvā āha –

Thus this Jātaka reached its proper connection. Then the female wanderer thought: ‘Even with this, the wise one’s virtues are not yet widely known. I will make his virtues manifest in the midst of all the city-dwellers, like spreading oil poured upon the surface of the ocean.’ Taking the king and descending from the palace, she had a seat prepared in the royal courtyard and seated him there. Having assembled the citizens, she again questioned the king from the very beginning about the water-demon’s problem. When he replied in the same manner as stated before, she addressed the citizens and said:

“Idaṃ suṇātha pañcālā, cūḷaneyyassa bhāsitaṃ;

Paṇḍitaṃ anurakkhanto, pāṇaṃ cajati duccajaṃ.

“Listen to this, O people of Pañcāla, the words spoken by Cūḷaneyya; while protecting the wise one, he gives up his life, which is so difficult to give up.

“Mātu [P 6.0478] bhariyāya bhātucca, sakhino brāhmaṇassa ca;

Attano cāpi pañcālo, channaṃ cajati jīvitaṃ.

“The Pañcāla king gives up the lives of six: of his mother, his wife, and his brother; of his friend, of the brahmin, and even of himself.”

“Evaṃ mahatthikā paññā, nipuṇā sādhucintinī;

Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāya, samparāyasukhāya cā”ti. (jā. 1.16.255-257);

“Thus, wisdom is of great consequence, subtle, and well-pondered by the virtuous; it is for benefit in this very life and for happiness in the future life.”

Tattha mahatthikāti mahantaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā. Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāyāti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve hitatthāya ca paraloke sukhatthāya ca hotīti.

In this context, ‘mahatthikā’ means it stands having encompassed a great benefit. ‘Diṭṭhadhammahitatthāya’ means it is for the sake of benefit in this very existence and for the sake of happiness in the next world.

Iti sā ratanagharassa maṇikkhandhena kūṭaṃ gaṇhantī viya mahāsattassa guṇehi desanākūṭaṃ gaṇhīti.

Thus, as if crowning a jeweled house with a great gem, she reached the pinnacle of the discourse by means of the Great Being’s virtues.

Dakarakkhasapañho niṭṭhito.

The Question of the Water-Demon is concluded.

Satthā [V 6.0311][M 6.0332] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva tathāgato paññavā, pubbepi paññavāyevā”ti jātakaṃ samodhānento osānagāthā āha –

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher identified the birth-story and spoke these concluding verses: “Not only now, bhikkhus, is the Tathāgata wise; in the past also he was wise.”

“Bherī uppalavaṇṇāsi, pitā suddhodano ahu;

Mātā āsi mahāmāyā, amarā bimbasundarī.

“Bherī was Uppalavaṇṇā; the father was Suddhodana; the mother was Mahāmāyā; and Amarā was Bimbasundarī.

“Suvo ahosi ānando, sāriputto ca cūḷanī;

Devadatto ca kevaṭṭo, calākā thullanandinī.

Suvo was Ānanda; Cūḷanī was Sāriputta; Kevaṭṭa was Devadatta; Calākā was Thullanandinī.

“Pañcālacandī sundarī, sāḷikā mallikā ahu;

Ambaṭṭho āsi kāmindo, poṭṭhapādo ca pukkuso.

Pañcālacandī was Sundarī; Sāḷikā was Mallikā; Ambaṭṭha was Kāminda; Poṭṭhapāda was Pukkusa.

“Pilotiko ca devindo, senako āsi kassapo;

Udumbarā maṅgalikā, vedeho kāḷudāyako;

Mahosadho lokanātho, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti.

“Pilotika was the Lord of Devas; Senaka was Kassapa; Udumbarā was Maṅgalikā; Vedeha was Kāḷudāyaka; and Mahosadha was the Lord of the World—thus you should remember the birth-story.”

Umaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth, the Commentary on the Umaṅga Jātaka.

(Chaṭṭho bhāgo niṭṭhito.)

(The sixth portion is concluded.)
